3. Verify cluster is operational kubectl get nodes Should return node list. If still failing, check kubelet also restarted.
4. Set up certificate monitoring Deploy cert-exporter or a CronJob that runs kubeadm certs check-expiration and alerts when certs are within 30 days of expiry.
5. Back up the new certificates cp -r /etc/kubernetes/pki /backup/pki-$(date +%Y%m%d) After renewal, back up the PKI directory. If the node fails, you need these certificates to restore etcd.
💡 Personal Advice:
Certificate expiry is the most predictable K8s outage. kubeadm certificates expire in exactly 1 year. Mark your calendar. Set up monitoring. Renew at 11 months. This catches every new kubeadm user off guard — don't be one of them.
CKS exam tests certificate renewal. You may be asked to renew certificates, check expiration, or troubleshoot an expired-cert cluster. Know: kubeadm certs check-expiration and kubeadm certs renew.
CS14
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS14
API Server Profiling Enabled — Sensitive Data Exposure via /debug/pprof

🔍 Symptom: kube-apiserver is running with --profiling=true (the default). Anyone with API access can retrieve heap dumps, CPU profiles, and goroutine stacks from /debug/pprof. These profiles contain sensitive information including Secret names, request paths, and internal memory structures. A compromised pod with minimal RBAC can exfiltrate the entire API server's memory state.

  kubectl get --raw /debug/pprof/heap?debug=1
  # runtime.MemStats
  # Alloc = 248392184
  # Heap objects with references to Secret names,
  # request tokens, and internal API structures...

  kubectl proxy &
  go tool pprof http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/heap
  (pprof) top
  Showing nodes accounting for 512MB, 78% of 656MB total
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. --profiling=true left as default: kube-apiserver profiling is ENABLED by default. Most clusters never disable it. Anyone with /debug/pprof access can retrieve detailed memory and CPU profiles.
  2. No RBAC restriction on /debug/pprof endpoint: The profiling endpoints are accessible to ANY authenticated user — not just cluster-admin. A compromised ServiceAccount with minimal permissions can access them.
  3. kubectl proxy exposes profiling to localhost: Developer runs kubectl proxy for debugging, which exposes the API server including /debug/pprof on localhost. A local process can dump the API server's memory.
  4. Profiling data contains secrets in plaintext: Heap profiles include objects in memory — Secret data decoded from etcd, request tokens, and TLS private keys may appear in profiling dumps.
  5. --contention-profiling and --profiling both enabled:
    6. Contention profiling adds mutex profiling data, revealing internal locking patterns that can be used for timing attacks against the API server.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Profiling data cached in monitoring system:
    2. Prometheus or monitoring agent scraped /debug/pprof and stored profiles in long-term storage. Sensitive data persists in metrics backend.
  2. Third-party profiler attached to API server:
    3. A commercial APM tool or profiler agent connects to /debug/pprof and exfiltrates data to an external service.
  3. Profiling endpoint exposed via Ingress accidentally:
    4. Someone created an Ingress or Service that routes /debug/pprof externally. The API server's internals are now accessible from the internet.
  4. Debug container attached to API server static pod:
    5. kubectl debug used to attach an ephemeral container to kube-apiserver. Profiling data accessed from within the pod.
  5. Core dump of API server process:
    6. API server crashed and wrote a core dump containing its entire memory. The core file is world-readable on the control plane node.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Profiling ON by default in kubeadm clusters:
    2. kubeadm doesn't disable profiling. New clusters always have /debug/pprof accessible.
  2. No security review of API server flags:
    3. Post-installation, teams focus on application deployment, not API server hardening. Profiling remains enabled indefinitely.
  3. Developer uses kubectl proxy unaware of profiling exposure:
    4. kubectl proxy exposes ALL API server endpoints including /debug. Developer unaware of the security implications.
  4. CIS benchmark not yet run:
    5. CIS benchmark check 1.2.22 specifically checks --profiling=false. If kube-bench hasn't been run, this is missed.
  5. Monitoring agent with broad permissions:
    6. Cluster monitoring system has cluster-admin and scrapes /debug/pprof by default. Profiling data stored in metrics system accessible to ops team.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get --raw /debug/pprof/ If this returns a list of profiling endpoints, profiling is enabled and accessible.
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep profiling Check the actual flag. --profiling=false should be present. If absent, profiling defaults to ON.
kube-bench run --targets master --check 1.2.22 CIS check for profiling. Should be PASS. If FAIL, profiling is enabled.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: kube-apiserver --profiling flag defaults to TRUE and is rarely disabled. The /debug/pprof endpoints are accessible to any authenticated user, exposing heap dumps, goroutine stacks, and memory structures that may contain Secret data, request tokens, and TLS key material.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Disable profiling on the API server sed -i '/- kube-apiserver/a \ - --profiling=false' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml Add --profiling=false to the kube-apiserver static pod manifest. The API server restarts automatically.
2. Verify profiling is disabled kubectl get --raw /debug/pprof/ Should return Forbidden or 404 Not Found. If it still returns data, profiling is still on.
3. Also disable on kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler Both also have --profiling flags that default to true. Disable them in their respective static pod manifests.
4. Run kube-bench to verify kube-bench run --targets master --check 1.2.22 Should show PASS. If FAIL, check that the flag took effect after API server restart.
5. Restrict via RBAC if profiling is needed temporarily If profiling is needed for debugging, restrict access to /debug/pprof to a specific cluster-admin group via an admission webhook or API server flag.
💡 Personal Advice:
Disable profiling in production. Always. Profiling is a diagnostic tool, not a production feature. It exposes internal memory structures that can contain sensitive data. Disable it on ALL control plane components.
CIS benchmark 1.2.22 tests this specifically. Run kube-bench regularly. If --profiling is not set to false, it's a FAIL. This is a quick win for your CIS compliance score.
CS15
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS15
CoreDNS Security Misconfiguration — Open DNS Resolver & Cache Poisoning

🔍 Symptom: CoreDNS is configured as an OPEN resolver — it accepts and processes DNS queries from ANY source IP, not just cluster pods. External attackers can use the cluster's CoreDNS for DNS amplification DDoS attacks. Additionally, CoreDNS is not configured with DNSSEC validation, making it vulnerable to cache poisoning. dig @<node-ip> google.com returns results from outside the cluster.

  dig @<coredns-service-external-ip> google.com
  ;; ANSWER SECTION:
  google.com.  300  IN  A  142.250.80.46  ← Open resolver!

  kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml
  Corefile:
    .:53 {
        errors
        health
        kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
        prometheus :9153
        forward . /etc/resolv.conf  ← No ACL, no DNSSEC
        cache 30
    }
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CoreDNS exposed via LoadBalancer or NodePort: The kube-dns Service has type: LoadBalancer or a NodePort, exposing CoreDNS to the internet. External attackers can query it.
  2. No ACL restricting CoreDNS queries to cluster CIDR: CoreDNS accepts queries from ALL IPs. A prometheus plugin in the Corefile should include an ACL restricting sources to the pod/service CIDR.
  3. DNSSEC validation not enabled: CoreDNS doesn't validate DNSSEC signatures. An attacker can poison the DNS cache with forged responses, redirecting cluster traffic to malicious IPs.
  4. Forward plugin sends queries to untrusted upstream: forward . /etc/resolv.conf forwards to whatever DNS the node uses — often the cloud provider's default DNS (8.8.8.8). Queries can be intercepted or modified in transit.
  5. CoreDNS Service has no NetworkPolicy restricting access: No NetworkPolicy limits which pods or external IPs can reach CoreDNS. Any pod (including compromised ones) can query CoreDNS for ANY domain.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CoreDNS cache size too large: Large cache with long TTL increases the window for cache poisoning attacks. Reduce cache TTL and maximum cache size.
  2. CoreDNS version with known CVEs: Older CoreDNS versions have vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-1010228, CVE-2022-27191). Update CoreDNS regularly.
  3. DNS-over-TLS not configured for upstream forwarding:
    4. Forwarding to upstream via plain UDP allows MITM attacks on DNS queries leaving the cluster. Use TLS for upstream forwarding.
  4. CoreDNS health endpoint exposed:
    5. The health plugin exposes :8080/health. If reachable externally, it leaks CoreDNS version and internal configuration.
  5. DNS rebinding attack via CoreDNS:
    6. Attacker registers a domain that resolves to an internal cluster IP. Pods connecting to that domain are rebinded to internal services.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default CoreDNS Corefile without security hardening:
    2. kubeadm installs CoreDNS with a basic Corefile — no ACLs, no DNSSEC, no rate limiting. New clusters are open resolvers by default.
  2. CoreDNS Service type LoadBalancer for "external monitoring":
    3. Team exposes CoreDNS via LoadBalancer so external monitoring can check DNS health. This creates an open resolver accessible from the internet.
  3. No egress NetworkPolicy limiting DNS forwarding:
    4. CoreDNS can forward queries to ANY upstream server. A compromised CoreDNS or cache poison could redirect all cluster DNS traffic.
  4. Default cloud DNS resolver used as upstream:
    5. No internal DNS infrastructure. CoreDNS forwards to the cloud provider's DNS (AWS .2 resolver, GCP metadata server). Traffic leaves the cluster unencrypted.
  5. No monitoring on CoreDNS query patterns:
    6. No alerts for unusual query volumes, failed lookups, or queries from external IPs. DNS abuse goes undetected.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system Check the Service TYPE. If LoadBalancer or NodePort with external IP, CoreDNS is exposed externally.
kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A20 Corefile Review the Corefile configuration. Look for ACLs, DNSSEC, rate limiting, and upstream forwarding settings.
dig @<coredns-cluster-ip> google.com +short From outside the cluster, test if CoreDNS responds. If it does, you have an open resolver.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: CoreDNS default configuration has no ACLs, no DNSSEC validation, and the kube-dns Service may be exposed externally. This creates an open DNS resolver that can be exploited for DDoS amplification and is vulnerable to cache poisoning attacks.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Ensure CoreDNS Service is ClusterIP only kubectl patch svc kube-dns -n kube-system -p '{"spec":{"type":"ClusterIP"}}' CoreDNS should NEVER be exposed outside the cluster. Internal DNS resolution only.
2. Add ACL to Corefile restricting query sources Add acl plugin to Corefile, allowing only pod/service CIDRs. Block everything else.
3. Enable DNSSEC validation Add dnssec plugin to Corefile. This validates DNSSEC signatures on responses, preventing cache poisoning.
4. Configure DNS-over-TLS for upstream forwarding forward . tls://1.1.1.1 tls://1.0.0.1 Encrypt upstream DNS queries. Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) and Quad9 (9.9.9.9) support DNS-over-TLS.
5. Apply NetworkPolicy restricting CoreDNS access Only pods in the cluster should reach CoreDNS. Block all external traffic to CoreDNS port 53.
💡 Personal Advice:
An open DNS resolver is a liability. Your cluster can be used for DNS amplification attacks — your infrastructure sends the attack traffic. Cloud providers may suspend your account for hosting an open resolver.
DNS is the foundation of cluster security. If DNS is compromised, every service in your cluster can be redirected to attacker-controlled endpoints. Treat CoreDNS hardening with the same priority as API server hardening.

🛡️ Category 2: Cluster Hardening (15 Issues)CH1-CH15

🟢 Cluster Hardening — RBAC, Secrets, Admission Control, Pod Security

Cluster Hardening focuses on locking down the control plane and core security mechanisms. RBAC misconfigurations are the #1 cause of privilege escalation. Secrets stored in plaintext, overly permissive ClusterRoleBindings, and disabled admission controllers create gaping security holes. For anihpj/jobpost, every ServiceAccount must have least-privilege RBAC, every Secret must be encrypted at rest, and every admission controller must enforce security policy.

📌 CH1–CH3: RBAC & ServiceAccount Failures

CH1
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH1
Overly Permissive ClusterRoleBinding — User Has cluster-admin

🔍 Symptom: A developer in the anihpj namespace can delete nodes, list all Secrets across all namespaces, and create new ClusterRoles. kubectl auth can-i --list --as=dev-user shows [*] [*] [*] — the user has FULL cluster-admin privileges despite only needing access to the anihpj namespace. A single compromised developer account gives an attacker complete control of the cluster.

  kubectl auth can-i --list --as=dev-user
  Resources   Non-Resource URLs   Resource Names   Verbs
  *.*         []                   []               [*]
  []          [*]                  []               [*]   ← FULL cluster-admin!

  kubectl get clusterrolebinding dev-user-binding -o yaml
  roleRef:
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
    kind: ClusterRole
    name: cluster-admin   ← Should be a custom Role, not cluster-admin!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ClusterRoleBinding directly binds to cluster-admin: The most common RBAC mistake. Instead of creating a custom Role with specific permissions, someone ran kubectl create clusterrolebinding dev-user --clusterrole=cluster-admin --user=dev-user. The user now has unrestricted access.
  2. ClusterRoleBinding used instead of RoleBinding: A ClusterRoleBinding grants permissions across ALL namespaces. Even a Role with limited permissions becomes cluster-wide when bound via ClusterRoleBinding. Use RoleBinding (namespaced) for namespace-scoped access.
  3. Wildcard resources and verbs in custom ClusterRole: The ClusterRole has resources: ["*"] and verbs: ["*"] — effectively equivalent to cluster-admin. Even a "custom" role with wildcards grants full control.
  4. Multiple ClusterRoleBindings stacking permissions: The user is bound to multiple ClusterRoles — none is cluster-admin individually, but combined they grant full access (e.g., one grants secrets:*, another grants pods:*, another nodes:*).
  5. Group membership grants cluster-admin: The user belongs to a group (e.g., system:masters) that has a ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin. kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep system:masters reveals the group binding.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Certificate subject maps to system:masters: The user's client certificate has O=system:masters in the subject. The API server automatically grants cluster-admin to this group. Check: openssl x509 -in user.crt -text | grep Subject.
  2. Impersonation escalation via ServiceAccount: A ServiceAccount with impersonate verb on users resource allows anyone with access to that SA to impersonate cluster-admin. The dev-user can impersonate system:admin.
  3. RBAC aggregation rules grant unintended permissions: A ClusterRole with aggregationRule automatically picks up permissions from other ClusterRoles matching a label. An unintended label match escalates privileges.
  4. Token from kubeconfig with embedded cluster-admin cert: The dev-user's kubeconfig contains a client certificate issued with O=system:masters. The certificate IS the cluster-admin credential, regardless of what RBAC says.
  5. Webhook authorizer bypass: A misconfigured authorization webhook (e.g., OPA/Gatekeeper in non-enforcing mode) returns allow: true for all requests — effectively granting cluster-admin to everyone.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default kubeconfig uses cluster-admin certificate: kubeadm creates /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf with a certificate for O=system:masters. Developers given this file have cluster-admin.
  2. No RBAC review process in place: New cluster, no policy for reviewing ClusterRoleBindings. Admin creates bindings quickly without auditing permissions.
  3. Copy-paste YAML with cluster-admin roleRef: Tutorial or StackOverflow snippet uses cluster-admin. Applied without understanding the implications.
  4. ServiceAccount with cluster-admin created for CI/CD: CI/CD pipeline given cluster-admin "so it just works." Every commit can now modify cluster resources.
  5. No audit logging to detect RBAC abuse: Without audit log enabled, privilege abuse goes undetected. No one knows the dev-user has cluster-admin until a breach occurs.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=dev-user The definitive RBAC audit — shows every verb the user can perform on every resource. *.* [*] means cluster-admin.
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B5 -A5 "dev-user" Find all ClusterRoleBindings referencing the user or their groups.
kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A -o yaml | grep -E "name:|namespace:|kind:|subjects" Full RBAC dump — check for wildcard roleRefs and unintended cluster-wide bindings.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: A ClusterRoleBinding directly references cluster-admin instead of a custom least-privilege Role. This is the most common RBAC anti-pattern — granting full cluster control when namespace-scoped access was intended.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Delete the ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin kubectl delete clusterrolebinding dev-user-binding Immediately revoke cluster-admin. The user will lose all access — this is intentional. You'll grant proper access next.
2. Create a namespaced Role with only needed permissions kubectl create role anihpj-dev -n anihpj --verb=get,list,create,update,patch,delete --resource=pods,deployments,services,configmaps,secrets Grant only the permissions needed for the anihpj namespace. Avoid --verb=* and --resource=*.
3. Bind the Role via RoleBinding (NOT ClusterRoleBinding) kubectl create rolebinding anihpj-dev-rb -n anihpj --role=anihpj-dev --user=dev-user RoleBinding is namespace-scoped. The user can only access the anihpj namespace.
4. Verify least privilege kubectl auth can-i --list --as=dev-user -n anihpj Should show limited resources only in anihpj. Outside anihpj, kubectl auth can-i list pods -n kube-system --as=dev-user should return "no."
5. Implement RBAC audit review Regularly run kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<each-user> and review all ClusterRoleBindings. Use tools like kubectl-who-can or rbac-lookup for automated auditing.
💡 Personal Advice:
ClusterRoleBinding ≠ RoleBinding. Know the difference cold. ClusterRoleBinding grants access across ALL namespaces — even if the role is intended for one namespace. RoleBinding is ALWAYS namespace-scoped. This is one of the most tested concepts on the CKS exam.
Audit with kubectl auth can-i --list --as=USER. Before giving ANY user access, run this command to see exactly what they can do. It's your RBAC crystal ball.
system:masters group is cluster-admin by default. Any certificate with O=system:masters is cluster-admin. Never distribute the admin.conf kubeconfig. Create individual kubeconfigs with limited certs.
RBAC is additive — check all bindings. A user may have 3 ClusterRoleBindings, none individually cluster-admin, but combined they grant full access. Audit the UNION of all permissions, not each binding in isolation.
CH2
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH2
ServiceAccount Token Auto-Mounted — Unnecessary API Access in Pods

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-web pod never calls the Kubernetes API, but kubectl exec anihpj-web -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ shows ca.crt namespace token. The ServiceAccount token is auto-mounted into every pod that doesn't explicitly disable it. If an attacker compromises anihpj-web (e.g., via an RCE in the Django app), they can read the token and make authenticated API calls with the pod's ServiceAccount permissions. Every pod is a potential API attack vector.

  kubectl exec anihpj-web -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
  ca.crt
  namespace
  token   ← SA token mounted, but anihpj-web NEVER calls the API!

  kubectl exec anihpj-web -- curl -s --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj/secrets
  { "items": [ ... all Secrets in anihpj namespace ... ] }   ← Token has excessive RBAC!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. automountServiceAccountToken: true (the default): Every pod mounts a ServiceAccount token unless explicitly disabled. automountServiceAccountToken: false is not set in the Pod spec. This is the #1 unnecessary token exposure.
  2. ServiceAccount has RBAC permissions it doesn't need: The default ServiceAccount often has more permissions than needed. A compromised pod reading its token inherits those permissions. Check: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default.
  3. Application never calls the API but token is still mounted: Most web apps, workers, and databases NEVER call the Kubernetes API. They don't need a token. The auto-mount is pure attack surface.
  4. Token is a long-lived JWT with no expiry: By default, ServiceAccount tokens are long-lived JWTs that never expire. If an attacker steals the token, it remains valid indefinitely — even after the pod is deleted.
  5. Pod spec inherited automount from ServiceAccount: Both the Pod spec AND the ServiceAccount have automountServiceAccountToken settings. If the SA has it set to true, it overrides the pod-level setting. Check: kubectl get sa anihpj-web-sa -o yaml | grep automount.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Token projected volume with excessive audience: The pod uses a projected volume for the token, but the audience includes the API server. The token can be used anywhere.
  2. Legacy token (non-time-limited) still in use: The cluster was upgraded from an older version where tokens were not time-limited. Old tokens remain valid until the SA is recreated.
  3. ServiceAccount token leaked to logs: Application code accidentally logs the token value (e.g., echo $TOKEN in entrypoint). The token is now in persistent log storage accessible to ops teams.
  4. Token accessible via /proc filesystem: Even with automountServiceAccountToken: false, a container with securityContext.privileged: true can read the node's token from /proc on the host.
  5. Sidecar proxy auto-injects token mount: A service mesh sidecar (Istio/Linkerd) automatically mounts a ServiceAccount token for mTLS. This token may have broader permissions than the application needs.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default ServiceAccount in every namespace has API access: kubeadm creates a default SA in every namespace with auto-mount enabled. All pods without an explicit SA use it.
  2. No organization policy on automountServiceAccountToken: No admission controller or policy enforcing automountServiceAccountToken: false for pods that don't need it.
  3. Developers unaware of SA token security implications: Token auto-mount is invisible. Developers don't know it exists or that it's an attack vector.
  4. RBAC granted to default ServiceAccount during initial setup: Admin granted cluster-wide read to default SA "for debugging." Every pod can now list all resources.
  5. ServiceAccount token never verified in application security review: No step in the deployment checklist checks for unnecessary SA token mounting.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -B2 automountServiceAccountToken Check if any pods explicitly set automountServiceAccountToken: false. If absent, token is mounted.
kubectl exec <pod> -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ The definitive check — if token file exists, the SA token is mounted.
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default See exactly what API access the pod's ServiceAccount has. Should be "no" for everything.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: automountServiceAccountToken defaults to TRUE. Pods that never call the Kubernetes API still mount a ServiceAccount token, creating unnecessary API attack surface for every compromised container.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Disable auto-mount in Pod spec automountServiceAccountToken: false Add to spec.template.spec in Deployment. The pod will no longer have a mounted token.
2. Disable auto-mount on the ServiceAccount itself kubectl patch sa anihpj-web-sa -n anihpj -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}' Any pod using this SA will NOT mount a token by default (can be overridden per-pod).
3. Remove RBAC from unnecessary ServiceAccounts kubectl delete rolebinding --all -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default If the token is mounted, at least ensure it has ZERO permissions. The default SA should have no RBAC bindings.
4. Enforce via OPA/Gatekeeper policy Create a policy requiring automountServiceAccountToken: false unless a specific annotation allows it. Catch violations at admission time.
5. Use projected tokens with short TTL when API access IS needed For pods that genuinely need API access, use projected ServiceAccount tokens with expirationSeconds: 3600 (1-hour TTL) instead of the default long-lived token.
💡 Personal Advice:
Default = Vulnerable. Always opt out. automountServiceAccountToken: false should be on EVERY pod that doesn't call the API. That's 90%+ of your workloads. Make it the default in your Deployment templates.
Token mounting is invisible attack surface. An attacker who RCEs into your web app immediately has a Kubernetes API token. If the SA has any RBAC, the attacker has that access. Disable auto-mount and you eliminate this entire attack path.
Projected tokens with short TTL are the secure alternative. If a pod genuinely needs API access, use a projected ServiceAccount token with a 1-hour expiry. The token auto-rotates and is audience-bound.
CH3
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH3
Default ServiceAccount Used — All Pods Share the Same Identity

🔍 Symptom: All pods in the anihpj namespace use the SAME default ServiceAccount. kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep serviceAccount shows serviceAccount: default for every pod — anihpj-web, anihpj-api, anihpj-db, and anihpj-redis all share one identity. If any ONE pod is compromised, the attacker gains the RBAC permissions of the default SA. Furthermore, you can't grant different API permissions to different pods — it's all-or-nothing for the entire namespace.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name:.metadata.name, sa:.spec.serviceAccountName}'
  { "name": "anihpj-web-7d8f9",    "sa": "default" }
  { "name": "anihpj-api-5c3b2",    "sa": "default" }
  { "name": "anihpj-db-0",         "sa": "default" }
  { "name": "anihpj-redis-9f1a4",  "sa": "default" }   ← ALL share "default"!

  kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default
  Resources: secrets, configmaps   Verbs: get, list   ← Shared RBAC for ALL pods!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No serviceAccountName specified in Pod spec: When serviceAccountName is omitted from the Pod spec, Kubernetes uses the default ServiceAccount. Every pod without an explicit SA gets the same identity.
  2. Dedicated ServiceAccounts never created: No one created separate SAs for web, api, db, and redis. The default SA is used as a convenience — there's no RBAC differentiation between components.
  3. RBAC bindings applied to default SA: Someone granted get,list on Secrets and ConfigMaps to the default SA for the web pod. Now the db and redis pods also inherit these permissions — a privilege leak across components.
  4. Copy-paste Deployment YAML without customizing SA: Tutorials and sample YAML rarely specify serviceAccountName. Teams deploy from templates without adding SA configuration.
  5. Lack of understanding of SA per-component security model: Developers treat ServiceAccounts as "just a pod setting" rather than a security identity. The concept of least-privilege per component isn't applied to SAs.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Namespace created without SA planning: Namespace created first, pods deployed second, SAs were never in the plan. The default SA is an afterthought.
  2. Existing dedicated SA deleted during cleanup: Someone deleted the anihpj-web-sa during a cleanup, and pods fell back to default. Kubernetes doesn't warn about missing SAs — it silently uses default.
  3. Helm chart doesn't template serviceAccountName: The Helm chart for anihpj doesn't support custom SAs per component. All pods default to default.
  4. PodSecurityPolicy/PSA migration incomplete: During migration from PSP to Pod Security Admission, SAs were not re-established. All pods fell back to default SA.
  5. RBAC broken after SA rename: Someone renamed the SA but didn't update RoleBindings. To "fix" it quickly, they reverted to using the default SA with existing bindings.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. default ServiceAccount automatically created in every namespace: kubeadm creates it. New teams deploy pods without knowing they should create dedicated SAs.
  2. No SA naming convention or policy established: No standards for SA naming, RBAC per component, or rule that every Deployment must specify serviceAccountName.
  3. CI/CD pipeline doesn't create ServiceAccounts: Pipeline deploys Deployments but doesn't include SA creation. SAs are manual afterthoughts.
  4. Security review missed SA-per-component requirement: Initial security assessment focused on NetworkPolicy and TLS — ServiceAccount isolation wasn't on the checklist.
  5. No admission control enforcing dedicated SAs: No OPA/Gatekeeper policy requiring pods to use non-default ServiceAccounts. Pods silently use default.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name:.metadata.name, sa:.spec.serviceAccountName}' Check which SA each pod uses. If all show default, no dedicated SAs exist.
kubectl get sa -n anihpj List all ServiceAccounts in the namespace. At minimum, you should see one per component (web, api, db, redis).
kubectl describe rolebinding -n anihpj Check which SAs have RBAC bindings. If all bindings reference default, all pods share the same permissions.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No dedicated ServiceAccounts were created for individual components. All pods use the default ServiceAccount, which means any RBAC granted to default is shared by ALL pods — a compromised database pod can read Secrets meant only for the web pod.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create dedicated ServiceAccounts per component kubectl create sa anihpj-web -n anihpj kubectl create sa anihpj-api -n anihpj kubectl create sa anihpj-db -n anihpj kubectl create sa anihpj-redis -n anihpj Each component gets its own identity. RBAC can now be scoped per component.
2. Update Deployments to use dedicated SAs kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"anihpj-web"}}}}' Each Deployment references its dedicated SA. Restart pods to pick up the new SA.
3. Create per-component RBAC (least privilege) anihpj-web: get Secrets (for TLS). anihpj-api: get ConfigMaps. anihpj-db: NO RBAC. anihpj-redis: NO RBAC. Bind each Role to only the SA that needs it.
4. Remove all RBAC from default ServiceAccount kubectl delete rolebinding --all -n anihpj The default SA should have ZERO permissions. Any pod accidentally using it will have no API access.
5. Enforce non-default SA via admission policy OPA/Gatekeeper policy: reject pods with serviceAccountName: default. Require explicit dedicated SAs for all workloads.
💡 Personal Advice:
One SA per component. Always. Treat ServiceAccounts like application identities — each component gets its own. The default SA should NEVER have RBAC bindings. It's a honeypot that silently grants permissions to pods that forget to specify a dedicated SA.
Audit with jq one-liners. kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | {ns:.metadata.namespace, name:.metadata.name, sa:.spec.serviceAccountName}' | grep '"default"' Find every pod using the default SA. This is your hit list for security hardening.
Distinct SAs enable forensic isolation. When SA-per-component is in place, audit logs show exactly WHICH component made an API call. With shared default SA, you can't tell if it was the web pod or the db pod that listed Secrets.

📌 CH4–CH6: RBAC Wildcards, Secrets Exposure & Anonymous Access

CH4
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH4
RBAC Role With Wildcard Verbs/Resources — Privilege Escalation via "*"

🔍 Symptom: A Role in the anihpj namespace has resources: ["*"] and verbs: ["*"]. The developer only needed get,list on Pods and Deployments, but the Role grants every verb on every resource. kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web shows the SA can create Roles, delete Secrets, and exec into pods — full namespace admin. This is the RBAC equivalent of chmod 777.

  kubectl get role anihpj-web-role -n anihpj -o yaml
  rules:
  - apiGroups: ["*"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["*"]          ← WILDCARD EVERYTHING

  kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web -n anihpj
  Resources: pods, secrets, deployments, roles, rolebindings, ...
  Verbs: get, list, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection, watch
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Role created with kubectl create role --verb=* --resource=*: The quick-and-dirty approach: kubectl create role anihpj-web-role --verb=* --resource=* -n anihpj. It "works" but grants everything. Replace with specific verbs and resources.
  2. apiGroups: ["*"] grants access to ALL API groups: Including rbac.authorization.k8s.io — the SA can now create new Roles and RoleBindings. This is a PRIVILEGE ESCALATION vector: the SA can grant itself more permissions.
  3. verbs: ["*"] includes escalate and bind: The escalate verb (on Roles) and bind verb (on RoleBindings) are included in *. The SA can create a new Role with cluster-admin and bind itself to it — full namespace takeover.
  4. No one reviewed the Role YAML before applying: The YAML was applied directly without a security review. The wildcards weren't caught because there's no RBAC audit process.
  5. Tutorial or template used wildcards for simplicity: Online examples often use resources: ["*"] and verbs: ["*"] to keep examples short. Teams copy-paste without restricting to actual needs.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Aggregated ClusterRole picking up wildcard labels: A ClusterRole with aggregationRule.clusterRoleSelectors matching a broad label picks up wildcard permissions from other ClusterRoles.
  2. Role with subresource wildcards: resources: ["pods/*"] grants access to all pod subresources including pods/exec, pods/log, pods/portforward — equivalent to shell access into every pod.
  3. nonResourceURLs: ["*"] grants access to /healthz, /version, /metrics: The SA can access API server health and metrics endpoints — information disclosure about control plane internals.
  4. Wildcard in resourceNames field: resourceNames: ["*"] is NOT a wildcard in resourceNames (it's a literal string), but teams mistakenly think it restricts by name — it actually only grants access to a resource literally named "*".
  5. Role template from Helm chart with wildcards: The chart's default values.yaml has wildcards. Teams deploy the chart without overriding RBAC rules.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No RBAC policy or standard defined: New cluster, no guidelines on least-privilege RBAC. Everyone uses wildcards because it's the path of least resistance.
  2. RBAC created by developers, not security team: Developers create Roles with wildcards because they don't know the exact resources needed. They just want the app to work.
  3. No admission controller validating RBAC rules: No OPA/Gatekeeper policy rejecting Roles with wildcard verbs or resources. Wildcards are accepted without question.
  4. RBAC not tested before deployment: No CI step runs kubectl auth can-i --list against the proposed Role. The first time anyone sees the permissions is in production.
  5. No RBAC audit tool in CI pipeline: Tools like kubescape, kube-bench, or rbac-police not integrated into the CI/CD pipeline.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get roles,clusterroles -A -o yaml | grep -E "^\s+(resources|verbs|apiGroups):" | grep "\*" Find every Role and ClusterRole with wildcard entries. Each match is a potential privilege escalation vector.
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web -n anihpj | grep -E "roles|rolebindings|secrets" Check specifically for RBAC modification and Secret access — these indicate privilege escalation capability.
kubectl describe role anihpj-web-role -n anihpj Review the exact rules. If apiGroups: ["*"] includes rbac.authorization.k8s.io, the SA can escalate.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Role created with wildcard verbs: ["*"] and resources: ["*"] for convenience rather than defining specific least-privilege permissions. This grants the ServiceAccount full namespace admin including the ability to create new Roles and escalate its own privileges.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Delete the wildcard Role and create a least-privilege replacement kubectl delete role anihpj-web-role -n anihpj kubectl create role anihpj-web-role -n anihpj --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods,deployments,services,configmaps Only grant the specific verbs and resources actually needed. Never use *.
2. Restrict apiGroups to only what's needed apiGroups: [""] for core resources, apiGroups: ["apps"] for Deployments, etc. Never use apiGroups: ["*"] — it includes RBAC API groups enabling escalation.
3. Verify no privilege escalation possible kubectl auth can-i create roles --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web -n anihpj Should return "no." If "yes," the SA can escalate its own privileges — fix immediately.
4. Add OPA/Gatekeeper policy rejecting wildcard RBAC Policy: reject any Role/ClusterRole with verbs: ["*"] or resources: ["*"] or apiGroups: ["*"]. Block at admission time.
5. Integrate RBAC audit into CI Run kubectl auth can-i --list for each SA in CI before deployment. Fail the build if any SA has wildcard permissions or RBAC modification capability.
💡 Personal Advice:
Wildcards in RBAC are time bombs. verbs: ["*"] includes escalate and bind — the two most dangerous verbs in Kubernetes. A wildcard Role gives the SA the ability to make itself cluster-admin. Never use wildcards in production RBAC.
The CKS exam WILL test this. Expect a scenario where you audit RBAC permissions and identify which Role/ClusterRole grants privilege escalation capability. Look specifically for apiGroups: ["*"] — it includes rbac.authorization.k8s.io.
rbac.authorization.k8s.io access = game over. If a SA can create Roles and RoleBindings in its namespace, it can grant itself ANY permission on ANY resource in that namespace. This is not a bug — it's how RBAC works. Don't give it out.
CH5
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH5
Secret Exposed as Environment Variable — Plaintext in /proc and Logs

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-db PostgreSQL pod has database credentials injected via env: from a Secret. kubectl exec anihpj-db -- env | grep POSTGRES_PASSWORD returns the password in PLAINTEXT. Any compromised process in the container can read /proc/<pid>/environ and extract the password. Additionally, if the application crashes and dumps environment variables in error logs, the password is preserved in persistent log storage. The Secret is also visible in kubectl describe pod (though masked in kubectl get pod -o yaml).

  kubectl exec anihpj-db -- env | grep POSTGRES
  POSTGRES_USER=anihpj_admin
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD=SuperSecretP@ss123!   ← PLAINTEXT in env!

  kubectl exec anihpj-db -- cat /proc/1/environ | tr '\0' '\n' | grep PASSWORD
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD=SuperSecretP@ss123!   ← Readable from /proc!

  kubectl get pod anihpj-db -o yaml | grep -A3 env
  env:
  - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:         ← Referenced, but still in container env
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Secret injected via env: instead of volume mount: env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef puts the Secret value in the container's ENVIRONMENT — it's visible to env, /proc/<pid>/environ, and any process that can enumerate environment variables. Use volumes[].secret.secretName to mount as a FILE instead.
  2. Application logs environment variables on startup: The Django app has DEBUG=True or prints environment at startup. Error pages and debug logs expose the database password to anyone with log access.
  3. Password visible in kubectl describe pod output: While kubectl get pod -o yaml masks Secret values, kubectl describe pod may reveal values in certain edge cases. Anyone with get pods RBAC can potentially see the password.
  4. Container crash dump includes environment: If the container crashes and core dumps are enabled, the environment variables (including passwords) are written to disk. The core file may be world-readable.
  5. No filesystem-level encryption for mounted Secrets: Even when mounted as a file, Secrets are stored in tmpfs (RAM). However, if swap is enabled, Secret data can be swapped to disk unencrypted.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Secret exposed via Kubernetes API to unauthorized SA: A compromised pod with get secrets RBAC can read the Secret directly from the API. The env injection is just the easiest path — RBAC access is the deeper problem.
  2. Secret stored in etcd without encryption at rest: The Secret exists in etcd as base64 (NOT encrypted). Anyone with etcd access can decode all Secrets. Enable EncryptionConfiguration for etcd.
  3. Secret leaked via image layers: The Dockerfile has ENV POSTGRES_PASSWORD=... baked into an image layer. Anyone with image pull access can docker history and extract the password.
  4. CI/CD pipeline exposes Secret in build logs: The pipeline echoes the Secret value during deployment. Build logs are often retained for months and accessible to all developers.
  5. Heap dump / memory dump contains Secret: A JVM heap dump or Node.js memory snapshot captures all environment variables. If the dump is written to a PersistentVolume, the Secret is persisted.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No Secret encryption at rest configured: Fresh kubeadm cluster stores Secrets as base64 in etcd — NOT encrypted. Anyone with etcdctl access can read ALL Secrets in the cluster.
  2. No policy on Secret injection method: No standard dictating that Secrets MUST be mounted as files, not injected as environment variables.
  3. etcd not using TLS: Without TLS, Secret data is transmitted in plaintext between API server and etcd. A network capture reveals every Secret.
  4. No external Secret management (Vault/SealedSecrets): Kubernetes Secrets are the only secret store. No integration with HashiCorp Vault, Sealed Secrets, or cloud KMS for encryption at rest and audit.
  5. Secrets committed to Git before migration to K8s: The team migrated from docker-compose where .env files were committed. The Secrets might still be in git history.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -B2 "secretKeyRef" Find every pod injecting Secrets via environment variables. Each one is a plaintext exposure vector.
kubectl exec <pod> -- env Check which environment variables are visible inside the container. Any Secret values will appear here in plaintext.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/environ | tr '\0' '\n' The /proc filesystem exposes environment variables to any process in the container. Verify Secret values are accessible.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Secret values injected as environment variables (env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef) are visible to any process inside the container via /proc/<pid>/environ. Environment variables are NOT a secure way to pass Secrets — they should be mounted as files via volumes[].secret.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Mount Secrets as files, not environment variables Replace env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef with a volume mount: volumes: [{name: db-secret, secret: {secretName: anihpj-db-secret}}] and volumeMounts: [{name: db-secret, mountPath: /etc/secrets/db, readOnly: true}].
2. Update app to read from file POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/etc/secrets/db/password PostgreSQL supports *_FILE variants. Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE instead of POSTGRES_PASSWORD.
3. Enable etcd encryption at rest Create EncryptionConfiguration with aescbc provider. Mount it to kube-apiserver via --encryption-provider-config. All new Secrets will be encrypted in etcd.
4. Restrict Secret RBAC to minimum kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web -n anihpj Only the pods that genuinely need Secret values should have get access. db needs its own Secret; web doesn't need db's password.
5. Use external Secret management Integrate with HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or use Sealed Secrets. External secret stores provide encryption, audit, rotation, and access control beyond Kubernetes RBAC.
💡 Personal Advice:
Environment variables are NOT for Secrets. Period. env vars leak everywhere: /proc, crash dumps, debug logs, child processes, docker inspect. Mount Secrets as files with readOnly: true and restricted permissions (defaultMode: 0400).
etcd encryption is NOT enabled by default. In a default kubeadm cluster, Secrets in etcd are base64-encoded — NOT encrypted. Anyone with etcd access can read every Secret. This is a CIS benchmark requirement (1.1.34).
Use the *_FILE convention. Most databases and frameworks support reading credentials from files: POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE, MYSQL_PASSWORD_FILE, AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE. Use them.
CH6
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH6
Anonymous Authentication Enabled on kube-apiserver — Unauthenticated Access

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get pods --token="" --certificate-authority=/dev/null --insecure-skip-tls-verify returns pod listings WITHOUT any authentication. The kube-apiserver is running with --anonymous-auth=true (the default), meaning ANY request without credentials is processed as system:anonymous. If any ClusterRoleBinding grants permissions to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated, anyone on the network can access those resources without authentication.

  curl -k https://api-server:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods
  { "kind": "PodList", "items": [...] }   ← NO AUTH REQUIRED!

  kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B5 "system:anonymous"
  - apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
    kind: ClusterRole
    name: view
  subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: system:anonymous   ← Anonymous users get "view" access!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. --anonymous-auth=true is the DEFAULT: kube-apiserver starts with anonymous authentication ENABLED by default. All unauthenticated requests are assigned the system:anonymous user and system:unauthenticated group. This is the #1 control plane hardening oversight.
  2. RBAC permissions granted to system:anonymous group: Someone created a ClusterRoleBinding granting view ClusterRole to system:anonymous — perhaps for "internal monitoring" or "ease of access." Now anyone can list all resources.
  3. RBAC permissions granted to system:unauthenticated group: Similar to above but using the system:unauthenticated group. Both groups represent users without valid credentials.
  4. --authorization-mode includes AlwaysAllow: The API server has --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow (extremely dangerous). Every request, authenticated OR anonymous, is allowed. This overrides all RBAC.
  5. Insecure port (8080) still open: kube-apiserver's insecure port bypasses ALL authentication and authorization. If port 8080 is still accessible, anonymous users have full cluster-admin access with no credentials.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Anonymous access to /healthz, /version, /metrics endpoints: Even without RBAC, anonymous users can access non-resource URLs like /healthz, /version, and /metrics — information disclosure about API server version and configuration.
  2. Anonymous access to Discovery API: /api and /apis endpoints list all available API groups and resources. Attackers use this for reconnaissance — mapping the cluster's attack surface without authentication.
  3. Webhook authorizer returning allow for unknown users: A misconfigured webhook authorizer returns allow: true instead of deny for unauthenticated requests. The webhook effectively bypasses authentication.
  4. PKI certificate with empty subject treated as anonymous: A misconfigured client certificate with no CN or O is treated as system:anonymous by the API server — but it passes TLS verification, so it's a "valid" anonymous request.
  5. Proxy/subpath-based anonymous bypass: A misconfigured apiserver proxy or aggregated API server forwards anonymous requests without re-authentication. The downstream API server sees the request as authenticated.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Anonymous auth enabled by default in kubeadm: All kubeadm clusters start with --anonymous-auth=true. The CIS benchmark recommends disabling it (1.2.19).
  2. No RBAC audit for system:anonymous bindings: New cluster, no one has checked if system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated have any ClusterRoleBindings.
  3. kube-bench not run post-installation: CIS benchmark check 1.2.19 would flag anonymous auth. kube-bench hasn't been run yet.
  4. API server flags not reviewed after upgrade: During an upgrade, --anonymous-auth may have been reset to default (true). Post-upgrade flag review was missed.
  5. NetworkPolicy not restricting API server access: Even with anonymous auth enabled, if a NetworkPolicy restricts which IPs can reach the API server, the risk is contained. But no such policy exists.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B10 "system:anonymous\|system:unauthenticated" Find any ClusterRoleBindings granting permissions to unauthenticated users. If any exist, anonymous users have those permissions.
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep anonymous-auth Check the actual flag. --anonymous-auth=false should be present. If absent or true, anonymous auth is enabled.
curl -k https://api-server:6443/api --header "Authorization:" If this returns API group listings, anonymous access is working. It should return 403 Forbidden.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: --anonymous-auth defaults to TRUE on kube-apiserver. Combined with a ClusterRoleBinding granting any permissions to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated, this allows anyone on the network to access Kubernetes resources without any credentials.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Disable anonymous authentication on API server Add --anonymous-auth=false to kube-apiserver manifest. All unauthenticated requests will be rejected with 401. Note: this may break liveness probes that don't authenticate.
2. Remove ALL ClusterRoleBindings to system:anonymous and system:unauthenticated kubectl delete clusterrolebinding <binding-name> These users/groups should have ZERO permissions. Even with anonymous-auth=false, removing bindings is defense-in-depth.
3. Ensure authorization mode is Node,RBAC (NOT AlwaysAllow) ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep authorization-mode Should show --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC. If AlwaysAllow is present, REMOVE it immediately — it bypasses all authorization.
4. Verify insecure port is closed ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep insecure-port Should NOT show port 8080. --insecure-port=0 disables it. The insecure port bypasses ALL authentication and authorization.
5. Run kube-bench CIS check 1.2.19 kube-bench run --targets master --check 1.2.19 Verifies anonymous-auth is disabled. Should show PASS.
💡 Personal Advice:
Anonymous auth enabled + system:anonymous RBAC = no authentication needed. This combination means anyone who can reach your API server can read (or modify) Kubernetes resources. It's one of the first things to check on a security audit.
Check the CIS benchmarks — they cover this. CIS 1.2.19 tests anonymous-auth. CIS 1.2.18 tests AlwaysAllow. CIS 1.2.16 tests insecure-port. Run kube-bench on your API server nodes regularly.
Defense in depth: even with anonymous-auth=false, remove anonymous RBAC. If a misconfiguration re-enables anonymous auth, the lack of RBAC bindings ensures anonymous users still can't do anything. RBAC for system:anonymous should ALWAYS be empty.

📌 CH7–CH9: etcd Encryption, Admission Control & Pod Security

CH7
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH7
etcd Unencrypted at Rest — All Secrets Visible in Plaintext

🔍 Symptom: etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj/anihpj-db-secret --cacert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key returns the Secret value in base64 — trivially decodable to plaintext. All Secrets, ConfigMaps, and resource metadata stored in etcd are UNENCRYPTED. Anyone with direct etcd access (or a compromised control plane node) can read every Secret in the cluster: database passwords, TLS private keys, API tokens — everything.

  ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj/anihpj-db-secret --cacert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
  ... k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:kms: ...   ← EXPECTED: encrypted prefix. NOT FOUND!
  ... anihpj-db-secret ...   ← ACTUAL: plain base64-encoded Secret data

  kubectl get secret anihpj-db-secret -n anihpj -o json | jq '.data.password | @base64d'
  "SuperSecretP@ss123!"   ← Same as in etcd — just decode base64
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. EncryptionConfiguration never created: etcd encryption at rest is NOT enabled by default. It requires creating an EncryptionConfiguration YAML and passing it to kube-apiserver via --encryption-provider-config. Most clusters skip this step.
  2. EncryptionConfiguration created but not applied to API server: The config file exists but --encryption-provider-config flag is MISSING from the kube-apiserver manifest. The API server doesn't know to encrypt.
  3. identity provider listed FIRST in EncryptionConfiguration: The identity: {} provider (which does NO encryption) is first in the providers list. Since the first provider is used for writes, all new Secrets are written UNENCRYPTED. Move aescbc or kms to first position.
  4. Encryption key stored on same node as etcd: The encryption key file is on the control plane node at /etc/kubernetes/pki/encryption-config.yaml. A node compromise gives the attacker both the encrypted data AND the key.
  5. Existing Secrets not re-encrypted after enabling encryption: Enabling encryption only encrypts NEW Secrets. All EXISTING Secrets remain unencrypted until rewritten. Run kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f - to re-encrypt all existing Secrets.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. EncryptionConfiguration syntax error — API server silently ignores it: A YAML indentation error causes the config to be unparseable. API server starts without encryption, no error is logged. Check: kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep etcd.
  2. KMS plugin unreachable — encryption fails open: If using kms provider and the KMS plugin (e.g., AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) is unreachable, the API server may fall back to no encryption or fail to start.
  3. Encryption key rotated but new key not propagated: Key rotation requires updating the EncryptionConfiguration and restarting the API server. If only one of multiple API servers is updated, different servers encrypt differently — causing read failures.
  4. AES-CBC without HMAC — malleability risk: aescbc without a separate authentication mechanism could allow ciphertext manipulation. Use secretbox (XSalsa20+Poly1305) or KMS for authenticated encryption.
  5. Backup of etcd stored without encryption: etcd snapshots taken for backup purposes contain the UNENCRYPTED data. Even if runtime etcd is encrypted, the backup file on disk exposes all Secrets.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Encryption not configured during kubeadm init: kubeadm does NOT set up encryption. The cluster starts with all Secrets stored as base64 in etcd.
  2. CIS benchmark 1.1.34 not checked: CIS requires etcd encryption at rest. New clusters haven't been audited against this benchmark.
  3. etcd peer/client TLS not configured: Without TLS, Secret data is transmitted in plaintext between API server and etcd — network captures reveal everything.
  4. No encryption in CI/CD pipeline: Pipeline doesn't validate that --encryption-provider-config is present in API server flags. Encryption is an afterthought.
  5. No external KMS integration for key management: Encryption key stored locally on control plane node. No integration with cloud KMS for centralized key management, rotation, and audit.
🔍 What to Look At:
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep encryption-provider-config If this flag is absent, encryption is NOT configured. All Secrets are unencrypted in etcd.
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep -A3 encryption-provider-config Check the static pod manifest for the encryption flag and the config file path.
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get "" --from-key --keys-only | grep secrets List all Secrets stored in etcd. If the key names don't start with k8s:enc:, they're unencrypted.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: EncryptionConfiguration was never created and passed to kube-apiserver via --encryption-provider-config. etcd encryption at rest is an opt-in security feature — it is NOT enabled by default in any Kubernetes distribution.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create EncryptionConfiguration YAML apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1 kind: EncryptionConfiguration resources: - resources: [secrets] providers: - aescbc: keys: - name: key1 secret: <base64-encoded-32-byte-key> - identity: {} Place at /etc/kubernetes/pki/encryption-config.yaml. aescbc first means it's used for writes; identity last for read fallback.
2. Mount config to API server Update /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml: add volume mount for encryption-config.yaml and flag --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/pki/encryption-config.yaml. API server restarts automatically.
3. Re-encrypt ALL existing Secrets kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f - Rewrite every Secret to trigger encryption. Without this, existing Secrets remain unencrypted indefinitely.
4. Verify encryption is active ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj/anihpj-db-secret ... The output should have k8s:enc:aescbc:v1: prefix — confirming the Secret is encrypted in etcd.
5. Run CIS benchmark check 1.1.34 kube-bench run --targets master --check 1.1.34 Verifies --encryption-provider-config is set. Should show PASS.
💡 Personal Advice:
etcd encryption is the most critical CKS hardening step. Without it, every Secret in your cluster is one etcdctl get away from exposure. This is a CIS benchmark MUST-PASS and a CKS exam requirement. Enable it on every cluster.
Re-encrypt existing Secrets — enabling encryption only covers NEW writes. After enabling encryption, run kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f - to re-encrypt all existing Secrets. Otherwise they remain unencrypted forever.
identity provider must be LAST in the list. The FIRST provider in EncryptionConfiguration is used for writes. If identity: {} is first, encryption is effectively disabled. Put aescbc or kms FIRST.
CH8
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH8
AlwaysAllow Admission Controller Enabled — No Security Gate

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f privileged-pod.yaml succeeds even though the pod has hostNetwork: true, privileged: true, and mounts /etc/kubernetes. No admission controller is blocking dangerous configurations. The kube-apiserver is missing critical admission controllers like NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, and DenyServiceExternalIPs. Additionally, --disable-admission-plugins removes security-critical plugins that were enabled by default.

  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata: {name: evil-pod}
  spec:
    hostNetwork: true
    hostPID: true
    privileged: true
    containers:
    - name: evil
      image: busybox
      command: ["sleep","3600"]
  EOF
  pod/evil-pod created   ← SHOULD HAVE BEEN REJECTED!

  ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep enable-admission-plugins
  --enable-admission-plugins=AlwaysAdmit   ← MISSING security plugins!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. --enable-admission-plugins overrides defaults: Specifying --enable-admission-plugins REPLACES the default list — it doesn't append to it. If you only enable NamespaceLifecycle, you DISABLE all other default plugins including security-critical ones.
  2. Security-critical plugins explicitly disabled: --disable-admission-plugins=PodSecurity,NodeRestriction REMOVES these from the active set. This is sometimes done during debugging and never reverted.
  3. NodeRestriction not enabled: Without NodeRestriction, a kubelet can modify ANY node's labels, taints, and status — not just its own. This enables node-to-node attacks via kubelet credential theft.
  4. PodSecurity admission plugin missing: Without PodSecurity (or PodSecurityPolicy on older clusters), there is NO enforcement of pod security standards. Privileged pods, hostPath mounts, and hostNetwork are all allowed.
  5. AlwaysPullImages not enabled: Without this, pods can use cached images with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent. A compromised node can serve a malicious cached image without the registry being checked.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. EventRateLimit not configured: Without rate limiting, a compromised pod can flood the API server with events — denial of service against the control plane.
  2. DenyServiceExternalIPs not enabled: A Service with externalIPs can redirect cluster traffic to arbitrary external IPs. Without this plugin, Service external IP attacks are possible.
  3. ImagePolicyWebhook not configured: No webhook to validate container images before admission. Images from untrusted registries or with known CVEs are admitted without checks.
  4. MutatingAdmissionWebhook misconfigured: A mutating webhook that adds a privileged sidecar to every pod in a namespace — silently escalating every deployment.
  5. Admission plugin ordering issues: Mutating webhooks run BEFORE validating webhooks. A mutating webhook can add privileged: true and the validating webhook never sees the original (safe) pod spec.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default admission plugins not reviewed: kubeadm enables a set of default plugins, but teams not aware of what they are or which ones should be added.
  2. PodSecurity admission not configured per namespace: The plugin is enabled but no namespace labels (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce) are set. No security standard is applied.
  3. CIS benchmark checks for admission plugins not run: CIS 1.2.14-1.2.18 test admission plugin configuration. kube-bench not run.
  4. No ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or OPA/Gatekeeper: Beyond built-in admission plugins, no custom policy engine is deployed. The admission pipeline relies entirely on defaults.
  5. Admission plugin configuration not in infrastructure-as-code: No git-managed API server manifest. Plugin changes are made manually on nodes and not documented.
🔍 What to Look At:
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -oE 'enable-admission-plugins=[^ ]*' | tr ',' '\n' List ALL enabled admission plugins. Verify security-critical ones are present.
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -oE 'disable-admission-plugins=[^ ]*' Check which plugins are DISABLED. Any security plugin in this list is a RED FLAG.
kubectl api-resources | grep admissionregistration Verify that ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration CRDs exist.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: --enable-admission-plugins was set manually, OVERRIDING the Kubernetes default admission plugin list. Security-critical plugins like NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, and AlwaysPullImages were omitted.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Review required admission plugins Minimum security set: NamespaceLifecycle, NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, AlwaysPullImages, ServiceAccount, LimitRanger, ResourceQuota, MutatingAdmissionWebhook, ValidatingAdmissionWebhook, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy. Ensure ALL are in --enable-admission-plugins.
2. Remove explicit --enable-admission-plugins to use defaults If you only need default plugins, REMOVE --enable-admission-plugins entirely. kube-apiserver uses the compiled-in recommended list which includes security-critical plugins.
3. Enable Pod Security admission with namespace labels kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted Set enforce, audit, and warn labels per namespace. restricted blocks privileged pods, hostPath, and hostNetwork.
4. Never disable security plugins Remove any --disable-admission-plugins entries that reference security-critical plugins. This flag should be empty or only disable specific non-security plugins.
5. Deploy OPA/Gatekeeper for custom policies Beyond built-in admission control, deploy a policy engine that can enforce organization-specific rules (e.g., "no pods without resource limits," "no image from :latest tag").
💡 Personal Advice:
--enable-admission-plugins REPLACES defaults, not appends. This is the #1 admission controller trap. If you specify --enable-admission-plugins=NamespaceLifecycle, you DISABLE ALL OTHER default plugins. Either don't set this flag at all, or explicitly include every plugin you need.
PodSecurity admission with "restricted" profile is the modern baseline. Apply pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted label to every namespace. This blocks privileged containers, hostPath volumes, hostNetwork, and hostPID by default.
CH9
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH9
Pod Security Standards Not Enforced — Privileged Pod Escapes Container

🔍 Symptom: A pod in the anihpj namespace runs with privileged: true, hostPID: true, and mounts the entire node filesystem via hostPath: /. kubectl exec <pod> -- nsenter --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid --target 1 gives a ROOT SHELL ON THE NODE. No Pod Security Standard (PSS) is enforced — the namespace has no pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label. Any pod, from any developer, can break out to the node.

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api-v2 -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E "privileged|hostPID|hostNetwork|hostPath"
  privileged: true
  hostPID: true
  hostPath: {path: /}

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-v2 -- nsenter --mount --pid --target 1 -- bash -c "crictl ps; cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml"
  CONTAINER           IMAGE
  kube-apiserver      registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.32   ← NODE ACCESS!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No Pod Security Standard labels on namespace: The anihpj namespace is missing pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted label. Without it, the PodSecurity admission plugin does NOT block privileged pods, hostPath, or hostNetwork.
  2. Pod created by a cluster-admin ServiceAccount: The Deployment uses a ServiceAccount with cluster-admin RBAC. Pod Security admission allows cluster-admin to bypass PSS restrictions — privileged pods from admin SAs are not blocked.
  3. Security context explicitly sets privileged: true: The Pod spec has securityContext: {privileged: true}. This disables ALL container isolation — all Linux capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor, and cgroup restrictions are removed.
  4. hostPID: true enables node process manipulation: The pod shares the node's PID namespace. nsenter --target 1 gives direct access to the node's init process and all other processes — including the container runtime and kubelet.
  5. hostPath: / mounts the entire node filesystem: The pod can read/write /etc/kubernetes, /var/lib/kubelet, and /var/log/pods. An attacker can modify static pod manifests (kube-apiserver, etcd) and take over the control plane.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. PodSecurity admission plugin not enabled: Even with namespace labels, if the PodSecurity admission plugin is not in --enable-admission-plugins, labels are ignored.
  2. Pod created before PSS labels were applied: Existing pods are NOT re-validated when labels are added. The privileged pod was created before enforce=restricted was applied.
  3. Additional capabilities grant effective root: Even without privileged: true, adding CAP_SYS_ADMIN and CAP_NET_ADMIN allows kernel-level operations including mount namespace manipulation and iptables modification.
  4. Seccomp profile explicitly set to Unconfined: The pod has seccompProfile: {type: Unconfined} — allowing ANY syscall including mount, reboot, and kexec.
  5. NO_NEW_PRIVILEGES not set: Without allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, a setuid binary inside the container can escalate to root even if the container was started as non-root.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. PodSecurity admission not configured during cluster setup: kubeadm 1.25+ enables PodSecurity by default but namespace labels are not set. All namespaces are effectively privileged.
  2. No security policy for pod specs: No review process, no OPA/Gatekeeper policy, no PSP/PSS migration plan. Developers deploy whatever pod spec they want.
  3. Legacy PSP migration incomplete: Cluster upgraded from pre-1.25 where PodSecurityPolicy was used. PSPs removed but Pod Security admission labels never added to namespaces.
  4. Testing/development mindset carried to production: privileged: true used during development for convenience. Never locked down before production deployment.
  5. No runtime detection of privileged pods: Falco or similar runtime security tool not deployed. Privileged pod breakouts would not generate alerts.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep pod-security Check for PSS labels. If enforce is missing or set to privileged, no pod restrictions are in place.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E "privileged:\s*true|hostPID:\s*true|hostNetwork:\s*true" Find all pods with dangerous security contexts. Each one is a potential container escape vector.
kubectl describe ns anihpj | grep -A5 "pod-security" Review the PSS violation warnings. The audit log shows which pods would be blocked if enforce mode were enabled.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label on the namespace. Without this, the PodSecurity admission plugin does not block privileged pods, hostPath mounts, hostNetwork, or hostPID — all of which enable container-to-node escape.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Apply Pod Security Standard labels to namespace kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted restricted blocks privileged pods, hostPath, hostNetwork, hostPID, and requires non-root user. Existing pods are grandfathered — new pods must comply.
2. Fix the Deployment to comply with restricted profile Remove privileged: true, hostPID: true, and hostPath mounts. Add runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}. Use emptyDir or PVC instead of hostPath.
3. Audit and restart non-compliant pods kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E "privileged.*true|hostPID.*true" Find non-compliant pods, fix their Deployments, and restart. After restart, PSS will enforce compliance.
4. Apply restricted to ALL namespaces kubectl label ns <ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted Every namespace should have at minimum audit=restricted. Gradually move critical namespaces to enforce=restricted.
5. Deploy Falco for runtime detection Even with PSS enforcement, deploy Falco to detect: privileged container launches, nsenter into host namespaces, unexpected filesystem mounts. Runtime detection catches what admission misses.
💡 Personal Advice:
privileged: true = total container escape. A privileged container has ALL Linux capabilities and all devices accessible. Combined with hostPID and hostPath, it IS a root shell on the node. Never use privileged: true in production. There is always a better way.
Use the audit → warn → enforce progression. Start with audit=restricted to log violations without blocking. Then add warn=restricted to notify users. Finally, enforce=restricted to block. Don't jump straight to enforce on existing namespaces — you'll break running workloads.

📌 CH10–CH12: Audit Logging, Kubelet Auth & Token Expiry

CH10
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH10
Audit Logging Not Configured — Zero Visibility Into API Activity

🔍 Symptom: A developer accidentally deleted the anihpj-db StatefulSet and its PVC — the PostgreSQL database and all customer data are gone. kubectl get events -n anihpj shows the deletion event but NOT who did it. There's no audit trail — no record of which user, which IP, or which token was used. The kube-apiserver is running without --audit-policy-file and --audit-log-path. The delete was destructive, irreversible, and untraceable.

  kubectl get events -n anihpj --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | grep anihpj-db
  2m    DELETED   StatefulSet anihpj-db   ← WHAT happened, but not WHO

  ls /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log
  ls: cannot access '/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log': No such file or directory

  ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep audit
  <no output>   ← Audit logging is NOT configured!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. --audit-policy-file not configured: The API server has no audit policy file. Without it, no audit events are logged. This is the most basic audit configuration step — and it's skipped by default.
  2. --audit-log-path not set: Even with an audit policy, without a log path the events go nowhere. --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log must be specified.
  3. Audit policy only logs Metadata level — not RequestResponse: The audit policy has level: Metadata which only logs request metadata (user, resource, verb) — not the request body. For deletions of Secrets and StatefulSets, you need level: RequestResponse to capture the full request.
  4. Audit log file not mounted from host: The audit log path is specified but the directory is not a hostPath volume mount. The API server writes to its container filesystem — which disappears on restart. Logs are ephemeral.
  5. No audit log retention or rotation: The audit log file grows indefinitely, filling the control plane disk. Without --audit-log-maxage, --audit-log-maxsize, and --audit-log-maxbackup, the disk fills and the API server crashes.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Audit webhook misconfigured: --audit-webhook-config-file points to a non-existent webhook. Audit events are sent to a black hole — no error is logged.
  2. Audit log file permissions prevent API server from writing: The host directory has wrong ownership. API server starts but silently fails to write audit events. Check: tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log should show events flowing.
  3. Audit policy omits critical resources: The policy logs Deployments but omits Secrets, ConfigMaps, and RBAC resources. The most security-critical operations are invisible.
  4. Audit log shipped but not monitored: Logs are sent to an external system (Elasticsearch, Splunk) but no alerts are configured. The delete event is ingested but no one is notified.
  5. Multiple API servers writing to the same audit log file: On multi-master clusters, each API server writes to the same NFS path — race conditions corrupt the audit log or cause lost events.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Audit logging not set up during kubeadm init: kubeadm does NOT configure audit logging by default. It's an entirely manual post-installation step.
  2. No audit policy file created: The cluster is running without any audit policy. No one has written the YAML or added the flags to kube-apiserver.
  3. CIS benchmark 1.2.22-1.2.25 not checked: Multiple CIS checks relate to audit logging. kube-bench hasn't been run.
  4. No centralized logging infrastructure: Even if audit logs were generated, there's no aggregation system (ELK, Loki, Splunk). Logs would exist only on the control plane node.
  5. Audit policy not tailored to organizational needs: The default approach is to enable audit logging "later." Later never comes until an incident happens.
🔍 What to Look At:
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -E "audit-policy-file|audit-log-path" Verify both flags are present. If either is missing, audit logging is not functional.
cat /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml Review the audit policy. At minimum, it should have level: RequestResponse for Secrets and RBAC resources.
tail -10 /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log | jq . Check that audit events are actually being written. Each line should be a JSON object with user, verb, objectRef, and sourceIPs.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: kube-apiserver is running without --audit-policy-file and --audit-log-path. Audit logging is NOT configured by default — it must be explicitly enabled with a policy file, log path, and volume mount.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create audit policy file on control plane node vim /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml Include rules for level: RequestResponse on Secrets, ConfigMaps, RBAC resources. level: Metadata for everything else. omitStages: [RequestReceived] to reduce noise.
2. Add audit flags to kube-apiserver manifest --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log --audit-log-maxage=30 --audit-log-maxsize=100 --audit-log-maxbackup=10 Mount /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml and /var/log/kubernetes/audit/ as hostPath volumes in the API server static pod manifest.
3. Create audit log directory on host mkdir -p /var/log/kubernetes/audit; chmod 700 /var/log/kubernetes/audit The directory must exist with correct permissions before the API server starts.
4. Verify audit events are flowing tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log | jq '.user.username, .verb, .objectRef.resource' Run a kubectl command and confirm it appears in the audit log.
5. Set up audit log forwarding and alerting Forward audit logs to a centralized system. Create alerts for: delete on secrets, delete on clusterrolebindings, create on clusterroles.
💡 Personal Advice:
Audit logging is your forensic safety net. Without audit logs, you cannot answer: Who deleted the production database? Who accessed that Secret? Who created that ClusterRoleBinding? Audit logging answers these questions. Enable it BEFORE you need it.
The audit policy determines what you can investigate. If your policy only logs Metadata, you'll know WHO did WHAT, but not the request body. For Secrets and RBAC, use RequestResponse to capture the full request and response body.
CH11
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH11
Kubelet Anonymous Authentication Enabled — Unauthenticated Node Access

🔍 Symptom: curl -k https://<node-ip>:10250/pods returns a list of ALL pods running on the node WITHOUT any authentication. The kubelet is running with --anonymous-auth=true (the default), allowing anyone with network access to the kubelet's port 10250 to list pods, retrieve logs, execute commands, and access container filesystems. An attacker who gains network access to a node can enumerate and compromise every pod on that node without credentials.

  curl -k https://10.0.0.1:10250/pods
  { "kind": "PodList", "items": [ ... all pods on node ... ] }   ← NO AUTH!

  curl -k https://10.0.0.1:10250/run/default/anihpj-web/anihpj-web -d "cmd=env"
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD=SuperSecretP@ss123!
  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA123...   ← Commands executed without auth!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. --anonymous-auth=true is the DEFAULT for kubelet: Kubelet starts with anonymous authentication ENABLED. Unauthenticated requests to port 10250 are assigned the system:anonymous user. This is the #1 kubelet hardening oversight.
