  3. No RBAC restriction on ConfigMap access: The default RBAC allows all ServiceAccounts in the namespace to read ConfigMaps. A compromised redis pod can read the ConfigMap and extract the database password — then connect directly to the database and exfiltrate data.
  4. ConfigMap committed to Git: The ConfigMap YAML is in the infrastructure repo. The database password is now in Git history — accessible to every developer with repo access and anyone who clones the repo.
  5. etcd encryption not enabled: Even Kubernetes Secrets are stored as base64 in etcd by default. Without etcd encryption, both ConfigMap AND Secret data is plaintext. But Secrets at least have RBAC and audit protections that ConfigMaps lack.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ConfigMap printed in CI/CD pipeline logs: The CI pipeline does echo "$CONFIGMAP_YAML" | kubectl apply -f -. The ConfigMap content — including passwords — is captured in CI logs visible to the entire engineering team.
  2. ConfigMap exposed via Kubernetes API without authentication: Anonymous auth on the API server combined with RBAC for anonymous users exposes the ConfigMap to unauthenticated network access.
  3. ConfigMap mounted as file readable by any container: volumes: [{name: config, configMap: {name: anihpj-config, defaultMode: 0644}}] — the file is world-readable. Any process in the container, including compromised ones, can read it.
  4. Templating tool (Helm/Kustomize) renders secrets into ConfigMap: The Helm chart has {{ .Values.db.password }} rendered into a ConfigMap instead of a Secret. The template is correct — the resource type is wrong.
  5. No Secret rotation mechanism: The password in the ConfigMap is 2 years old. Even if migrated to a Secret, rotation is needed — but there's no process for it.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Quick-and-dirty migration from docker-compose: The .env file from docker-compose was directly converted to a ConfigMap without reviewing which values are sensitive.
  2. Developers unaware of Secret resource type: Kubernetes Secrets are unknown to developers coming from non-Kubernetes backgrounds. ConfigMap is the "configuration thing" they know about.
  3. No pre-commit hook or CI check for secrets in YAML: No detect-secrets or trufflehog scanning YAML files for embedded passwords before commit or during CI.
  4. No External Secrets Operator or Vault integration: No integration with HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or External Secrets Operator. Kubernetes Secrets are the only option — and even that wasn't used.
  5. No secret detection in code review checklist: PR review doesn't include checking for secrets in ConfigMap YAML. The password slipped through review unnoticed.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cm -A -o yaml | grep -iE "password|secret|token|key|api.key" Scan all ConfigMaps for sensitive keywords. Every match is a potential plaintext secret. Migrate to Kubernetes Secrets.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E "configMapRef|secretRef" Check if pods mount ConfigMaps as environment variables (envFrom.configMapRef). If the ConfigMap has secrets, they're in the container's environment.
git log -p | grep -iE "password|secret|token" --color Search Git history for any sensitive data that may have been committed in ConfigMap YAML files. Every finding needs immediate rotation.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Sensitive data (passwords, API keys, JWT secrets) is stored in plaintext in a ConfigMap instead of a Kubernetes Secret. ConfigMaps provide no confidentiality guarantees — they're readable by anyone with namespace access, printed in plaintext by kubectl, and stored without encryption in etcd.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Migrate sensitive data from ConfigMap to Secret kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secrets -n anihpj --from-literal=DATABASE_URL='postgresql://...' --from-literal=JWT_SECRET='...' Secrets are stored separately from ConfigMaps. They can be encrypted at rest and have stricter RBAC controls.
2. Mount Secret as file, not environment variable Use volumes[].secret.secretName and volumeMounts instead of envFrom.secretRef. Secrets mounted as files are NOT visible in /proc/<pid>/environ.
3. Delete sensitive data from ConfigMap kubectl delete cm anihpj-config -n anihpj; kubectl create cm anihpj-config -n anihpj --from-literal=non-sensitive-key=value Remove all sensitive entries from the ConfigMap. Only non-sensitive configuration should remain.
4. Rotate all exposed credentials Every password, key, and token that was in the ConfigMap MUST be rotated. Assume they've been compromised — anyone with Git access, CI log access, or namespace RBAC could have read them.
5. Enable etcd encryption at rest Even Secrets are stored as base64 without encryption. Enable EncryptionConfiguration with aescbc provider to encrypt Secrets in etcd.
💡 Personal Advice:
ConfigMap ≠ Secret. Know the difference. ConfigMap: for non-sensitive app settings (timeouts, feature flags, log levels). Secret: for passwords, tokens, keys, certificates. Putting secrets in ConfigMaps is like writing your password on a sticky note on your monitor — everyone in the room can read it.
Secrets in Git are secrets FOREVER. If a ConfigMap with passwords was committed to Git, deleting the file doesn't remove it — it's in the commit history permanently. Use git filter-branch or BFG Repo-Cleaner to scrub it, AND rotate every exposed credential.
MV11
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV11
Debug Endpoint Exposed in Production — Heap Dumps and Env Leakage

🔍 Symptom: curl https://anihpj-api:8000/actuator/heapdump downloads the JVM heap dump of the production API server. curl https://anihpj-api:8000/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2 returns all goroutine stacks. These debug endpoints expose: all environment variables (including Secrets), request tokens in memory, database connection strings, and internal API routes. Spring Boot Actuator, Django Debug Toolbar, and Go pprof are production-accessible without authentication — every developer debugging tool is an attacker's reconnaissance goldmine.

  curl https://anihpj-api:8000/actuator/env
  {"activeProfiles":["prod"],"propertySources":[{"name":"systemEnvironment",
    "properties":{"POSTGRES_PASSWORD":{"value":"****"},"JWT_SECRET":{"value":"****"}}}

  curl https://anihpj-api:8000/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 -o heap.bin
  # Heap dump contains request tokens, session data, and decrypted Secrets in memory!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Spring Boot Actuator endpoints exposed without auth: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* exposes ALL actuator endpoints (heapdump, env, threaddump, mappings, configprops) on the main application port. No authentication required.
  2. Go pprof endpoints bound to 0.0.0.0: net/http/pprof is imported and bound to 0.0.0.0:6060 — the debug server listens on ALL interfaces. Any pod in the cluster can access /debug/pprof/ and retrieve heap/CPU profiles.
  3. Django DEBUG=True enables debug toolbar: Django Debug Toolbar shows SQL queries, template context (with variables), and request headers. In production with DEBUG=True, anyone can access the debug panel.
  4. No NetworkPolicy restricting access to debug ports: The debug port (6060, 8081, 5005 for Java debugging) has no NetworkPolicy. Any compromised pod or external attacker that reaches the pod network can access debug endpoints.
  5. Debug endpoints not behind authentication middleware: The API gateway routes external traffic to the app, but the app also listens on a separate debug port that bypasses the API gateway entirely. No auth middleware protects the debug port.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Java JMX/RMI port open with default credentials: -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.port=9010 -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=false — JMX is accessible without authentication, allowing remote code execution via MBeans.
  2. Node.js inspector port exposed: node --inspect=0.0.0.0:9229 exposes the Chrome DevTools debugging protocol. An attacker can attach a debugger and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the production process.
  3. Debug endpoint leaks internal IPs and routes: /actuator/mappings exposes every API endpoint including internal-only routes. Attackers use this to map the application's attack surface.
  4. Health endpoint returns excessive detail: /actuator/health shows {"db":{"status":"UP","details":{"url":"postgresql://..."}}} — database connection strings in health checks. Set management.endpoint.health.show-details=never.
  5. Debug endpoints included in production Docker image: The same Docker image is used for dev and prod. The dev image includes debug tools — and they're present (and running) in production because no prod-specific config disabled them.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No production-specific application config: Dev config enables debug tools. Prod config should disable them — but uses the same config file with just a different database URL.
  2. Actuator/pprof not disabled in application.properties: Default Spring Boot and Go framework settings expose debug endpoints. No one explicitly disabled them for the production profile.
  3. No NetworkPolicy default-deny for debug ports: No baseline NetworkPolicy blocks traffic to debug ports (6060, 8081, 9010, 9229). Attackers can probe these ports freely.
  4. Container image uses same build for dev and prod: The same Docker image tag is deployed to dev and prod. Security is "we'll harden it later" — but later never comes.
  5. No external pentest or security scan: A basic vulnerability scan would immediately flag /actuator/env, /debug/pprof/, and JMX ports. No scan has ever been performed.
🔍 What to Look At:
curl -s https://anihpj-api:8000/actuator; curl -s https://anihpj-api:8000/debug/pprof/; curl -s https://anihpj-api:8000/__debug__/ Probe common debug endpoint paths. If ANY return data, debug endpoints are exposed in production.
kubectl exec <pod> -- ss -tlnp Check which ports the container listens on. Any port other than the main app port (8000) could be a debug endpoint — especially 6060 (pprof), 8081 (actuator), 9010 (JMX).
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E "DEBUG|ACTUATOR|PPROF|JMX" -i Check environment variables and arguments for debug-related settings that should be disabled in production.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Framework debug endpoints (Spring Boot Actuator, Go pprof, Django Debug Toolbar) are enabled and accessible without authentication. These endpoints expose heap dumps, environment variables (including Secrets), database connection strings, and internal API routes — providing attackers with complete application reconnaissance.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Disable debug endpoints in production config Spring Boot: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info. Go: don't import net/http/pprof in production builds. Django: DEBUG=False.
2. Bind debug ports to localhost only --pprof-listen-address=127.0.0.1:6060 If debug endpoints are needed, bind to 127.0.0.1 — they're only accessible from within the container. External access requires kubectl port-forward.
3. Add NetworkPolicy blocking debug ports Default-deny all traffic to ports 6060, 8081, 9010, 9229, 5005. Only specific developer IPs (via kubectl port-forward) should reach debug endpoints.
4. Use separate prod and dev Docker images Build a production image that excludes debug tools: use a multi-stage build where the final stage doesn't include pprof, debug toolbar, or actuator (beyond health/info).
5. Add WAF rules blocking known debug paths Block at the API gateway: /actuator/*, /debug/*, /__debug__/*, /.env. These paths should never be accessible from outside the cluster.
💡 Personal Advice:
Heap dumps contain EVERYTHING in memory. A heap dump from a production JVM contains: decrypted Secrets, request tokens, session cookies, database passwords, and user PII — all in plaintext. Exposing /actuator/heapdump or /debug/pprof/heap is equivalent to handing an attacker a memory image of your application. NEVER expose these in production.
The same image for dev and prod is a security anti-pattern. Dev images have debug tools, verbose logging, and expanded error messages. Production images should be hardened: no debug endpoints, no shell, no package manager. Build a separate production image or use a prod-specific entrypoint that disables debug features.
MV12
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV12
CORS Misconfiguration — Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

🔍 Symptom: curl -H "Origin: https://evil.com" -v https://anihpj-api:8000/api/jobs returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com. The API server ECHOES any Origin back — it's configured with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (or a reflector pattern). A malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the anihpj API FROM the user's browser. If the user is logged into the job board, visiting evil.com triggers API calls using the user's authenticated session — exfiltrating personal data, posting fake job listings, or deleting the user's account.

  curl -H "Origin: https://evil.com" -v https://anihpj-api:8000/api/jobs
  < HTTP/2 200
  < Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com   ← REFLECTS ANY ORIGIN!
  < Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

  curl -H "Origin: https://attacker-phish.site" -v https://anihpj-api:8000/api/users/me
  < Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker-phish.site   ← REFLECTED AGAIN!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS = True in Django: Django CORS middleware has CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS = True — every Origin is accepted. The API is callable from ANY website the user visits.
  2. Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials: The server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * AND Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. These are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE per the CORS spec. Browsers should reject this — but some accept it anyway, leaking authenticated responses.
  3. Origin header reflected back to client: The server reads the Origin request header and echoes it back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. This accepts ANY origin — equivalent to * but harder to detect in configuration reviews.
  4. Pre-flight OPTIONS request returns 200 with wildcard: The OPTIONS handler (CORS preflight) returns Access-Control-Allow-Methods: * and Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * — accepting any HTTP method and any header from any origin.
  5. CORS configured for development never tightened for production: CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS = True was set during development for convenience. The production config never changed it to a specific allowlist.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS regex too permissive: CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_REGEXES = [r"^https?://.*\.jobpost\.com$"] — matches ANY subdomain including evil.jobpost.com. Subdomain takeovers make this a vulnerability.
  2. No CSRF protection alongside CORS: CORS restricts cross-origin requests in browsers — CSRF tokens protect against state-changing requests. If CSRF is disabled and CORS is permissive, attackers can POST data as authenticated users.
  3. CORS configured at wrong layer: CORS headers are set by the Ingress controller (nginx-ingress annotations) which adds * for all services regardless of whether they need it. Application-level CORS settings are overridden.
  4. API key authentication bypasses CORS entirely: CORS only protects browser-based requests. If the API accepts API keys in headers, non-browser clients (curl, Python requests) can call the API from anywhere. CORS is a browser control, not server-side auth.
  5. WebSocket CORS not configured: The WebSocket endpoint doesn't validate the Origin header. Any website can open a WebSocket connection to the API and stream data as the authenticated user.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CORS_ORIGIN_ALLOW_ALL defaults to True in some frameworks: Django CORS Headers and some Express.js middleware default to wide-open CORS. The team never changed the default.
  2. No CORS audit in security review: CORS configuration is often overlooked in security assessments. The team assumes "CORS is fine" because the app works in the browser.
  3. CORS set to * for "compatibility" with unknown clients: The API serves both a web frontend AND mobile apps. The team used * because "we don't know all the client domains."
  4. No CORS testing in CI pipeline: No automated test verifies that the API rejects requests from unauthorized origins. CORS configuration is assumed correct.
  5. CORS treated as "just a frontend thing": Backend developers consider CORS a frontend concern. The backend just sends headers — the security implications of permissive CORS are not understood.
🔍 What to Look At:
curl -H "Origin: https://evil.com" -v https://anihpj-api:8000/api/jobs 2>&1 | grep -i "access-control" If Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com or * appears, the API accepts cross-origin requests from any domain.
curl -X OPTIONS -H "Origin: https://evil.com" -v https://anihpj-api:8000/api/jobs 2>&1 | grep -i "access-control" Check the CORS preflight response. If it returns Allow-Methods: * and Allow-Headers: *, CORS is wide open.
kubectl exec <pod> -- env | grep -i cors Check environment variables for CORS settings in the application container. CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS=true is a red flag.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: CORS is configured with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (or an Origin-reflector pattern). Any malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin API requests using the victim's browser session, enabling data theft, account manipulation, and CSRF-style attacks.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Restrict CORS to specific allowed origins CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS = ["https://anihpj.jobpost.com", "https://admin.jobpost.com"] Never use * or an Origin reflector. Explicitly list every domain that should access the API. Reject everything else.
2. Never combine * with credentials Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is spec-violating and dangerous. If you need credentials, you MUST specify exact origins.
3. Do NOT echo the Origin header Check your CORS middleware: it should compare the Origin against a WHITELIST, not just echo it back. Reflection is equivalent to * but harder to detect.
4. Restrict CORS preflight methods and headers CORS_ALLOW_METHODS = ["GET", "POST", "PUT"] — only allow methods your API actually needs. Never *.
5. Add CORS validation test to CI Automated test: send request with Origin: https://evil.com and assert the response does NOT contain Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that origin.
💡 Personal Advice:
CORS with * is open season for cross-origin attacks. Any website you visit can make authenticated API calls to your backend — using YOUR cookies, YOUR session, YOUR identity. You'd never know. CORS is not just a "browser thing" — it's a critical API security control. Configure it correctly.
CORS is NOT server-side authentication. CORS restricts cross-origin requests from BROWSERS. Non-browser clients (curl, Postman, Python requests) ignore CORS entirely. Never rely on CORS as your only API protection — always implement proper authentication and authorization on the server side.

📌 MV13–MV16: Rate Limiting, WebSockets, gRPC & Health Leaks

MV13
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV13
Rate Limiting Not Configured — API Abuse and Credential Stuffing

🔍 Symptom: An attacker can make 10,000 login attempts per minute against /api/auth/login without any throttling. curl -X POST https://anihpj.jobpost.com/api/auth/login -d '{"user":"admin","password":"guess123"}' returns 200 or 401 with no delay. There's no rate limiting at the API gateway, no exponential backoff, and no IP-based blocking. Brute-force attacks against user accounts, credential stuffing with leaked passwords, and API scraping (job listings, user profiles) all proceed at unlimited speed. The API has no defense against automated abuse.

  for i in {1..100}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X POST https://anihpj.jobpost.com/api/auth/login -d '{"user":"admin","password":"guess'$i'"}'; echo; done
  401  401  401  401  401 ...  401  401  200 !   ← 100th attempt found the password!
  # All 100 requests completed in 3 seconds — NO RATE LIMITING!

  curl -I https://anihpj.jobpost.com/api/jobs | grep -i "X-RateLimit"
  # No rate limit headers — no throttling mechanism deployed
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No rate limiting at API gateway or Ingress: nginx-ingress doesn't have nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps annotation. Istio doesn't have RequestAuthentication + AuthorizationPolicy with rate limiting. Every request reaches the backend unchecked.
  2. No application-level rate limiting: Django doesn't have django-ratelimit or throttling middleware. The login endpoint has no @ratelimit(key='ip', rate='5/m') decorator. There's no per-user or per-IP throttling.
  3. No account lockout after failed attempts: Even with rate limiting, account lockout (5 failed attempts = 15 min lockout) prevents targeted brute-force. Neither rate limiting NOR account lockout is implemented.
  4. No distinction between authenticated and unauthenticated limits: Authenticated users should have higher limits than anonymous requests. Without this, an attacker can DoS the API by exhausting the global rate limit — blocking legitimate users.
  5. No WAF with rate-based rules: Cloud WAF (AWS WAF, Cloud Armor) can block IPs that exceed request thresholds. No WAF is deployed — rate limiting relies entirely on application or gateway config.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Rate limiting configured but bypassed via header manipulation: The rate limiter uses X-Forwarded-For header — which the attacker sets to a different IP on every request. The rate limiter sees 10,000 unique IPs instead of 10,000 requests from the same attacker.
  2. Distributed brute-force from botnet: The attack comes from 10,000 unique IPs. Per-IP rate limiting allows 1 request per second per IP — but 10,000 IPs × 1 req/s = 10,000 attempts per second. Global rate limiting is needed.
  3. Rate limit counter stored in local memory: If the rate limiter uses in-memory counters (not Redis), each pod replica has its own counter. With 5 replicas, the attacker gets 5× the rate limit by distributing requests across pods.
  4. Rate limiting on wrong resource: Rate limit is on /api/jobs but the login endpoint /api/auth/login has NO rate limit. Attackers target the un-throttled endpoint.
  5. GraphQL endpoint with no query complexity limiting: GraphQL allows deeply nested queries that consume massive resources. A single un-throttled GraphQL request can DoS the database equivalent of 1,000 REST API calls.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Rate limiting considered "premature optimization": Early-stage teams deprioritize rate limiting — "we'll add it when we have traffic." The traffic arrives as an attack.
  2. No API gateway with built-in rate limiting: Using basic nginx-ingress without the rate-limiting annotations enabled. No API management layer (Kong, Ambassador, APISIX) deployed.
  3. No DDoS protection service: No Cloudflare, AWS Shield, or similar DDoS mitigation. The cluster's bandwidth is the only protection against volumetric attacks.
  4. No observability on request rates: No Prometheus metrics tracking requests per second per endpoint. Rate anomalies aren't detected because request rates aren't monitored.
  5. No incident response plan for API abuse: When brute-force attacks happen, there's no runbook. The team doesn't know how to identify the attack source, block the IP, or apply emergency rate limits.
🔍 What to Look At:
curl -I https://anihpj.jobpost.com/api/auth/login | grep -i "ratelimit\|retry-after" Check for rate limit headers. Absence of X-RateLimit-* or Retry-After headers means no rate limiting is active.
kubectl get ingress -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E "limit-rps|limit-rpm|limit-connections" Check Ingress annotations for nginx-ingress rate limiting. If absent, the Ingress forwards all requests without throttling.
kubectl exec anihpj-api -- env | grep -i "ratelimit\|throttle" Check if the application has rate limiting configured via environment variables. Absence means no app-level throttling.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No rate limiting is configured at ANY layer — Ingress, API gateway, or application. Brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and API scraping proceed at unlimited speed with no throttling, no backoff, and no IP blocking.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Configure rate limiting at the Ingress nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "10" nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rpm: "100" nginx-ingress supports per-IP rate limiting via annotations. Start with 10 req/s per IP for login endpoints, higher for general API.
2. Add application-level rate limiting on auth endpoints Django: REST_FRAMEWORK = {'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES': ['rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle'], 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {'anon': '5/min', 'user': '100/min'}}. Login: 5 attempts/minute/IP. API: 100 req/min/authenticated user.
3. Implement account lockout After 5 failed login attempts, lock the account for 15 minutes. Notify the user via email. This stops targeted brute-force even if rate limiting is bypassed.
4. Deploy WAF with rate-based rules AWS WAF rate-based rule: block IPs making >1000 requests in 5 minutes. This catches botnets and volumetric attacks before they reach your cluster.
5. Monitor and alert on rate anomalies Prometheus metric: rate(http_requests_total{path="/api/auth/login"}[5m]). Alert if login request rate exceeds baseline by 10× — early warning of brute-force attack.
💡 Personal Advice:
Rate limiting is your API's immune system. Without it, your API has no defense against automated abuse. Rate limit at every layer: WAF → Ingress → Gateway → Application. Each layer catches what the previous misses. No single layer is sufficient.
Auth endpoints need the strictest limits. Login, password reset, and registration endpoints are the #1 target for brute-force attacks. 5 attempts/minute per IP, account lockout after 5 failures. These are table-stakes security controls — implement them before going to production.
MV14
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV14
WebSocket Connection Not Authenticated — Unauthorized Real-Time Data Stream

🔍 Symptom: wscat -c ws://anihpj-api:8000/ws/updates/ connects without ANY authentication token. The WebSocket endpoint streams real-time job updates, user notifications, and internal event data to anyone who connects. There's no JWT validation on WebSocket upgrade, no session cookie check, and no Origin header validation. An attacker can open a WebSocket and receive a firehose of real-time data — new job postings, user registrations, and internal system events — without ever authenticating.

  wscat -c ws://anihpj-api:8000/ws/updates/
  Connected (press CTRL+C to quit)
  < {"event":"job_created","data":{"title":"Senior Dev","salary":"$150k"}}
  < {"event":"user_registered","data":{"email":"john@company.com"}}
  < {"event":"internal_metrics","data":{"db_connections":42,"cache_hits":1523}}
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. WebSocket handshake doesn't require auth token: The WebSocket upgrade handler doesn't check for a JWT in the query string (?token=...) or in the initial HTTP headers (Authorization: Bearer ...). Anyone who can establish a TCP connection gets a WebSocket stream.
  2. JWT validated on HTTP but not on WebSocket: The REST API validates JWT — but WebSocket connections use a DIFFERENT code path. The Django Channels or Socket.IO handler doesn't call the auth middleware. WebSocket connections bypass authentication entirely.
  3. No Origin header validation on WebSocket: Browsers send the Origin header on WebSocket upgrade. The server should validate it — but doesn't. Any website can open a WebSocket to your backend. Combined with CORS bypass, this leaks real-time data to malicious sites.
  4. WebSocket broadcasts all events to all connections: The WebSocket server doesn't implement channel-based routing. Every connected client receives ALL events — there's no per-user or per-role filtering. An anonymous connection sees admin events and internal metrics.
  5. No timeout or idle disconnect: The WebSocket stays open indefinitely with no heartbeat or timeout. An attacker can maintain hundreds of persistent connections, exhausting server file descriptors and memory.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. WebSocket token passed in URL logged everywhere: The auth token is in the query string (ws://host/ws?token=eyJhbG...). Server access logs, proxy logs, and browser history capture the token in plaintext.
  2. No CSWSH (Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking) protection: Without Origin validation, a malicious website can open a WebSocket using the victim's cookies. The WebSocket inherits the authenticated session — the attacker reads the victim's real-time data.
  3. No message-level authentication: Even if the initial handshake is authenticated, individual WebSocket messages are not signed or verified. An attacker who MITMs the connection can inject false events after the handshake.
  4. WebSocket compression enables CRIME/BREACH attacks: Per-message deflate enabled on the WebSocket allows attackers to infer secret data byte-by-byte by observing compressed message sizes. Disable compression on authenticated WebSockets.
  5. No TLS for WebSocket (ws:// not wss://): The WebSocket uses ws:// (plaintext) instead of wss:// (TLS). All data — including auth tokens in the URL — is transmitted in plaintext across the network.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. WebSocket authentication not in initial development scope: The WebSocket was added for real-time features. Auth was "phase 2" — which never happened.
  2. No WebSocket security review: REST API security was reviewed. WebSocket security was overlooked because it's a different protocol with different attack vectors.
  3. Django Channels default allows anonymous connections: Django Channels doesn't enforce authentication by default. AuthMiddlewareStack is in the routing but doesn't REJECT unauthenticated connections — it just sets scope["user"] to AnonymousUser.
  4. No NetworkPolicy restricting WebSocket port: The WebSocket port is accessible from any pod. A compromised pod can connect and stream data without triggering any auth check.
  5. No monitoring on WebSocket connections: No metrics tracking WebSocket connection count, authentication failures, or data egress. Unauthorized connections go undetected.
🔍 What to Look At:
wscat -c ws://anihpj-api:8000/ws/updates/ Try connecting without any auth token. If the connection succeeds and data flows, WebSocket authentication is missing.
curl -H "Upgrade: websocket" -H "Connection: Upgrade" -v http://anihpj-api:8000/ws/updates/ 2>&1 | grep "101" If the server returns 101 Switching Protocols without checking authentication, WebSockets are unauthenticated.
kubectl exec <pod> -- env | grep -i "websocket\|channels\|socket" Check WebSocket configuration. Django Channels should have AuthMiddlewareStack but must also implement connection rejection for anonymous users.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The WebSocket upgrade handler does not validate authentication tokens. WebSocket connections use a separate code path from REST API calls, bypassing the JWT/session authentication middleware. Anyone who can establish a TCP connection receives a real-time stream of internal data.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Authenticate WebSocket connections Django Channels: use AuthMiddlewareStack and in the consumer, call self.scope["user"] — if is_anonymous, self.close(). Node.js: validate JWT from ws.upgradeReq.headers['authorization'] before accepting.
2. Validate Origin header on WebSocket upgrade Compare Origin header against an allowlist. Reject connections from unexpected origins. This prevents cross-site WebSocket hijacking from malicious websites.
3. Implement per-user channel routing Don't broadcast all events to all connections. Route events to specific user channels based on the authenticated user ID. Each connection only receives events relevant to that user.
4. Enforce wss:// (TLS) for all WebSockets Never use ws:// in production. Always wss://. The WebSocket uses the same TLS certificate as the HTTPS endpoint. All data is encrypted in transit.
5. Add WebSocket connection limits and timeouts Max 5 concurrent WebSockets per user. Max 100 per IP. Idle timeout: 5 minutes. Ping/pong heartbeat every 30 seconds. Drop connections that don't respond to pings.
💡 Personal Advice:
WebSocket is NOT just "long-lived HTTP." The WebSocket upgrade handshake goes through HTTP, but AFTER that, it's a different protocol. Authentication middleware that works for REST may NOT apply to WebSocket connections. Always test WebSocket endpoints WITHOUT a token — if they connect, they're unauthenticated.
Anonymous WebSocket + public events = data leak firehose. If your WebSocket streams real-time data without authentication, you're broadcasting your entire application's internal state to anyone who knows the endpoint URL. This includes competitors scraping your data in real-time.
MV15
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV15
gRPC Service Without TLS — Plaintext Protobuf Traffic

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api exposes a gRPC endpoint on port 9000 for internal service communication. grpcurl -plaintext anihpj-api:9000 list returns all gRPC services and methods WITHOUT any TLS handshake. gRPC traffic — including serialized Protobuf messages with user data, JWT tokens in metadata, and internal API calls — flows in plaintext across the pod network. Any pod on the same network can intercept, replay, or modify gRPC calls because there's no TLS encryption and no mutual authentication.

  grpcurl -plaintext anihpj-api:9000 list
  anihpj.jobpost.v1.JobService
  anihpj.jobpost.v1.UserService
  grpc.reflection.v1alpha.ServerReflection   ← ALL SERVICES LISTED WITHOUT TLS!

  grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"user_id":"123"}' anihpj-api:9000 anihpj.jobpost.v1.UserService/GetUser
  {"id":"123","email":"admin@jobpost.com","role":"admin"}   ← USER DATA WITHOUT AUTH!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. gRPC server started without TLS credentials: grpc.NewServer() (Go) or grpc.server(async_server) (Python) without grpc.Creds(). The server accepts all connections in plaintext — no TLS certificate configured.
  2. gRPC client connects with grpc.WithInsecure(): The client explicitly disables TLS: grpc.Dial("anihpj-db:9000", grpc.WithInsecure()) — bypasses any server TLS configuration and sends data in plaintext.
  3. No mutual TLS (mTLS) between gRPC services: Even with server-side TLS, the server doesn't verify the client's certificate. Any client with a valid TCP connection can call gRPC methods — there's no client identity verification.
  4. gRPC reflection enabled in production: grpc.reflection.v1alpha.ServerReflection is registered — allowing anyone to list ALL gRPC services and methods. This is gRPC's equivalent of an unauthenticated API schema dump. Disable in production.
  5. No JWT or token authentication on gRPC methods: The gRPC server doesn't validate auth metadata (JWT in gRPC metadata headers). Any client can call any method with any parameters. There's no per-method authorization.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. TLS certificate mismatch between gRPC and HTTP: The gRPC server uses a different TLS certificate than the HTTPS endpoint — one that's self-signed or expired. Clients configured to verify TLS reject the connection and silently fall back to insecure mode.
  2. gRPC load balancer terminates TLS but backend is plaintext: The gRPC-aware load balancer (e.g., nginx with HTTP/2) terminates TLS at the edge but forwards plaintext to the backend gRPC server. Pod-to-pod traffic is unencrypted.
  3. No gRPC interceptor for auth/audit: gRPC supports interceptors (middleware) for auth, logging, and rate limiting. No interceptors are configured — the gRPC server is a raw passthrough to business logic.
  4. gRPC streaming RPC consumes unlimited resources: Bidirectional streaming RPCs have no message size limits, no timeout, and no rate limiting. An attacker can open a stream and send unlimited data — memory exhaustion attack.
  5. Protobuf binary data deserialized without validation: Malformed Protobuf messages can cause buffer overflows or panic the gRPC server. No input validation beyond Protobuf parsing — large fields or deeply nested messages cause crashes.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. gRPC used as "internal-only" with no security: Team assumes the pod network is trusted. gRPC is deployed with WithInsecure() because "it's just internal traffic." Zero-trust principle not applied to gRPC.
  2. Service mesh doesn't cover gRPC port: Istio sidecar only intercepts HTTP ports. gRPC on port 9000 is not in the sidecar's port list — traffic bypasses the mesh entirely (no mTLS, no policies).
  3. No gRPC security awareness: Team is experienced with REST API security. gRPC security (TLS, mTLS, interceptors, JWT in metadata) is unfamiliar territory — security is skipped.
  4. gRPC started as an experiment and graduated to production: The gRPC endpoint was a proof-of-concept with -plaintext for easy testing. It was promoted to production without ever adding TLS.
  5. No NetworkPolicy for gRPC port: Port 9000 is accessible from ALL pods. A compromised frontend pod can call internal gRPC methods on the backend — no network-level restriction.
🔍 What to Look At:
grpcurl -plaintext anihpj-api:9000 list If this returns service listings, the gRPC server accepts plaintext connections AND has reflection enabled. Both are production anti-patterns.
kubectl exec <pod> -- ss -tlnp | grep 9000 Check if the gRPC port is listening. Then verify if it's covered by the service mesh sidecar (Istio).
istioctl proxy-config listener <pod> -n anihpj | grep 9000 If the gRPC port is not in the sidecar's listener list, Istio is NOT intercepting this traffic — no mTLS, no auth policies.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The gRPC server is configured without TLS (WithInsecure()) and gRPC reflection is enabled in production. All gRPC traffic flows in plaintext — Protobuf messages with user data and JWT metadata are visible to any pod on the network. Any client can discover and call all gRPC methods without authentication.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enable TLS on gRPC server Go: creds, _ := credentials.NewServerTLSFromFile("tls.crt", "tls.key"); grpc.NewServer(grpc.Creds(creds)). Mount TLS cert from Kubernetes Secret. All connections require TLS handshake.
2. Enable mTLS for gRPC client authentication Server: tls.Config{ClientAuth: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert}. Client: grpc.WithTransportCredentials(creds). Both sides present certificates — mutual trust established.
3. Disable gRPC reflection in production // Don't register reflection.Register(s) in production builds Reflection exposes your entire API schema. It's for development tools (grpcurl, grpcui) — attackers love it for reconnaissance. Disable in production.
4. Add JWT auth interceptor gRPC interceptor extracts JWT from authorization metadata. Validates signature, expiry, and claims before passing to the handler. Reject unauthenticated calls at the interceptor level.
5. Ensure service mesh covers gRPC port Istio: add port 9000 to the pod's traffic.sidecar.istio.io/includeInboundPorts annotation. The sidecar will intercept gRPC traffic and provide automatic mTLS.
💡 Personal Advice:
Plaintext gRPC = plaintext everything. gRPC carries serialized Protobuf with metadata headers. If it's plaintext, every piece of data — user info, JWT tokens, service method names — is visible to anyone sniffing the network. gRPC TLS is not optional in production. It's table stakes.
gRPC reflection is a free API map for attackers. With reflection enabled, grpcurl list shows every service, every method, every parameter. It's like hosting your Swagger docs without authentication. Always disable reflection in production builds.
MV16
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV16
Health Endpoint Leaks Sensitive Information — /health Returns Full Status

🔍 Symptom: curl https://anihpj.jobpost.com/health returns a detailed JSON response including database connection strings, Redis cluster topology, upstream service health, and internal IP addresses. The health endpoint — designed for load balancer probes — exposes: "postgresql":"postgresql://anihpj-db:5432/jobpost", "redis_nodes":["10.244.3.5:6379","10.244.3.6:6379"], "internal_api": {"status":"ok","url":"http://payment-svc.internal:8080"}. Attackers use health endpoints for reconnaissance — mapping the internal infrastructure without triggering any alerts.

  curl -s https://anihpj.jobpost.com/health | python3 -m json.tool
  {
    "status": "ok",
    "database": {"status":"up","url":"postgresql://anihpj_admin:****@anihpj-db:5432/jobpost"},
    "redis": {"status":"up","nodes":["10.244.3.5:6379","10.244.3.6:6379"]},
    "internal_api": {"payment":"http://payment.internal:8080","notifications":"http://notify:9000"},
    "memory_usage": "67%",
    "uptime": "15d 4h 23m"   ← ATTACKER RECON GOLDMINE!
  }
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Health endpoint returns full component status: The health check doesn't just return 200 OK — it returns detailed JSON with database URLs, Redis IPs, and internal service endpoints. This is far more information than a load balancer needs — which only cares about HTTP status codes.
  2. Health endpoint not authentication-protected: /health and /healthz are accessible to unauthenticated users. Load balancers need them, but they don't need detailed component status — just HTTP 200/503. The detailed endpoint should be protected.
  3. Database connection strings in health response: The health check connects to the database and reports the connection URL — including the database name and host. Even if the password is masked, the hostname reveals internal network topology.
  4. Internal service discovery exposed: Health check calls downstream services (payment, notifications, message queue) and returns their status and URLs. This is a complete map of the internal microservice architecture — exposed on the public endpoint.
  5. Memory/uptime metrics in health response: The health endpoint reports memory usage and uptime. Attackers use uptime to determine patch schedules and memory usage to gauge the impact of memory-based DoS attacks.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes use detailed endpoint: livenessProbe.httpGet.path: /health calls the detailed health endpoint every 10 seconds. The kubelet logs (readable via kubectl logs by anyone with pod log access) capture the full health response.
  2. Health endpoint exposes version numbers: "version":"1.2.3","python_version":"3.9.18","django_version":"4.2.7" — attackers use version numbers to target known CVEs. Version information should NEVER be in public headers or health endpoints.
  3. Separate /healthz and /readyz not configured:
    4. Kubernetes needs two endpoints: liveness (/healthz) and readiness (/readyz). If both point to the same detailed /health, the detailed info is exposed to the kubelet at high frequency.
  4. Health check performs expensive operations: The health endpoint connects to every downstream service on EVERY call. A single probe triggers 5+ internal requests. An attacker can DoS the system by repeatedly calling /health — the health check becomes the attack vector.
  5. Health endpoint cached by CDN/proxy: The detailed health response is cached at the CDN or reverse proxy. The internal architecture map is now available from edge caches globally — and the CDN logs show who accessed it.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Health endpoint copied from framework tutorial: Django/Spring Boot health check tutorials show detailed output. The team copied the tutorial code without realizing the security implications.
  2. Health endpoint designed for internal dashboard: The detailed health JSON was built for an internal monitoring dashboard. It was accidentally exposed on the public API because no one realized the same endpoint serves both purposes.
  3. No architecture review of public endpoints: The security review covered /api/* but didn't audit /health, /status, /info, or /metrics. These endpoints are invisible to typical security assessments.
  4. No WAF rule masking sensitive response patterns: The WAF doesn't inspect response bodies for patterns like postgresql:// or internal IP addresses. Data leak via response body goes undetected.
  5. Health endpoint in public Ingress: The Ingress routes /health to the backend. The health endpoint should only be accessible from the load balancer's health check IP ranges — not the entire internet.
🔍 What to Look At:
curl -s https://anihpj.jobpost.com/health | python3 -m json.tool | wc -l If the output is more than 5 lines, the health endpoint is returning excessive detail. A secure health check returns {"status":"ok"} or just HTTP 200.
curl -s https://anihpj.jobpost.com/health | grep -iE "postgres|mysql|redis|mongo|elastic|http://|internal" Check for database URLs, service endpoints, and internal IPs in the health response. Any matches are information leaks.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 "livenessProbe\|readinessProbe" | grep path Check which endpoint the probes call. If it's /health (detailed), it's called every 10s. Use separate /healthz and /readyz.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The health endpoint returns detailed internal infrastructure information — database URLs, Redis node IPs, downstream service endpoints, and version numbers — to anyone who queries it. What should be a simple load balancer probe has become an attacker's reconnaissance goldmine.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Split health into minimal and detailed endpoints /healthz: returns HTTP 200 if process is alive (liveness — no dependencies checked). /readyz: returns HTTP 200 if ready to serve (readiness — checks DB/Redis connectivity, returns 200/503 only). /health: detailed JSON for authenticated monitoring only.
2. Never expose database URLs or internal IPs A health check should return: {"status":"ok"} or {"status":"degraded","checks":{"db":"down"}}. Never include the actual connection string, IP address, or hostname.
3. Require authentication for detailed health /health (detailed): require valid JWT or API key, and restrict to monitoring service IPs. Public probes hit /healthz and /readyz which return minimal responses.
4. Configure kubelet probes to use minimal endpoints livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz}}; readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /readyz}} Probes run every 10 seconds. Don't have them call the detailed health endpoint — it's unnecessary load and a log spam vector.
5. Restrict /health to load balancer IPs only Ingress annotation or NetworkPolicy: only allow /healthz and /readyz from the load balancer's health check IP range. Block /health at the Ingress level — it's only for internal monitoring.
💡 Personal Advice:
Your health endpoint is an attacker's first recon target. Attackers probe /health, /status, /info, and /actuator before attempting any exploit. If your health endpoint returns database URLs and internal service maps, you've just handed the attacker your entire infrastructure blueprint. A health check should return one thing: "I'm alive."
Three endpoints: healthz, readyz, health (auth-protected). This pattern separates concerns: liveness (is the process alive?), readiness (can it serve traffic?), detailed health (what's the internal state?). Only the first two are public.

📌 MV17–MV20: DNS Discovery, Resource Limits, CA Bundles & Startup Probes

MV17
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV17
Internal Service Discoverable via External DNS — Service Enumeration

🔍 Symptom: nslookup anihpj-db.jobpost.com returns the internal ClusterIP of the PostgreSQL database. The internal Kubernetes service DNS name has been added to the public DNS zone as a CNAME or A record. Attackers performing DNS enumeration discover: anihpj-db.jobpost.com (database), anihpj-redis.jobpost.com (cache), anihpj-api.internal.jobpost.com (API), payment-svc.jobpost.com (payment service). The public DNS zone maps the entire internal microservice architecture — attackers know exactly which services exist and their hostnames before sending a single HTTP request.

  dig AXFR jobpost.com   # Zone transfer attempt
  ;; ANSWER SECTION:
  anihpj-db.jobpost.com.     300 IN A  10.244.1.10   ← INTERNAL IP IN PUBLIC DNS!
  anihpj-redis.jobpost.com.   300 IN A  10.244.1.11
  payment-svc.jobpost.com.    300 IN A  10.244.2.20

  curl http://anihpj-db.jobpost.com:5432/
  curl: (52) Empty reply from server   ← PostgreSQL port OPEN and reachable!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Internal Kubernetes service DNS published to public DNS: anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local was added to the public jobpost.com DNS zone — either as a CNAME or by configuring the internal DNS resolver to respond to public queries. Internal hostnames are now visible externally.
  2. Service type LoadBalancer with public DNS name: The anihpj-db Service has type: LoadBalancer — the cloud provider assigns a public hostname that resolves to the internal service IP. External DNS picks this up and publishes it.
  3. External-dns controller publishing internal services: The external-dns controller is configured to publish ALL Services with specific annotations — including internal-only database and cache services. The annotation filter is too broad.
  4. Internal DNS zone transfer not restricted: The public DNS server allows zone transfers (AXFR) from any IP. Attackers can download the ENTIRE DNS zone — enumerating every internal service in one request. Restrict zone transfers to authorized secondary DNS servers.
  5. Wildcard DNS pointing to cluster Ingress: *.jobpost.com points to the Ingress controller's external IP. ANY subdomain — including anihpj-db.jobpost.com — routes to the Ingress. The Ingress forwards to the backend service based on the Host header.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Service hostname leaked in HTTP response headers: The API returns X-Backend-Service: anihpj-api or X-Powered-By: Express (anihpj-api) in response headers. Attackers passively discover service names from HTTP responses.
  2. Internal hostnames in JavaScript source maps: Frontend source maps (.js.map) contain internal API URLs like http://anihpj-api.internal:8000. Source maps are publicly accessible and reveal internal hostnames.
  3. Kubernetes API server exposes service DNS via CoreDNS: The cluster's CoreDNS is configured as an open resolver. Attackers can query anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local from outside the cluster if CoreDNS is exposed.
  4. Certificate Transparency logs reveal internal hostnames: TLS certificates issued for internal services are logged in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs. Attackers search CT logs for *.jobpost.com and discover all internal hostnames with valid certificates.
  5. DNS resolution via cloud metadata service: The cloud provider's internal DNS (Route 53 Resolver, Cloud DNS) resolves internal hostnames. If a pod with a public IP queries it, the resolution leaks internal IPs to external observers.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. external-dns deployed with default broad scope: New cluster, external-dns installed with default settings. It publishes all annotated Services to public DNS — including database and cache services that should stay internal.
  2. No DNS zone architecture separating internal/external: Single DNS zone for everything. No split-horizon DNS: internal.jobpost.com for internal services, jobpost.com for public services.
  3. Public DNS managed by same team as Kubernetes: Developers add DNS records for debugging. Internal service records leak into public DNS because there's no approval process for DNS changes.
  4. No DNS enumeration monitoring: No alerting on zone transfer attempts, high-volume DNS queries, or queries for non-public hostnames. DNS enumeration goes undetected.
  5. No certificate authority restrictions: Internal hostnames get public TLS certificates (Let's Encrypt). These appear in CT logs — permanently recording the existence of internal services.
🔍 What to Look At:
dig <service>.jobpost.com +short; dig <service>.internal.jobpost.com +short Try resolving internal service names from OUTSIDE the cluster. If they resolve, internal DNS is publicly exposed.
kubectl get svc -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.type=="LoadBalancer") | {name,namespace,hostname: .status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}' Find all LoadBalancer services. Each one with a public hostname is potentially exposing an internal service.
dig AXFR jobpost.com Attempt a zone transfer. If it succeeds, your entire DNS zone is downloadable — fix your DNS server configuration immediately.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Internal Kubernetes Service DNS names are published to the public DNS zone either via external-dns, Service type LoadBalancer auto-registration, or manual DNS entries. Attackers can enumerate internal services, discover their hostnames and IPs, and map the entire microservice architecture without sending a single HTTP probe.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Implement split-horizon DNS Public DNS (jobpost.com): only public-facing endpoints (web, api gateway). Internal DNS (internal.jobpost.com or svc.cluster.local): only resolvable from within the VPC/cluster.
2. Restrict external-dns to specific annotations --annotation-filter=external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/publish=public Only Services with the publish=public annotation get DNS records. Internal services (db, redis, payment) don't have this annotation.
3. Use ClusterIP (not LoadBalancer) for internal services Database, cache, and message queue services should be type: ClusterIP. Only the API gateway and web frontend need LoadBalancer or Ingress exposure.
4. Disable DNS zone transfers from public IPs Configure your DNS provider to REJECT AXFR requests from unauthorized IPs. Zone transfers should only be allowed to your secondary DNS servers.
5. Monitor DNS for enumeration Alert on: zone transfer attempts, >100 unique subdomain queries/minute, queries for known internal patterns (db.*, redis.*, internal.*).
💡 Personal Advice:
DNS is your infrastructure map. Don't publish it publicly. Every internal hostname in public DNS is a free hint to attackers. "They have a PostgreSQL database at anihpj-db.jobpost.com" — now the attacker knows exactly what to target. Keep internal DNS internal.
Certificate Transparency logs are permanent and public. Every TLS certificate issued for an internal hostname is logged FOREVER in CT logs. Even if you remove the DNS record, the hostname is discoverable via CT log search. Use wildcard certs for internal services or don't expose them at all.
MV18
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV18
No Resource Limits — Noisy Neighbor Denial of Service

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api Deployment has no resources.limits or resources.requests. A memory leak in the Django app causes it to consume 4GB of RAM — starving anihpj-db and anihpj-redis on the same node. The node becomes unresponsive, the kubelet can't report status, and the node gets tainted as NodeMemoryPressure. Without resource limits, a single misbehaving pod can crash ALL pods on the node. This is the "noisy neighbor" problem — one pod's failure cascades to the entire node.

  kubectl top pod -n anihpj
  NAME            CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
  anihpj-api      3500m        4200Mi   ← CONSUMING ALL NODE RESOURCES!
  anihpj-db       200m         256Mi
  anihpj-redis    50m          128Mi

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 resources
  resources: {}   ← NO LIMITS, NO REQUESTS!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No resources.limits set in container spec: resources.limits: {cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi"} is missing. Without limits, the container can consume ALL CPU and memory on the node — starving the kubelet, container runtime, and neighboring pods.
  2. No resources.requests set for scheduling: resources.requests: {cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi"} is missing. The scheduler doesn't know how much the pod needs — it may place a memory-hungry pod on a node with insufficient resources.
  3. No LimitRange in the namespace: A LimitRange resource sets default resource limits for all containers in the namespace. Without it, containers with no explicit limits have unbounded resource access.
  4. Memory leak in application code: Django or Python memory leak causes RSS to grow unbounded. Without memory limits, the leak consumes all node memory — the OOM killer terminates the pod, but not before it impacts other pods.
  5. No ResourceQuota in the namespace: A ResourceQuota limits the TOTAL resources all pods in the namespace can consume. Without it, one namespace can starve other namespaces on the same node.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. OOMKiller terminates critical pod first: When node memory is exhausted, the Linux OOM killer selects a process to kill based on oom_score. The database (anihpj-db) might be killed instead of the memory-leaking api pod — corrupting data.
  2. CPU throttling without visible symptoms: The pod has no CPU limits — it consumes all available CPU. Other pods get CPU starved, request latencies spike, and health probes timeout. The node appears healthy but services are degraded.
  3. No Pod Priority/Preemption configured: Without priorities, critical pods (database, kube-proxy) and non-critical pods (batch processing) compete equally for resources. A batch job can evict the database pod.
  4. Limits set but requests not set: limits: {memory: "1Gi"} without requests: {memory: "256Mi"}. The scheduler doesn't reserve memory — it may place pods assuming no memory pressure, leading to overcommit and OOM kills.
  5. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler creates too many replicas: HPA scales based on CPU, but memory is the bottleneck. HPA creates 20 replicas — all hit memory limits simultaneously, causing cascading OOM kills.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No resource management policy: New cluster, no standard for setting requests/limits. Developers deploy without specifying resources — "it works fine on my laptop."
  2. No LimitRange enforcing defaults: LimitRange not applied to namespaces. Pods without explicit limits run unbounded.
  3. No ResourceQuota preventing namespace overrun: No quota on total CPU/memory a namespace can consume. The anihpj namespace can consume the entire cluster's resources.
  4. No OPA policy requiring resource limits: No admission policy rejecting pods without resources.limits and resources.requests. Pods without limits are admitted silently.
  5. No resource usage monitoring or alerting: No Prometheus alert on high node memory pressure, pod memory growth, or pods without resource limits. Resource issues discovered only after node failure.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, resources: .spec.containers[].resources}' Find all pods without resources.limits or resources.requests. Each one is a potential noisy neighbor that can starve the node.
kubectl top nodes; kubectl top pods -A Check actual resource usage. If any node is >90% memory or CPU, pods are at risk of OOM kill or CPU starvation.
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Allocated resources" Shows total resource requests vs node capacity. If requests > capacity, the node is overcommitted — OOM kills are likely.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No resources.limits or resources.requests are set on container specs. Without limits, a single pod with a memory leak or CPU spike can consume all node resources — starving neighboring pods, the kubelet, and the container runtime, causing node-level failure.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set resource requests and limits on every container resources: requests: {memory: "128Mi", cpu: "100m"} limits: {memory: "512Mi", cpu: "500m"} Requests = guaranteed minimum for scheduling. Limits = hard maximum — container is OOM killed if exceeded. Set after profiling actual app usage.
2. Apply LimitRange to all namespaces kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion: v1 kind: LimitRange metadata: {name: anihpj-limits, namespace: anihpj} spec: limits: - default: {memory: "512Mi", cpu: "500m"} defaultRequest: {memory: "128Mi", cpu: "100m"} type: Container EOF All containers without explicit limits get these defaults. Prevents unbounded resource consumption.
3. Apply ResourceQuota to namespaces ResourceQuota limiting total requests/limits per namespace: requests.cpu: "10", requests.memory: "20Gi". Prevents one namespace from consuming the entire cluster.
4. Configure Pod PriorityClasses Critical pods (database, kube-proxy) get high priority. Batch jobs get low priority. When resources are tight, low-priority pods are evicted first — protecting critical services.
5. Deploy OPA policy requiring resource limits Reject pods without resources.limits and resources.requests for both CPU and memory. This enforces resource hygiene at admission time — no pod runs without limits.
💡 Personal Advice:
No limits = everyone's problem. When your API pod has a memory leak and consumes 4GB, it's not just YOUR pod that crashes — the database, cache, and kubelet on the same node all get OOM killed. Resource limits protect the ENTIRE node, not just your pod.
Requests = scheduling guarantee. Limits = hard cap. Both are mandatory. Requests tell the scheduler what the pod NEEDS. Limits tell the kernel when to OOM kill. Use both. Set requests to 50-70% of limits — the pod gets guaranteed resources but can burst when available.
MV19
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV19
Root CA Certificate Bundled in Container Image — Trust Anchor Leaked

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api Docker image includes the company's private Root CA certificate and private key at /etc/ssl/certs/internal-ca.crt and /etc/ssl/private/internal-ca.key. Anyone who pulls the container image (public registry!) can extract the Root CA private key by running docker run anihpj-api cat /etc/ssl/private/internal-ca.key. With the Root CA key, an attacker can sign certificates for ANY domain — impersonating any internal or external service. The trust anchor of the entire PKI is available to anyone with image pull access.

  docker run --rm anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 ls /etc/ssl/certs/ /etc/ssl/private/
  /etc/ssl/certs/internal-ca.crt
  /etc/ssl/private/internal-ca.key   ← PRIVATE KEY IN CONTAINER IMAGE!

  docker run --rm anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 cat /etc/ssl/private/internal-ca.key
  -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
  MIIEpAIBAAKCAQEA...   ← ROOT CA PRIVATE KEY EXTRACTED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Private key copied into Docker image during build: COPY internal-ca.key /etc/ssl/private/ in the Dockerfile. The CA private key is now permanently embedded in the image layer — accessible to anyone with docker pull access.
  2. CA certificate bundled for "convenience": The team added the internal CA cert to the image so the app can trust internal services. The private key was accidentally included alongside the certificate — or the directory was copied recursively.
  3. Image pushed to public registry: The image containing the CA private key is on Docker Hub with public pull access. Anyone in the world can docker pull anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 and extract the key.
  4. Docker build context includes sensitive files: The build context directory contains the CA key file. Even without an explicit COPY, ADD . /app copies everything — including internal-ca.key — into the image.
  5. No .dockerignore excluding key files: There's no .dockerignore file. The build context sends ALL files to the Docker daemon — including *.key, *.pem, and .env files that should never leave the build host.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CA key stored in intermediate build layer: The Dockerfile copies the key in one layer and deletes it in another: COPY key /tmp; RUN use-key; RUN rm /tmp/key. The key is STILL in the previous layer — accessible via docker history or dive.
  2. CA key in environment variable baked into image: ENV CA_KEY=-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----... — the key is in the image metadata. docker inspect reveals all ENV values including the private key.
  3. Private key committed to Git alongside Dockerfile: The key file is in the same Git repo as the Dockerfile. Anyone with repo access — including CI systems, contractors, and departed employees — has the CA private key.
  4. CI pipeline logs print the key during build: The build script does echo "$CA_KEY" or cat ca.key during image build. CI logs — accessible to all developers — contain the private key.
  5. Backup or snapshot of registry contains all image layers: Registry backups are stored in object storage with broad access. The CA private key is in every backup of every image that included it. Rotating the CA means finding and deleting every backup.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No .dockerignore or .gitignore for key files: New project, no template files excluding *.key, *.pem, and secrets/ from Docker build context or Git.
  2. CA created without security around private key storage: The Root CA was created for internal mTLS. The private key was stored in the project directory "temporarily" — and was picked up by the Docker build.
  3. No image scanning for secrets: No trufflehog or ggshield scanning Docker images for private keys before pushing to the registry. The key went undetected.
  4. No private registry with access control: Images are on Docker Hub with public pull. Even if the team realizes the key is exposed, the image is already cached on every mirror and user's machine globally.
  5. No PKI compromise response plan: No documented process for rotating the Root CA, revoking all issued certificates, and re-issuing new certs to all services. CA compromise response is undefined.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker run --rm anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 find / -name "*.key" -o -name "*.pem" -o -name "*-ca.crt" 2>/dev/null Search the image for any private key or CA certificate files. Every key found in a container image is compromised — the image is publicly pullable.
docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --no-trunc | grep -E "COPY|ADD" Check what files were copied into each layer. If a layer copied a directory containing *.key files, the key is forever in that layer.
cat .dockerignore Verify that *.key, *.pem, secrets/, and .env are in .dockerignore. If the file doesn't exist or is missing these patterns, key files may be in the build context.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Root CA private key was copied into the Docker image during build — either via an explicit COPY or via ADD . /app without a .dockerignore. The image is in an accessible registry, meaning anyone who pulls the image can extract the CA private key and sign certificates for any internal or external service.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Revoke the compromised Root CA IMMEDIATELY The CA private key is in the wild. Revoke the CA, create a NEW Root CA, and re-issue ALL certificates signed by the old CA. Every service, every mTLS endpoint, every internal TLS cert must be replaced.
2. Remove CA key from Dockerfile and rebuild Delete any COPY or ADD that references CA keys. Remove from .dockerignore if present. Rebuild the image WITHOUT the key — verify with docker run.
3. Use cert-manager or Vault to inject CA certificates at runtime Instead of baking CA certs into images, mount them from Kubernetes Secrets or inject via init containers at pod startup. The CA cert (public key only) lives in a Secret, not in the image.
4. Add .dockerignore with key file exclusions *.key / *.pem / secrets/ / .env Every project must have a .dockerignore that excludes sensitive files from the Docker build context. This is table stakes for container security.
5. Scan images for secrets before pushing trufflehog filesystem /app; ggshield scan docker anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 Integrate secret scanning into CI. Fail the build if any private key, API token, or password pattern is found in the image layers.
💡 Personal Advice:
A CA private key in a Docker image is a PKI apocalypse. If your Root CA key is in an image, you must: (1) revoke the CA, (2) create a new CA, (3) re-issue EVERY certificate to EVERY service, (4) rotate ALL TLS secrets, (5) audit every system for unauthorized certs. This is a multi-week incident — prevent it with .dockerignore.
.dockerignore is your first line of defense. A single *.key line in .dockerignore prevents this entire class of vulnerability. Create the file before your first docker build — retroactively removing keys from Docker layers is nearly impossible.
MV20
🔗 CATEGORY 4: MICROSERVICE VULNERABILITIES — Issue MV20
Startup Probe Without Security Context — Slow-Start Container Exposed

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api pod takes 90 seconds to start (loading ML models, warming caches) but the liveness probe starts checking after 10 seconds. The pod is repeatedly killed by the kubelet as Liveness probe failed — causing a CrashLoopBackOff. To "fix" this, the team increased initialDelaySeconds: 120 on the liveness probe — but during those 120 seconds, the pod is ALREADY receiving traffic (readiness probe passes early). The partially-initialized pod serves traffic before security middleware is loaded — authentication, rate limiting, and input validation are not yet active. Early traffic to an uninitialized pod bypasses all security controls.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w | grep anihpj-api
  anihpj-api   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   0s
  anihpj-api   0/1   Running            10s   ← Liveness probe kills it
  anihpj-api   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   20s   ← Cycle repeats!

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "readinessProbe\|livenessProbe\|startupProbe"
  livenessProbe:  {initialDelaySeconds: 120, periodSeconds: 10}
  readinessProbe: {initialDelaySeconds: 10, periodSeconds: 5}   ← PASSES EARLY!
  # No startupProbe configured!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No startupProbe configured for slow-starting container: Kubernetes 1.20+ supports startupProbe — a probe that runs ONLY during startup. Once it succeeds, liveness and readiness take over. Without it, liveness kills the pod during initialization.
  2. Readiness probe passes before security middleware loaded: The readiness probe checks /healthz which returns 200 as soon as the HTTP server binds — BEFORE auth middleware, rate limiter, and input validation are initialized. The pod receives traffic without security controls.
  3. liveness initialDelaySeconds too short for app startup: initialDelaySeconds: 10 assumes the app starts in 10 seconds. The app takes 90 seconds — it's killed by liveness 8 times before the delay expires.
  4. Readiness and liveness probe same endpoint: Both probes hit /healthz. The readiness probe (which controls traffic) passes at the same time as liveness — there's no distinction between "alive" and "ready to serve traffic."
  5. Application doesn't signal readiness: The app starts accepting HTTP connections immediately when the port binds — regardless of whether initialization is complete. The readiness probe sees an open port and assumes the app is ready.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Graceful shutdown period too short: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 5 — the pod gets 5 seconds to shut down. The app needs 30 seconds to drain connections and save state. In-flight requests are killed mid-processing.
  2. PreStop hook not configured: No lifecycle.preStop hook to drain connections before the pod terminates. The pod is deleted while still serving traffic — clients get connection refused errors.
  3. Pod receives traffic before endpoint is registered: The readiness probe passes, but Service endpoint propagation takes 5-10 seconds due to kube-proxy iptables/ipvs update delay. During this window, the pod is "ready" but unreachable.
  4. Application crashes during initialization with no health reporting: The startup fails silently — the HTTP server never starts. The readiness probe never passes, but the pod stays in Running (not Ready) indefinitely without crashing.
  5. Sidecar not ready but main container is: The Istio sidecar is still initializing, but the main container's readiness probe passes. Traffic arrives at the pod but can't be routed by the sidecar — connection timeouts.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. startupProbe not used — team unaware it exists: Kubernetes 1.20 feature not widely known. Teams still use initialDelaySeconds hacks instead of startupProbe.
  2. Probes copied from tutorial without tuning: Default probe values from a getting-started guide used in production. The app has very different startup characteristics than the tutorial app.
  3. No load testing to determine probe thresholds: Probe initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, and failureThreshold are guesses — never validated against actual application startup timing under load.
  4. No readiness gate for security middleware: The app doesn't expose a separate endpoint (/ready/security) that only returns 200 when ALL security middleware is loaded. The readiness probe is a basic HTTP check.
  5. Probes not updated after adding heavy initialization: ML model loading and cache warming added after initial deploy. Probes still tuned for the old 10-second startup time — never updated.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <pod> -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A15 "startupProbe\|livenessProbe\|readinessProbe" Check all three probes. If startupProbe is missing and initialDelaySeconds on liveness is long, the pod is vulnerable to early traffic before security initialization.
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n anihpj | grep -E "Started|Ready|Restart" Check restart count and readiness state transitions. Frequent restarts during startup indicate probe misconfiguration.
curl -s --max-time 2 anihpj-api:8000/api/jobs Send a request immediately after pod creation. If it returns 200 before the app is fully initialized, the pod serves traffic without security controls.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No startupProbe is configured, and the readiness probe passes BEFORE security middleware (authentication, rate limiting, input validation) is loaded. The pod receives and processes traffic from clients without any security controls during the initialization window.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add startupProbe for slow-starting containers startupProbe: httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000} failureThreshold: 30 periodSeconds: 5 Gives the pod up to 150 seconds (30×5) to start. Liveness and readiness probes are DISABLED until startupProbe succeeds — preventing premature kills.
2. Use separate readiness endpoint that validates security init Readiness should check /ready — an endpoint that returns 200 ONLY when: (1) HTTP server is up, (2) auth middleware is loaded, (3) rate limiter is initialized, (4) database connection pool is ready.
3. Keep liveness simple and fast livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}, periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3} Liveness should ONLY check if the process is alive — not dependencies. A failed database should make the pod "not ready" (readiness fails) but NOT kill the pod (liveness still passes).
4. Add readiness gates for critical dependencies Use readinessGates with custom conditions — the pod is not "Ready" until all conditions are true. This is more granular than a single readiness endpoint.
5. Test probe configuration under load Profile app startup time under realistic conditions (cold start, cache miss, DB migration). Set startupProbe.failureThreshold to 2× the worst-case startup time. Validate that pods never CrashLoopBackOff during normal startup.
💡 Personal Advice:
startupProbe eliminates the initialDelaySeconds guessing game. Before startupProbe, ops teams set initialDelaySeconds: 120 and hoped the app started in time — but traffic still arrived early. startupProbe guarantees the pod is fully initialized before either liveness or readiness begin. Use it for any pod that takes >10 seconds to start.
Liveness ≠ Readiness. Know the difference. Liveness: "Is the process alive?" (should always pass). Readiness: "Is the process ready to serve traffic?" (can fail if dependencies are down). A pod that is alive but not ready doesn't get traffic — and doesn't get killed. This distinction is critical for microservice resilience.

📦 Category 5: Supply Chain Security (20 Issues)SC1-SC20

🟢 Supply Chain Security — Image Signing, SBOM, CI/CD Hardening, Provenance

Supply chain attacks are the fastest-growing threat vector in Kubernetes. Unsigned images, missing SBOMs, compromised CI/CD pipelines, and untrusted registries allow attackers to inject malicious code before it ever reaches the cluster. For anihpj/jobpost, every image must be Cosign-signed, every build must generate an SBOM, CI/CD ServiceAccounts must have least-privilege RBAC, and admission controllers must verify image signatures before any pod runs.

📌 SC1–SC4: Image Signing, SBOM, CI/CD & Registry Security

SC1
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC1
Image Not Signed — No Cosign Signature Verification at Admission

🔍 Symptom: cosign verify --key cosign.pub anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 returns Error: no signatures found. The image was pushed to the registry WITHOUT being signed. Any attacker with registry push access can replace the image — or anyone who compromises the CI pipeline can push a malicious image — and the cluster will run it without question. There's no Kyverno/OPA admission policy verifying Cosign signatures before pods are admitted. The entire image supply chain has zero integrity verification.

  cosign verify --key cosign.pub anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2
  Error: no signatures found for anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2   ← UNSIGNED!

  kubectl get deployment anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep image:
  image: anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2   ← Running unsigned image!

  kubectl get clusterpolicy -A | grep -i cosign
  # No output — no admission policy enforcing signature verification
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Cosign signing step not in CI pipeline: The CI pipeline builds and pushes the image but never runs cosign sign --key cosign.key <image>. Images reach the registry unsigned — there's no cryptographic proof of build origin.
  2. No admission controller verifying signatures: Kyverno or OPA policy to verify Cosign signatures at pod admission is not deployed. Even if images are signed, unsigned images are admitted without verification.
  3. Signing key not securely stored: The Cosign private key is needed for signing but isn't available in CI. The team skipped signing because key management wasn't set up. Use keyless signing with OIDC (Sigstore Fulcio) to eliminate key management.
  4. Developers push images manually without signing: Emergency hotfixes and manual deployments bypass CI. Developers push directly to the registry with docker push — no signing step, no audit trail, no accountability.
  5. Signing considered "too complex" or "not needed yet": The team views image signing as an advanced feature for "later." Meanwhile, every image running in production has no integrity guarantee — any image with the right name:tag is trusted blindly.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Signature verification fails silently: Kyverno policy is configured but the public key is wrong or the signature digest doesn't match the image. Verification failures are logged but pods are still admitted — fail-open instead of fail-closed.
  2. Keyless signing not configured: Sigstore Fulcio (OIDC-based keyless signing) eliminates the need for long-lived signing keys. The team doesn't know keyless signing exists and thinks key management is a prerequisite.
  3. Image re-tagged and the new tag has no signature: An image signed at @sha256:abc is re-tagged as :v1.2. The tag has no signature because signing happened before re-tagging. Admission checking tags (not digests) misses this.
  4. Signature stored in wrong registry: Cosign signs the image and stores the signature in the SAME registry. If the registry is changed (migration, replication), signatures are left behind — images appear unsigned in the new registry.
  5. Private key expired or rotated without re-signing: The Cosign private key was rotated but all existing images were not re-signed. Admission controller with the new public key rejects all existing images as "unsigned."
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
